E-Corporation has contacted its lead SAP HANA security consultant and requested help in defining a security model to accommodate its security requirements. The consultant has determined that a series of repository roles will need to be defined. Let’s look further at the consultant’s decision-making process and the four repository roles recommended for this project.

### 6.6.1    Consumer Repository Role

The first repository role will provide a base level of access to SAP HANA information views. The name of the repository role will be consumer. This role will grant SELECT and EXECUTE access to the \_SYS\_BI schema, which is required because additional metadata is published to this schema. The role will also grant SELECT access to the design-time calculation view e-corp.sales.models::SCV\_CUSTOMER\_SALES. Users will need to have SELECT access, at a minimum, to query the information views and metadata in the \_SYS\_BIC schema. When you reference the design-time calculation view in the repository role, the system will automatically grant access to its corresponding column view in the \_SYS\_BIC schema. An analytic privilege will also be granted. The analytic privileges will limit the consumer’s access to a series of information views and will dynamically filter the results of the views so that each user will be limited to one or more sales regions based on his predetermined security profile.

Data consumers also need access to the SAP HANA Info Access service hosted in the SAP HANA XS platform. To use this service, these users are granted the role sap.bc.ina.service.v2.userRole::INA\_USER. In addition, some consumers need the ability to change their passwords using a web interface hosted in the SAP HANA XS platform. The role sap.hana.xs.formLogin.profile::ProfileOwner must be granted to allow consumers access to this utility.

[Figure 6.17](#06_006.html#f6.17) shows the configuration of the consumer repository role script, which in our example, contains two catalog schema privileges and one analytic privilege.

[![Consumer Repository Role Script](bilderklein/klein06_017.png)](img-f6.17.html) 

**Figure 6.17**    Consumer Repository Role Script

### 6.6.2    Power User Repository Role

In addition to the standard users at E-Corporation, a small group of power users require unique permissions. These users need access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench to query information views and tables for debugging purposes. They’ll also need to access the SAP HANA packages to view the design-time versions of the SAP HANA information views. Therefore, they’ll need basic access to the SAP HANA repository. To accommodate this requirement, the security consultant recommends that an additional repository role named poweruser be created.

[![Poweruser Repository Role Script](bilderklein/klein06_018.png)](img-f6.18.html) 

**Figure 6.18**    Poweruser Repository Role Script

The poweruser repository role will be an extension of the consumer repository role, which means that power users will inherit all the privileges assigned to the consumer repository role. The poweruser repository role will grant access to the REPOSITORY\_REST stored procedure, which is required to access the package hierarchy within SAP HANA. It will also grant SELECT access to the schemas housing the data used by the SAP HANA information views. Finally, it will grant REPO.READ access to the e-corp package, which will allow a power user the ability to view the configuration of each information view within the repository.

[Figure 6.18](#06_006.html#f6.18) shows the configuration of the poweruser repository role script, which contains all the privileges necessary to accommodate the security requirements.

### 6.6.3    Developer Repository Role

The developers at E-Corporation will require access to SAP HANA and the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench. These users will be responsible for creating the development artifacts used by the analytic solution. At a high level, developers require the following privileges and accesses:

*   Developers will require at least the privileges assigned to the consumer and power user repository roles.
    
*   Developers need the ability to fully manage the staging and data mart schemas. They’ll also be responsible for creating and managing the tables used by the solution.
    
*   Developers will require access to the SAP HANA repository, system views, SAP HANA application lifecycle management, delivery units, analytic privileges, and import and export interfaces.
    
*   Developers will require access to all data when querying SAP HANA information views.
    
*   Developers will require full access to the e-corp package and its child packages.
    
*   Developers will require read access to all packages and development artifacts.
    
*   Developers will require access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench.
    

To accommodate these requirements, a repository role named developer will be created. [Figure 6.19](#06_006.html#f6.19) shows the repository role script designed to accommodate E‐Corporation’s requirements for developers.

Let’s look at how the developer repository role script shown in [Figure 6.19](#06_006.html#f6.19) fulfills the requirements:

*   By including three existing roles within the extends role section of the script, two requirements are achieved. Developers will gain all the privileges of the consumer and poweruser roles and will gain access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench.
    
*   The two schema privilege lines grant the role full access to the staging and data mart schemas using their design-time reference.
    
*   The items listed in the system privilege line grant access to the SAP HANA repository, system views, SAP HANA application lifecycle management, delivery units, analytic privileges, and import and export interfaces.
    
*   The catalog analytic privilege line grants full query access to all SAP HANA information views.
    
*   The first package line grants full access to the top-level e-corp package.
    
*   The second package line grants read-only access to the entire package hierarchy.
    

[![Developer Repository Role Script](bilderklein/klein06_019.png)](img-f6.19.html) 

**Figure 6.19**    Developer Repository Role Script

As you can see, developer requirements can be fulfilled by including a few existing roles and by specifying several specific privileges. Referencing existing roles is helpful by reducing redundancy within custom repository roles. These references also ensure that the developer role will inherit the same privileges as the lower-level power user and consumer roles. Two of the existing repository roles also provided application privileges specific to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench.

### 6.6.4    Security Administrator Repository Role

The final recommended repository role grants privileges to a select group of security administrators. This role must provide security administrators the ability to manage users, create repository roles, and grant permissions. [Figure 6.20](#06_006.html#f6.20) shows the privileges and additional roles that will be assigned to the repository role named SecurityAdmin.

As described in the comments within the script, the security administrator role is an extension of the developer role and three additional XS engine application-specific roles. The applications in the XS engine provide interfaces useful in managing a security model. Three additional system privilege lines are included to grant user, role, and audit management. The catalog sql object lines grant EXECUTE privileges for a series of stored procedures necessary to grant and revoke privileges for objects owned by \_SYS\_REPO. Finally, the package security lines are included to provide exclusive access to the top-level package that will be used to store security-related development artifacts.

[![SecurityAdmin Repository Role Script](bilderklein/klein06_020.png)](img-f6.20.html) 

**Figure 6.20**    SecurityAdmin Repository Role Script

Once the repository roles are activated and assigned to the appropriate users, E‐Corporation will have the makings of a sound security model. Because the company used repository roles, the model can easily be transported to other systems and managed using lifecycle management best practices. In addition, the \_SYS\_REPO system account will be the primary owner and grantor of the privileges.

## 6.7    Summary

Repository roles offer multiple advantages when managing an SAP HANA security model. With few exceptions, repository roles should be used as the basis for your SAP HANA security model. You can create repository roles using design-time scripts or a GUI interface within the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor. Repository roles can be configured to reference both runtime catalog objects and design-time objects within the repository. In addition, you can transport repository roles between SAP HANA systems for consistency.

# 7    System Privileges

In this chapter, we’ll explore the different system privileges that govern a broad spectrum of actions within the SAP HANA platform.

System privileges play an important role in the development of any SAP HANA security model. These privileges govern specific actions within the SAP HANA platform: in some cases, actions specific to administrators; in other cases, actions performed by developers. Throughout this chapter, we’ll explore the various system privileges that SAP HANA provides and the types of activities that they govern. We’ll also review the system privileges included with SAP HANA 2.0 and demonstrate how system privileges are granted using SQL, the SAP HANA cockpit, the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, and within repository-based roles. We’ll close the chapter with a case study outlining several commonly used administrative roles and their required system privileges.

## 7.1    What Are System Privileges?

System privileges govern various activities or actions that can be executed within the SAP HANA platform. Administrators must be granted system privileges to perform activities such as backups, license key management, audit management, Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) management, system configuration settings, user creation, and role creation. Developers must be granted system privileges to perform imports and exports of catalog objects and repository objects. Several system privileges also govern access to actions performed within the SAP HANA development repository.

System privileges are predefined and delivered with the SAP HANA system. System privileges can’t be created or customized as of SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 00. To clarify the role that system privileges play in a security model, let’s review each default system privilege and categorize them.

## 7.2    Default System Privileges

SAP HANA is delivered with multiple system privileges. To better explain how system privileges might be used within a security model, we’ve organized them into five broad categories: developer, security admin, system admin, environment monitoring, and environment performance. We defined these categories based on our experience, but they don’t exist natively within SAP HANA. Placing system privileges into categories will hopefully help you understand how to use them with the repository roles you’ll devise to support your security model.

### 7.2.1    Developer-Related System Privileges

The following system privileges are typically required by developers. In general, these privileges only grant access to areas within SAP HANA related to the development of content. For example, a developer creating SAP HANA information views would likely need many of these system privileges in the development environment.

#### Create R Script

The create R script system privilege grants roles the ability to create a stored procedure using the R language.

#### REPO.EXPORT

The REPO.EXPORT system privilege governs access to interfaces for exporting a delivery unit from an SAP HANA system to a delivery unit export file. Delivery units are logical organizational units that contain one or more SAP HANA development artifacts. Typically, delivery units are exported and then imported into another SAP HANA system to transport code between systems.

#### REPO.IMPORT

The REPO.IMPORT system privilege governs access to interfaces for importing a delivery unit file into an SAP HANA system.

#### REPO.MAINTAIN\_DELIVERY\_UNITS

The REPO.MAINTAIN\_DELIVERY\_UNITS system privilege governs access to interfaces for defining a delivery unit within the SAP HANA repository.

#### REPO.WORK\_IN\_FOREIGN\_WORKSPACE

The REPO.WORK\_IN\_FOREIGN\_WORKSPACE system privilege grants a role the ability to take ownership of inactive development artifact versions hosted in another user’s workspace.

#### REPO.CONFIGURE

The REPO.CONFIGURE system privilege is used within SAP HANA application lifecycle management. Specifically, this system privilege allows the grantee to configure change recording when enabled.

#### REPO.MODIFY\_CHANGE

The REPO.MODIFY\_CHANGE system privilege is used within SAP HANA application lifecycle management. Specifically, this system privilege allows the grantee to assign objects to a change list when change recording is enabled.

#### REPO.MODIFY\_OWN\_CONTRIBUTION

The REPO.MODIFY\_OWN\_CONTRIBUTION system privilege is used within SAP HANA application lifecycle management. Specifically, this system privilege allows the grantee to assign objects to a change list when change recording is enabled.

#### REPO.MODIFY\_FOREIGN\_CONTRIBUTION

The REPO.MODIFY\_FOREIGN\_CONTRIBUTION system privilege is used within SAP HANA application lifecycle management. Specifically, this system privilege allows the grantee to modify objects to a change list when change recording is enabled. The grantee can perform the action even if it doesn’t own the change list assignment.

### 7.2.2    Security Admin-Related System Privileges

Security administrators typically require the following system privileges. In general, these privileges grant access to actions within SAP HANA related to the management and maintenance of users, roles, auditing, and encryption.

#### Audit Admin

The AUDIT ADMIN system privilege governs the execution of auditing\-related SQL commands and actions performed using the various options within SAP HANA Studio or the SAP HANA cockpit. SQL commands such as CREATE AUDIT POLICY, DROP AUDIT POLICY, ALTER AUDIT POLICY, and SELECT \* FROM SYS.AUDIT\_LOG can’t be executed unless a user inherently has the AUDIT ADMIN system privilege. This rule also applies to graphical user interfaces (GUIs) because they execute the same SQL commands in the background when a user attempts to make changes to the various activities being audited.

#### Audit Operator

The AUDIT OPERATOR system privilege governs access to commands that can clear the audit logs when auditing is enabled. For example, with this privilege, the SQL command ALTER SYSTEM CLEAR AUDIT LOG ALL can be executed. This rule also applies to similar GUI options that allow the audit log to be cleared. Note that the act of clearing the audit log is always recorded to the audit log, a MandatoryAuditPolicy within the SAP HANA system. In other words, this audit policy is always active and can’t be circumvented. This system privilege also provides read access to the system audit log and the execution of SELECT \* FROM SYS.AUDIT\_LOG SQL statement.

#### Certificate Admin

The CERTIFICATE ADMIN system privilege governs access to SQL commands and GUIs for managing certificates within the SAP HANA in-database certificate store. This privilege provides data access when executing SELECT \* FROM SYS.CERTIFICATES or SELECT \* FROM SYS.PSE\_CERTIFICATES and allows for the execution of CREATE CERTIFICATE, DROP CERTIFICATE, and other related in-database certificate management commands.

#### Create Structured Privilege

The CREATE STRUCTURED PRIVILEGE system privilege grants access to the execution of the SQL command CREATE STRUCTURED PRIVILEGE. Structured privileges can be implemented to restrict data-level access to catalog views and column views.

Note that this system privilege is included in the MODELING and CONTENT\_ADMIN default roles. You might conclude that this privilege is required for all roles or users creating SAP HANA analytic privileges, a type of structured privilege. However, custom roles don’t need this privilege to activate analytic privileges created using SAP HANA Studio or SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA. The activation of SAP HANA analytic privileges is controlled using package privileges, and the navigation of the package hierarchy is controlled using the SYS.REPOSITORY\_REST stored procedure. The runtime object type of an SAP HANA analytic privilege artifacts is a special type of structured privilege but created by the system account \_SYS\_REPO. Therefore, only the \_SYS\_REPO system account requires the CREATE STRUCTURED PRIVILEGE system privilege.

#### Credential Admin

The CREDENTIAL ADMIN system privilege governs access to the CREATE CREDENTIAL, ALTER CREDENTIAL, and DROP CREDENTIAL SQL commands. Credentials are objects that store authentication information for remote sources used by SAP HANA smart data access and SAP HANA smart data integration.

#### Encryption Root Key Admin

The ENCRYPTION ROOT KEY ADMIN system privilege grants access to all SQL commands related to the management of root keys used to encrypt data, logs, and applications. SQL commands such as ALTER SYSTEM APPLICATION ENCRYPTION, ALTER SYSTEM PERSISTENCE ENCRYPTION, and ALTER SYSTEM LOG ENCRYPTION, which are governed by this system privilege. In addition to specific SQL commands, this privilege also grants access to any SAP HANA-related GUI that issues the same statements on behalf of a user.

#### LDAP Admin

The LDAP ADMIN system privilege governs the use of SQL statements that manage an SAP HANA Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) provider, such as CREATE, ALTER, DROP, and VALIDATE LDAP PROVIDER.

#### Role Admin

The ROLE ADMIN system privilege governs access to GUI interfaces and SQL commands that CREATE, ALTER, or DROP standard roles within the system. This privilege also governs interfaces and SQL statements that GRANT or REVOKE roles. The ROLE ADMIN system privilege is only applicable to standard catalog roles and doesn’t grant the same privileges to repository-based roles.

Although commonly granted to security administrators, this privilege isn’t necessarily required when repository-based roles are the basis of your security model. Repository roles are granted using special stored procedures, and security administrators only need EXECUTE access for those procedures.

#### SSL Admin

The SSL ADMIN system privilege governs access to SQL commands that establish the purpose of an SSL certificate, such as SET <STORE\_NAME> PURPOSE SSL. This privilege also grants data access to the SYS.PSES personal security environment (PSE) system view.

#### Structuredprivilege Admin

The STRUCTUREDPRIVILEGE ADMIN system privilege grants the grantee the ability to CREATE, ALTER, and DROP any structured privileges defined in the system. Roles with this privilege don’t need to be the owner of the structured privilege to perform the DROP or ALTER actions.

#### Trust Admin

The TRUST ADMIN system privilege governs access to GUIs and commands that manage SSL certificates within the trust store or certificate store. This privilege grants access to the CREATE PSE SQL command used to create a certificate store for in-database certificate management.

#### User Admin

The USER ADMIN system privilege governs access to GUIs and SQL statements used to CREATE, ALTER, and DELETE user accounts within the SAP HANA system.

### 7.2.3    System Admin-Related System Privileges

System administrators typically require many of the following privileges. Some of these privileges might seem related to other areas, which might be true in some cases. However, these privileges typically grant the ability to perform actions that have a profound impact on the stability and reliability of the SAP HANA system. Because these privileges deserve a higher level of scrutiny, we recommend limiting these privileges to only high-level system administrators. Also, system auditing and other critical rules must be enabled before these privileges are granted to administrators.

#### Adapter Admin

The ADAPTER ADMIN system privilege should be assigned to roles that manage the SAP HANA smart data integration adapter framework. This privilege must be granted to roles that will be responsible for issuing SQL statements such as CREATE ADAPTER, DROP ADAPTER, and ALTER ADAPTER. This privilege also provides data access to system views such as SYS.ADAPTERS, SYS.ADAPTER\_CAPABILITIES, and SYS.ADAPTER\_LOCATION.

#### Agent Admin

The BACKUP ADMIN system privilege should be assigned to roles that manage the SAP HANA smart data integration data provisioning agent framework. This privilege must be granted to roles that will be responsible for issuing SQL statements such as CREATE AGENT, DROP AGENT, and ALTER AGENT. This privilege also provides data access to system views such as SYS.AGENTS, SYS.AGENT\_CONFIGURATION, and SYS.AGENT\_GROUPS.

#### Backup Admin

The BACKUP ADMIN system privilege governs access to commands and GUIs that initiate backup and restoration activities related to the SAP HANA system. This privilege grants the ability to alter system configuration parameters related to the backup and recovery of the system and allows for the truncation of the backup catalog and its associated files. This privilege also grants access to query backup-related system views in the SYS schema, such as with SELECT \* FROM SYS.M\_BACKUP\_CATALOG.

On its own, this privilege doesn’t provide access to the backup console in SAP HANA Studio or interfaces within the SAP HANA cockpit. During our testing, we identified that the CATALOG READ system privilege was also required to use the backup console. However, with both privileges granted, such roles would be able to fully manage the backup and restore processes within SAP HANA.

#### Backup Operator

The BACKUP OPERATOR system privilege governs access to SQL commands that initiate system backups or that provide read access to backup-specific system views. However, this privilege doesn’t provide the ability to change backup settings, restore the system, or execute commands that manage the backup catalog. This privilege is most often granted to service accounts that initiate a system backup from the command line, for example, SAP HANA accounts that initiate scheduled backup jobs from a Linux cron scheduling engine.

#### Create Remote Source

The CREATE REMOTE SOURCE system privilege governs access to SQL commands and GUIs used to create remote sources used by SAP HANA smart data access or SAP HANA smart data integration. This privilege also provides read-only data access to system views such as SYS.REMOTE\_SOURCES and SYS.REMOTE\_SOURCE\_OBJECTS.

#### Create Scenario

The CREATE SCENARIO system privilege governs access to the execution of the CREATE CALCULATION SCENARIO SQL statement. Calculation scenarios are specialized catalog objects used by SAP HANA calculation views. SAP hasn’t published significant information about calculation scenarios, but we do know that they are fundamental to the creation of SAP HANA calculation views. The \_SYS\_REPO system account normally creates calculation scenarios in the \_SYS\_BIC schema on behalf of a developer activating a calculation view, so most roles don’t necessarily need this privilege.

However, if an application or highly skilled user is creating calculation views and storing calculation scenarios in a custom schema, this system privilege will be required. For example, the SAP Business Warehouse (SAP BW) service account creates calculation scenarios and column views within the SAP HANA service account schema. Therefore, the SAP BW service account requires this privilege.

Note that this system privilege is included in the MODELING and CONTENT\_ADMIN default roles. You might conclude that this privilege is required for all roles or users creating SAP HANA information views, but custom roles don’t need this privilege to activate SAP HANA information views using SAP HANA Studio or SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA. The activation of SAP HANA information views is controlled using package privileges and the navigation of the package hierarchy is controlled using the SYS.REPOSITORY\_REST stored procedure. Runtime SAP HANA information view artifacts are created by the \_SYS\_REPO system account. Therefore, only the \_SYS\_REPO system account requires the create scenario system privilege.

#### Create Schema

The CREATE SCHEMA system privilege grants the ability to execute the CREATE SCHEMA SQL command. The system usually creates a user schema for each standard user. However, if a user expects to create additional standard catalog schemas, he must be granted this system privilege.

#### Data Admin

The DATA ADMIN system privilege governs access to several items. Like the catalog read system privilege, this privilege grants full read-only access to all system views stored in the SYS schema.

This privilege also allows the execution of any Data Definition Language (DDL) statement. For example, the CREATE COLUMN TABLE command is considered a DDL statement. DDL statements can be issued towards objects in any schema, even if the grantee doesn’t have CREATE ANY privilege access for the schema. However, this privilege doesn’t grant the grantee access to issue Data Manipulation Language (DML) statements against catalog objects that it doesn’t own or otherwise have DML access to.

In addition to allowing the execution of any DDL statement, the DATA ADMIN system privilege also grants the ability to delete any table in the system regardless of any other granted privileges. For reference, you could delete system-related tables when granted this privilege. Grantees can delete a table even if they don’t own it or otherwise have the DELETE privilege granted. Therefore, this privilege should only be granted on an extremely limited basis.

#### Database Admin

The DATABASE ADMIN system privilege grants access to all SQL commands related to the tenant database, including tenant database SQL commands such as CREATE, DROP, ALTER, RENAME, BACKUP, and RECOVERY. In addition to specific SQL commands, this privilege also grants access to any SAP HANA-related GUI that issues the same statements on behalf of a user.

#### Export

The EXPORT system privilege governs the ability to export catalog objects and data using the EXPORT SQL command or GUIs, such as the SAP HANA database explorer, that provide options to export catalog objects to the SAP HANA database file system. Based on our testing, this privilege only applies to the issuing of the SQL command in the SQL console or when the export location is the SAP HANA database filesystem. In addition to the EXPORT system privilege, the grantee will also need the SELECT privilege for the catalog objects being exported.

Note that this privilege doesn’t govern access to the export catalog object wizard in the SAP HANA database explorer in the SAP HANA cockpit, where the export location is local computer. To perform a catalog export using this GUI interface, the grantee only requires the SELECT privilege on the schemas or tables being exported.

#### Extended Storage Admin

The EXTENDED STORAGE ADMIN system privilege grants the ability to manage SAP HANA extended storage and to issue SQL commands such as CREATE EXTENDED STORAGE, ALTER EXTENDED STORAGE, and DROP EXTENDED STORAGE. This privilege also governs read-only data access to extended storage system views such as SYS.M\_ES\_DBSPACES, SYS.M\_ES\_DELTA\_MEMORY, and others. In addition to specific SQL commands, this privilege also grants access to any SAP HANA-related GUI that issues the same statements on behalf of a user.

#### Import

The IMPORT system privilege governs the ability to import data into catalog tables using the IMPORT SQL command or GUIs, such as the SAP HANA database explorer, that provide options for importing catalog objects from the SAP HANA database file system. Based on our testing, this privilege only applies to the issuing of the SQL command in the SQL console or when the import location is the SAP HANA database file system. In addition to the import system privilege, grantees will also need the INSERT privilege on the target catalog table.

Note that this privilege doesn’t govern access to the import catalog object wizard in the SAP HANA cockpit’s SAP HANA database explorer, where the import location is local computer. To perform a catalog import using this GUI interface, the grantee also needs the INSERT, UPDATE, DROP, and CREATE ANY privileges on the target schema. If the schema doesn’t exist, the SCHEMA ADMIN system privilege will be required as well.

#### INIFILE Admin

The INIFILE ADMIN system privilege governs access to changes within the system settings. With this privilege, the system configuration can be changed by issuing ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION SQL statements in the SQL console.

#### License Admin

The LICENSE ADMIN system privilege governs access to GUIs and SQL statements for installing and removing license keys. SQL statements such as SET SYSTEM LICENSE can only be issued in the SQL console once the license admin system privilege is granted.

#### Log Admin

The LOG ADMIN system privilege governs access to the SQL command ALTER SYSTEM LOGGING. This command allows the redo logging mechanism to be enabled or disabled. When the redo logging mechanism is disabled, the relational database management system (RDBMS) can’t properly recover after an index server outage. Therefore, this privilege only should be granted as needed.

#### Optimizer Admin

The OPTIMIZER ADMIN system privilege governs access to ALTER SYSTEM SQL commands, such as ALTER SYSTEM CLEAR SQL PLAN CACHE. These commands can influence the query optimizer.

#### Resource Admin

The RESOURCE ADMIN system privilege governs access to a variety of SQL commands and GUIs used to affect system resources, table distribution, page file data encryption keys, and table partitioning. SQL commands such as ALTER SYSTEM RECLAIM DATAVOLUME and ALTER SYSTEM RESET MONITORING VIEW are managed by this system privilege. GUIs that reset memory statistics are also allowed when this system privilege is granted.

#### Savepoint Admin

The SAVEPOINT ADMIN system privilege governs access to the ALTER SYSTEM SAVEPOINT SQL command. Executing this command will commit all in-memory data to the data volume within the persistent storage layers of SAP HANA. By default, SAP HANA savepoints are executed automatically by the system every 5 minutes.

#### Scenario Admin

The SCENARIO ADMIN system privilege governs access to all calculation scenario-related activities, including the ability to create calculation scenarios. SAP hasn’t published significant information about calculation scenarios, but we do know that they’re fundamental to the creation of SAP HANA calculation views. Calculation scenarios normally are created by the \_SYS\_REPO account when SAP HANA information views are created.

#### Service Admin

The SERVICE ADMIN system privilege governs access to the SQL commands and GUIs used to start, stop, kill, cancel, and reconfigure SAP HANA system services, such as indexserver, compileserver, nameserver, and xsengine.

#### Session Admin

The SESSION ADMIN system privilege governs access to GUIs and SQL statements for canceling or changing a user session. SQL commands such as ALTER SYSTEM CANCEL SESSION and ALTER SYSTEM ALTER SESSION can’t be executed without this system privilege.

#### Tenant Admin

According to the documentation, the TENANT ADMIN system privilege governs GUIs and SQL statements for resuming and suspending a tenant database. Unfortunately, the SAP HANA documentation doesn’t provide any example SQL statements that you can use to suspend or resume a tenant database, so we weren’t able to fully test this functionality. We did attempt to execute ALTER SYSTEM SUSPEND TENANT <TENANT DATABASE>, but an error was returned: Alter Tenant deprecated and Was Never Fully Implemented.

#### Table Admin

The TABLE ADMIN system privilege governs GUIs and SQL statements used to unload columnar tables into memory, unload columnar tables from memory, and perform delta merges on columnar tables. Users granted this system privilege don’t require ownership of the table or schema, nor do they require any SQL object privileges to perform these actions.

#### Trace Admin

The TRACE ADMIN system privilege enables a role to configure traces within the SAP HANA system. This privilege also authorizes the ability to delete trace files from the system.

#### Version Admin

The VERSION ADMIN system privilege governs access to SQL statements used to manage the row-store garbage collector, for example, ALTER SYSTEM RECLAIM VERSION SPACE.

#### Workload Admin

The WORKLOAD ADMIN system privilege governs access to SQL statements used to CREATE, ALTER, and DROP workload mappings and workload classes. Workloads and workload classes are used to govern statement execution priority, statement memory limits, or statement thread limits based on user- or application-specific information.

### 7.2.4    Environment Monitoring-Related System Privileges

Individuals that monitor the SAP HANA system will typically require the following privileges. Thus, for example, the CATALOG READ system privilege is included with the MONITORING default role.

#### Catalog Read

The CATALOG READ system privilege provides full read-only data access to all catalog views within the SYS schema. No filter restrictions will be applied to the view, and no further privileges are required to access system view data.

#### Monitor Admin

The MONITOR ADMIN system privilege governs access to ALTER SYSTEM SQL commands specific to event management.

### 7.2.5    Environment Performance-Related System Privileges

For individuals using workload-related tools to capture, compare, or test the performance of a particular workflow, the following system privileges will likely be required.

#### Workload Analyze Admin

The WORKLOAD ANALYZE ADMIN system privilege governs access to workload analysis, capture, and replay actions within the SAP HANA system.

#### Workload Capture Admin

The WORKLOAD CAPTURE ADMIN system privilege governs data access to the SYS.M\_WORKLOAD\_CAPTURES system view and grants the EXECUTE privilege on the SYS.WORKLOAD\_CAPTURE stored procedure. Capturing and replaying workloads allows administrators to view performance impacts after changes are made in SAP HANA configuration or hardware.

#### Workload Replay Admin

The WORKLOAD REPLAY ADMIN system privilege governs data access to the SYS.M\_WORKLOAD\_REPLAY\_PREPROCESSES and SYS.M\_WORKLOAD\_REPLAYS system views. This privilege also grants the EXECUTE privilege on the SYS.WORKLOAD\_REPLAY stored procedure. Capturing and replaying workloads allows administrators to view performance impacts after changes are made in SAP HANA configuration or hardware.

## 7.3    Granting System Privileges

In this section, we’ll review the various options available to grant and revoke system privileges: SQL commands, the SAP HANA cockpit, the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, and repository-based role scripts or the repository-based role editor GUI.

### 7.3.1    Granting System Privileges with SQL

Using the SQL console and SQL statements, you can both grant and revoke privileges to roles or users. Let’s look at a series of example SQL statements used to grant system privileges to both users and roles.

With system privileges, the grantee can be either a user account or a role. A sound security model will grant privileges to roles and avoid directly granting individual privileges to individual users. Technically, you can grant system privileges to a grantee using the GRANT SQL syntax. However, as we’ve discussed, using repository-based roles, which don’t use SQL to grant system privileges, is best; we’ll review this benefit again in [Section 7.3.4](#07_003.html#h7.3.4). With that said, reviewing the process for granting system privileges to standard users or roles is still important. Although we’ve provided SQL script examples in several chapters, let’s take a moment to review the SQL statement for granting system privileges to a grantee. Note that a semicolon marks the end of each of the following SQL statements:

```
GRANT <SYSTEM_PRIVILEGE> TO <GRANTEE>;    
GRANT <SYSTEM_PRIVILEGE> TO <GRANTEE> WITH ADMIN OPTION;    
GRANT DATA ADMIN, EXPORT, IMPORT TO ROLE_SEC_ADMIN WITH ADMIN OPTION;
```

The first statement provides the general syntax, with variables indicated by text within angle brackets (<>). The variables must be replaced with items unique to your environment. The <SYSTEM\_PRIVILEGES> variable can be replaced with a comma-separated list of system privileges, as shown in the third statement. The <GRANTEE> variable will be replaced with the name of an activated role or user account within the system.

The second SQL statement includes the WITH ADMIN OPTION at the end, which allows the grantee of the role to subsequently grant the same privilege to another user or role. This option is typically reserved for user grantees that manage security models.

The final statement provides a complete example in which system privileges are granted to the ROLE\_SEC\_ADMIN role. This statement includes the WITH ADMIN OTPTION, allowing the role grantee to grant the same privileges to other users or roles.

You can also revoke system privileges using the REVOKE SQL syntax, as follows:

```
REVOKE <SYSTEM_PRIVILEGE> FROM <GRANTEE>;    
REVOKE DATA ADMIN, EXPORT, IMPORT FROM ROLE_SEC_ADMIN;
```

The first statement provides the general syntax, and the second SQL statement provides a full example, in which the listed system privileges are removed from the ROLE\_SEC\_ADMIN role.

### 7.3.2    Granting System Privileges with the SAP HANA Cockpit

Let’s review the workflows for granting and revoking system privileges with the SAP HANA cockpit. As an alternative to using SQL statements, you can use the SAP HANA cockpit links Assign Privileges or Manage Roles. Each interface allows you to both grant and revoke system privileges for a given user account or for a given role. Most users will find using the SAP HANA cockpit easier than memorizing and entering in SQL statements.

To access the Assign Privileges or Manage Roles area, start at the SAP HANA cockpit Home screen and locate an SAP HANA system in the Resource Directory. Connect to the desired tenant database or SYSTEMDB, which will take you to the System Overview window. Using the Filter by Area dropdown list, choose the option Security. Locate the Assign Privileges or Manage Roles in the User & Role Management tile.

[Section 7.1](#07_001.html#h7.1) shows the Assign Privileges interface within the SAP HANA cockpit for the TEST\_01 user account. In this window, you’ll see several tabs, one for each privilege category, starting with System Privileges, Object Privileges, Analytic Privileges, Application Privileges, Package Privileges, and Privileges on Users. You’ll find a similar interface when working with roles. However, the Role Details GUI has an additional link called Roles where you can grant existing roles to the selected role.

[![Managing Privileges Assigned to User Account in the SAP HANA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein07_001.png)](img-f7.1.html) 

**Figure 7.1**    Managing Privileges Assigned to User Account in the SAP HANA Cockpit

The first tab in the Assign Privileges window is named System Privileges. Use this tab to list, grant, or revoke system privileges for a given user account or for a given role.

Privileges listed in this interface are already granted to the user or role. If the list is blank, nothing is currently granted. To grant a system privilege, click Edit button located on the far-right side of the interface near the Search field. Once you click the Edit button, new buttons labeled Cancel, Add, and Remove will appear. Click the Add button to open the Select System Privileges popup window. Within this window, you’ll see a search bar and a list of system privileges with checkboxes to their left. Use the search bar to filter the list based on the entered text. Then, scroll through the list and select the checkbox beside the system privilege you want to grant. With one or more system privileges selected, click the OK button to add the desired items to the user. Your selected system privileges should now appear under the System Privileges tab, as shown in [Section 7.2](#07_002.html#h7.2).

[![List of Selected System Privileges](bilderklein/klein07_002.png)](img-f7.2.html) 

**Figure 7.2**    List of Selected System Privileges

To assign the Grantable to others privilege, locate a system privilege in the list. To the right, you’ll see a slider button to move to Yes, thus allowing the user to grant the same privilege to another user or role. Repeat this process for each system privilege in the list. Once you’ve added all the desired system privileges to the list, click the Save button to grant the privileges.

To revoke a system privilege, start by clicking the Edit button again, then select the checkbox beside each system privilege in the list, and click the Remove button to revoke the privileges. Repeat the process for each system privilege you want to revoke. Once you’ve removed all the desired system privileges, click the Save button. The removed privileges will be revoked, and the user object will be updated.

During the process of adding or removing, you can click the Cancel button to discard any unsaved changes. Clicking the Cancel button will deactivate the Add, Cancel, and Remove buttons and return you to a read-only list of currently granted system privileges.

### 7.3.3    Granting System Privileges with the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, hosted within the SAP HANA extended application services, classic model (SAP HANA XS) engine (XS engine), provides an interface that you can use to create users, create roles, or manage security for standard roles. This interface provides a web-based alternative to the SAP HANA cockpit and also serves as an alternative to issuing GRANT and REVOKE statement with SQL.

You can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench via a supported Internet browser. The following URLs can be customized to match the details of your environment:

*   http://sap-hana.myhost.com:8000/sap/hana/ide/security
    
*   http://<sap\_hana\_host>:80<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/security
    

In the last example, replace <sap\_hana\_host> with the host name of the SAP HANA system in your environment and <instance\_number> with the two-digit instance number corresponding to your SAP HANA system.

For secure access, the following examples should help you construct the correct URL:

*   https://<sap\_hana\_host>:43<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/security
    
*   https://sap-hana.myhost.com:4300/sap/hana/ide/security
    

Once you have access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, expand the Security node on the right. Expand Roles to reveal a list of standard roles defined in the system. Double-click a role to open the management interface for the given role. With the selected role management window open, you can begin granting and revoking privileges.

###### Note

To perform the same action for an individual user account, expand the Users node and double-click the desired user account.

Recall that we recommend the use of repository-based roles to support an SAP HANA security model. However, in this section, we’ll simply highlight the basic workflow if you chose to manage security with standard roles or directly on individual user accounts.

With the GUI management interface open for a given grantee, you can add a system privilege as follows. Locate the tab labeled System Privileges. Click the plus (+) button to add and search for the desired system privilege. The Find System Privileges window will appear where you can search for a specific system privilege. Select the desired system privileges and click OK to add them to the list. Choose Grantable to Other Users and Roles to the right of each listed system privilege as needed.

To save your changes, press (Ctrl)+(S) or click the disk icon at the top left to save and activate the privilege. To revoke a system privilege, select it in the list and click the red X. Once again, save the changes to make them active within the database system.

If any activation issues arise, warning messages will appear in the status pane at the bottom of the user management window. The status pane has a dark background. Error messages will appear in red text. Errors are only generated during an attempted activation or saving of changes.

### 7.3.4    Granting System Privileges with Repository Roles

When SAP HANA was initially released, assigning system privileges to standard roles was the best available option. Multiple GUIs and SQL statements were created to help organizations manage granting privileges to and revoking privileges from standard roles. As SAP HANA evolved, repository roles were introduced to aid in application development efforts. Because of their numerous benefits, we highly recommend that you use repository roles to generate security models. Now, let’s review the process for granting and revoking system privileges within repository-based roles.

#### Script-Based Repository Roles

In [Chapter 6](#06_001.html#h6), we introduced you to repository roles and outlined the workflows required to create and manage repository roles. In this section, we’ll again review the syntax necessary to assign system privileges to design-time repository-based role scripts. If you require more information about this process, refer to [Chapter 6](#06_001.html#h6).

When defining system privileges within design-time repository-based role scripts, you must start each line with system privilege:. After the colon, you can provide a comma-separated list of system privileges. At the end of the list, include a semicolon to finish the line. If you don’t want to include a comma-separated list, you can explicitly list each privilege on its own line, with each line beginning with system privilege:.

The following snippets of code show the definition of system privileges within a repository roles script. The first line includes three privileges, each separated by a comma; the remaining two lines only include a single system privilege each:

```
system privilege: AGENT ADMIN, AUDIT ADMIN, AUDIT OPERATOR;    
system privilege: AUDIT OPERATOR;    
system privilege: CREATE REMOTE SOURCE;
```

As you can see, you can reuse the system privilege: expression multiple times within the script. You can also consolidate them all into a single line in which each privilege is comma-separated. Note that the \_SYS\_REPO account has been granted all system privileges by default. The \_SYS\_REPO account also can grant all system privileges to other users or roles by default.

#### SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor, hosted within the XS engine, provides an interface that you can use to build and test development artifacts. From a security perspective, you can use this interface to create and manage repository-based roles. This interface offers all the advantages of repository-based roles without the need to define repository roles using scripts and SAP HANA domain-specific language. However, you can use this interface to edit the role via a GUI or open the role file in the text editor.

You can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor via a supported Internet browser. The following URLs can be customized to match the details of your environment:

*   http://sap-hana.myhost.com:8000/sap/hana/ide/editor
    
*   http://<sap\_hana\_host>:80<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/editor
    

Replace <sap\_hana\_host> with the host name of the SAP HANA system in your environment. Replace <instance\_number> with the two-digit instance corresponding to your SAP HANA system.

For secure access, the following examples should help you construct the correct URL:

*   https://<sap\_hana\_host>:43<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/editor
    
*   https://sap-hana.myhost.com:4300/sap/hana/ide/editor
    

To use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench and define a repository role, the user account first will need to be granted one of the roles listed in [Table 7.1](#07_003.html#t7.1). Users only need one of the two roles to use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench.

 
| Role Name || Summary |
| --- | --- |
| sap.hana.ide.roles ::EditorDeveloper || Within SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench, users can only access the editor. Within the editor, users can view, edit, create, delete, or activate repository-based roles or other repository-based development artifacts found in development packages or the development repository. Users must have package privileges in addition to this role to properly access and activate a repository role or other development artifacts. |
| --- | --- |
| sap.hana.ide.roles::Developer || This role grants a higher level of privileges for users that need full access to SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench. This role grants access to the editor, catalog, and security interfaces and is considered the parent to the sap.hana.ide.roles::EditorDeveloper role. |

**Table 7.1**    Roles Required to Use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor

###### Package Privileges Required to Use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor

In addition to the roles listed in [Table 7.1](#07_003.html#t7.1), a user will also need the appropriate package privileges for the package in which they plan to edit, create, or activate repository roles. This requirement also applies to script-based repository roles. For example, users will need the following package privileges to create repository roles using the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor interface:

*   REPO.READ
    
*   REPO.EDIT\_NATIVE\_OBJECTS
    
*   REPO.ACTIVATE\_NATIVE\_OBJECTS
    

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor interface, shown in [Figure 7.3](#07_003.html#f7.3), is quite similar to the development areas under the Repositories tab of SAP HANA Studio. On the left side of the interface is a Content folder, under which is the package hierarchy.

[![SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor](bilderklein/klein07_003.png)](img-f7.3.html) 

**Figure 7.3**    SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor

As you expand the package hierarchy nodes, you’ll begin seeing development artifacts, depending on what’s available in your environment. To create a repository role, right-click the package in which you want to store the role and choose New • Role. A small window will appear asking for the Role Name. Enter the desired name and click OK; a new tab-based window will appear on the right, as shown in [Figure 7.3](#07_003.html#f7.3), where the tab is named SECURITY\_ADMIN.hdbrole. Click the System Privileges tab to manage and list system privileges.

Under this tab, to add a system privilege, click the large plus (+) button on the subtab header. The Select System Privilege popup window will appear, as shown in [Figure 7.4](#07_003.html#f7.4).

A search box will appear in this window; enter a portion of the system privilege name to narrow the results or scroll through the unfiltered list to locate the desired system privilege. Select one or more privileges within the list, pressing the (Ctrl) key while clicking to select multiple items. The selected items are highlighted in light blue. Click the OK button at the bottom of the window to finalize the selection.

The selected privileges will now appear in the System Privileges tab. To remove an assigned system privilege, select the privilege from the list and click the large minus (–) button above the list. Items in the list must be deleted one at a time.

[![Searching for System Privileges within the Select System Privileges Dialog Box](bilderklein/klein07_004.png)](img-f7.4.html) 

**Figure 7.4**    Searching for System Privileges within the Select System Privileges Dialog Box

Once you’ve configured the desired list of system privileges, click the save all icon (three floppy disks) at the top left.

If any issues arise when saving and activating the repository role, messages will appear in red text within the console window just below the opened repository role tab. The console window has a dark background and is located at the bottom of the opened tab. Affirmative messages will appear in white text and error messages in red text.

To close the open repository role tab, click the small X to the right of the tab.

## 7.4    Case Study: Security Administrator System Privileges

E-Corporation has contacted its lead SAP HANA security consultant and has requested help defining a series of repository roles to be used by its security team to manage security within the SAP HANA environment. Based on previous experience, the consultant recommends defining four repository roles for the security team to allow for the separation of duties within the system. This separation helps reduce both fraud and negligence within the security model. The consultant suggests that the four roles be created based on the following groups:

*   Admins responsible for managing users
    
*   Admins responsible for creating roles
    
*   Admins that manage communication and data encryption
    
*   Admins that mange system auditing
    

To help E-Corporation better understand the consultant’s reasoning, he provided a justification for each activity and why they needed to be separated from each other. In addition, he also listed the capabilities and system privileges that were required for each broad activity. In this case study, we’ll examine the consultant’s suggestions and his justifications for each.

### 7.4.1    User Management Role

The first repository role recommended by the security consultant grants the necessary privileges to provision and administer user accounts. Grantees of this role will be responsible for the following tasks:

*   Provisioning user accounts
    
*   Resetting user account passwords
    
*   Assigning Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) and Kerberos identities
    

To ensure that best practices are followed and that the separation of duties is implemented properly, grantees with this role should not be able to perform the following tasks:

*   Creating or updating existing roles
    
*   Granting standard roles to users
    
*   Granting repository roles to users
    
*   Granting individual privileges to users
    
*   Managing system auditing
    

With these requirements and restrictions defined, the security consultant recommends that the user management repository role be limited to only those system privileges required to manage users. Grantees of this role should not have the ability to assign roles to user accounts. Allowing them to assign roles would grant the ability to both manipulate a user and assign privileges to the user. This level of access gives the grantee the ability to impersonate a user account, allowing it to perform fraudulent or malicious actions within the system. To achieve the listed requirements, the user management repository role only requires the USER ADMIN system privilege.

In addition to only granting the USER ADMIN system privilege, the following conditions must also exist for the user accounts within this repository role:

*   The user account must not have the ROLE ADMIN system privilege, which grants the ability to create standard roles and to grant them to other users.
    
*   The user account must not have EXECUTE access to the \_SYS\_REPO.GRANT\_ACTIVATED\_ROLE stored procedure or other stored procedures in the \_SYS\_REPO schema that are used to manage security. Granting such access to these procedures will allow repository roles to be granted or other privileges to be assigned.
    
*   The user account must not have been granted any other privileges using the WITH ADMIN OPTION or WITH GRANT OPTION. This rule prevents the user from granting any individual privileges to other user accounts directly. Note that a user will be able to grant others access to its own schema in SAP HANA 1.0. Starting with SAP HANA 2.0, users can be restricted from their own user schema and subsequently prevented from granting privileges to their own schema.
    
*   The grantee must be granted the sap.hana.ide.roles::SecurityAdmin role to use web-based GUIs for managing users.
    
*   To prevent access to the auditing mechanism, the AUDIT ADMIN and AUDIT OPERATOR system privileges must not be granted to the user.
    

When implemented according to these requirements, the grantee will not be able to elevate his own privileges or the privileges of another user account. In addition, because the grantee doesn’t have access to manipulate the auditing mechanisms, he won’t be able to cover his tracks. All actions he performs on a user account should be captured by the auditing mechanism. Now, let’s look at how the role management role should be structured and why.

### 7.4.2    Role Management Role

The second repository role recommended by the security consultant grants the necessary privileges to provision roles and grant roles to users. Grantees of this role will be responsible for the following tasks:

*   Creating repository-based roles and assigning all privileges
    
*   Creating standard roles when necessary
    
*   Mapping LDAP groups to roles
    
*   Managing structured privileges other than analytic privileges
    
*   Creating analytic privileges and assigning restrictions
    
*   Granting roles to and revoking roles from users
    

Grantees assigned this role shouldn’t be able to create or manipulate user accounts. This rule prevents these grantees from impersonating a user account, subsequently allowing them to perform fraudulent or malicious actions within the system while concealing their identity.

To ensure that best practices are followed and that the separation of duties is implemented properly, the following list contains tasks that the grantees should not be able to perform:

*   Creating user accounts or changing user account passwords
    
*   Granting individual privileges to users
    
*   Managing system auditing
    

To achieve the listed requirements, the role management repository role requires the following system privileges: ROLE ADMIN, LDAP ADMIN, and STRUCTUREDPRIVILEGE ADMIN. In addition to granting these system privileges, the following conditions must also exist for the user accounts within this repository role:

*   The grantee must have package privileges for the package hierarchy node used to store the repository roles and analytic privileges. Grantees must be able to create, edit, and activate repository-based roles within this package.
    
*   The grantee must have the REPO.READ package privilege on package nodes they intend to grant to repository roles using a GUI. This privilege is only required to view them in the graphical list.
    
*   The grantee must have the REPO.READ package privilege on packages containing information views that will be configured within analytic privileges.
    
*   The grantee and \_SYS\_REPO must have SELECT access to any tables containing data-level security information, for example, tables that map user accounts to data attributes. These tables are used to define dynamic analytic privileges.
    
*   The grantee must have EXECUTE privileges for stored procedures in the \_SYS\_REPO schema the names of which begin with GRANT\_ and REVOKE\_.
    
*   The grantee must have EXECUTE privileges for the SYS.REPOSITORY\_REST stored procedure. This privilege is required to work in the SAP HANA package hierarchy or repository in which repository roles are created.
    
*   If standard roles are used in the security model, the grantee must have been granted the grantable privileges using the WITH ADMIN OPTION or WITH GRANT OPTION. This privilege isn’t necessary if repository roles are used. With repository roles, the system account \_SYS\_REPO must be granted the grantable privileges using the WITH ADMIN OPTION or WITH GRANT OPTION.
    
*   The grantee must be granted the sap.hana.ide.roles::EditorDeveloper and sap.hana.ide.roles::SecurityAdmin roles to use web-based GUIs when creating repository roles or managing roles.
    
*   To prevent access to the auditing mechanism, the AUDIT ADMIN and AUDIT OPERATOR system privileges must not be granted to the user.
    

When implemented according to these requirements, the grantee won’t be able to use another user account to perform fraudulent or malicious actions in the SAP HANA system. In addition, because the grantee doesn’t have access to manipulate the auditing mechanisms, he can’t cover his tracks. All actions he performs using his assigned account should be captured by the auditing mechanism.

### 7.4.3    Data and Communication Encryption Role

The third repository role recommended by the security consultant grants the necessary privileges to administer communication protocol, log volume, and data volume encryption. Grantees of this role will be responsible for the following tasks:

*   Changing the root key
    
*   Enabling persistent data volume encryption
    
*   Enabling transaction log volume encryption
    
*   Managing credentials used by remote sources
    
*   Managing keystores and certificate files on the SAP HANA operating system
    
*   Administering SSL certificates used for authentication and secure communications
    

Given that a high degree of operating system and administrative level access is required by this role, system administrators will need to be assigned this role, and individuals on the security team won’t perform the listed actions. A separation of duties in this case has more to do with the amount of access required to manage end-to-end encryption. For example, a user administering a role doesn’t require operating system-level access or SAP HANA INI file access to perform her functions. Therefore, she shouldn’t automatically obtain administrative functionality just because she’s a member of the security team.

Regardless of how your organization decides to configure encryption-related administration access, limiting access to these activities is still important. If communication encryption is disabled, man-in-the-middle attacks may intercept data and credentials. If data volume or log volume encryption is disabled, unauthorized individuals with physical access to SAP HANA persistent storage devices might be able to access confidential or proprietary data. This vulnerability is especially important to consider when the SAP HANA system is hosted outside the physical security of your organization’s internal data center or network.

With that in mind, let’s look at the system privileges required to manage data and communication encryption. To manage all aspects of encryption, the CERTIFICATE ADMIN, ENCRYPTION ROOT KEY ADMIN, SSL ADMIN, TRUST ADMIN, INIFILE ADMIN, CREDENTIAL ADMIN, and CATALOG READ system privileges will be required. In addition, an operating system user account will be required if certificates are stored on the file system of the operating system.

### 7.4.4    System Auditing Role

The final repository role recommended by the security consultant grants the necessary privileges to manage auditing within the SAP HANA system. This critically important role should be limited to individuals that have no other security or system administration-related privileges within the system. Grantees of this role will be responsible for the following tasks:

*   Enabling or disabling auditing
    
*   Creating audit policies to track actions within the SAP HANA system
    
*   Clearing the audit database table, logs, or files
    

The AUDIT ADMIN and AUDIT OPERATOR system privileges must be granted to roles that will facilitate these requirements. The ability to maintain a separation of duties with this role is critical. Grantees of this role must not be able to cover their tracks within the system, which means they can’t simultaneously administer users, roles, and auditing. Granting a single user all these abilities would allow that user to commit fraud or perform malicious actions without accountability.

## 7.5    Summary

System privileges govern access to a variety of actions within an SAP HANA system. These actions can be categorized into development, security, administration, system monitoring, and performance testing areas. System privileges can be granted to users, roles, and repository roles, but using repository roles is best because the \_SYS\_REPO account has the necessary privileges by default to grant system privileges to other users.

# 8    Object Privileges

In this chapter, we’ll explore the different privileges that you can grant to catalog objects and walk you through the process of granting privileges.

Object privileges play an important role in the development of any SAP HANA security model and define the types of SQL script actions a user can perform on a catalog object. SAP HANA hosts multiple types of catalog objects. In [Chapter 3](#03_001.html#h3), we discussed the various types of catalog objects that you can create in SAP HANA and how the way you create catalog objects affects your security model.

As a reminder, catalog objects consist of various relational database management system (RDBMS) artifacts, such as schemas, tables, views, stored procedures, triggers, sequences, and a few other items. Items such as tables both store and define the structure of the data. Other items, such as views, express query logic.

Schemas are crucially important in the world of catalog objects. All catalog objects are assigned to a single schema. You could say that the schema is the parent object to all other catalog objects. SAP HANA allows security administrators the option of granting privileges on a schema, in which case all objects within the schema inherit the privileges assigned to the schema. Alternatively, security administrators can assign privileges to individual objects, in which case the security administrator will need to update the security model to grant the appropriate privileges to the catalog object each time a new object is created within a schema.

In this chapter, we’ll look at object privileges and demonstrate how you can grant object privileges to users or roles using SQL statements, using the SAP HANA cockpit, or within repository-based roles.

## 8.1    What Are Object Privileges?

When you grant privileges to a catalog object, you’re essentially specifying the types of actions that you can execute against the catalog object using SQL. Some of those actions correlate directly with the syntax you’ll use in a SQL statement. For example, you can query a table using the following SQL statement:

```
SELECT TOP 100 "FirstName" FROM "EDW"."DimCustomer" WHERE "Status" = 'Active'
```

Notice that this SQL statement starts with SELECT. To properly execute this SQL statement, a user or its associated role must be granted the SELECT privilege for the catalog table DimCustomer. You could also grant SELECT to the enterprise data warehouse (EDW) schema, allowing the user or associated role to query any table in that schema.

In the following sections, we’ll explore catalog object privileges related to schemas, tables, views, stored procedures, functions, remote sources, and sequences.

### 8.1.1    Catalog Object Privileges

Before we explore the process of granting privileges to catalog objects, let’s look at the different privileges that you can grant to each of the major types of catalog objects, starting with catalog schemas.

#### Granting All Privileges

SAP HANA 2.0 supports a special GRANT statement as a shortcut for granting all Data Definition Language (DDL) and Data Manipulation Language (DML) privileges currently granted to the grantor, for a given object, to a grantee. This GRANT statement is only applicable for schemas, tables, and view catalog objects. Based on testing, for schemas, this GRANT statement only seems to work if the grantor is also the owner of the schema. However, this special statement does work for tables and views even if the grantor is not also the owner. If the grantor has the ability to grant to others, he can use this special shortcut, which does partially grant privileges. If the grantor only has one privilege that is grantable to others, only that one privilege is applied to the target grantee.

The following example SQL statements can be used by a grantor to grant all currently granted privileges to another grantee:

```
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON SCHEMA <SCHEMA_NAME> TO <GRANTEE_NAME>;
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON <SCHEMA_NAME>.<TABLE_NAME> TO <GRANTEE_NAME> WITH GRANT OPTION;
```

#### Catalog Schemas

[Table 8.1](#08_001.html#t8.1) lists some frequently used SQL actions related to schemas. These actions can be granted to a user or roles. In [Table 8.1](#08_001.html#t8.1), we briefly describe how each action relates to a schema and the objects associated with that schema. Keep in mind that these actions will apply to all catalog objects within a schema. Schema privileges aren’t as restrictive as those applied to individual catalog objects, and therefore, you should heavily scrutinize schema privileges before they’re granted.

 
| Grantable Privileges for Catalog Schemas || Description of SQL Action |
| --- | --- |
| CREATE ANY || When granted, this privilege allows the creation of catalog objects within the specified schema. When a user creates a catalog object, he’s the owner of that object and has full privileges for it.Note: The privilege to create a catalog object is established at the schema level only. You can’t grant this privilege for each individual object type. |
| --- | --- |
| ALTER || This privilege allows changes to all objects within the schema. |
| DROP || This privilege allows any object within the schema to be deleted or dropped from the system. |
| EXECUTE || This privilege allows the grantee to execute of any stored procedure or function defined within the specified schema. |
| SELECT || This privilege allows the grantee to issue SQL SELECT statements against any applicable object defined within the referenced schema. This statement is typically used to query tables and views but also allows access to a sequence. |
| INSERT || This privilege allows the insertion of data into any table defined within the specified schema. |
| UPDATE || This privilege allows data to be updated within any table defined in the specified schema. |
| DELETE || This privilege allows data to be deleted within any table defined in the specified schema and applies to both the DELETE and TRUNCATE SQL actions. |
| INDEX || This privilege governs the ability to create, change, or remove an index for any table defined within the specified schema. |
| TRIGGER || This privilege governs the ability to create triggers associated with any table defined within the specified schema. |
| DEBUG || This privilege authorizes the debug functionality for any applicable object defined within the schema. |
| REFERENCES || This privilege allows the grantee to retrieve the name of the schema and its objects when using SAP HANA Studio, when using the SAP HANA database explorer, or when querying system views that contain basic table metadata. For example, the schema’s referenced table names will return when the granted user queries the system view tables using the SQL statement SELECT \* FROM SYS.TABLES. |
| CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE || This privilege allows the grantee to create a temporary local table used by stored procedures. This privilege is independent from the CREATE ANY privilege to limit users from creating any type of object in a schema. |
| CREATE VIRTUAL PACKAGE || This privilege allows the grantee to create virtual packages. A virtual package is a file that contains Java libraries and resource files. This file is an archived (ZIP) file that can be referenced in virtual procedures and functions. For example, custom Spark procedures are virtual procedures that are used to access a Spark remote source via SAP HANA smart data access. |
| SELECT CDS METADATA || This privilege grants access to all core data services (CDS) metadata stored in the catalog for a given CDS table. |
| UNMASKED || This privilege grants access to masked data stored in a table and allows the grantee to query the table or view and view the actual data stored within. |

**Table 8.1**    Privileges That Can Be Granted to Catalog Schemas

#### Catalog Tables

[Table 8.2](#08_001.html#t8.2) lists the frequently used SQL actions related to tables that can be granted to a user or role. In [Table 8.2](#08_001.html#t8.2), we briefly describe how each action relates to tables in general.

 
| Grantable Privileges for Catalog Tables || Description of SQL Action |
| --- | --- |
| ALTER || This privilege allows the grantee to make DDL changes to tables, for example, to add or delete a column. |
| --- | --- |
| DROP || This privilege allows the grantee to remove a table from the system. |
| SELECT || This privilege allows the grantee to use SELECT in SQL statements to retrieve data from a table. |
| INSERT || This privilege allows the grantee to use INSERT in SQL statements to add additional data to the table. |
| UPDATE || This privilege allows the grantee to use UPDATE in SQL statements to update existing rows within a table. |
| DELETE || This privilege allows the grantee to use DELETE in SQL statements to delete or truncate one or more rows within a table. This action supports both DELETE and TRUNCATE SQL statements. |
| INDEX || This privilege allows the grantee to govern the ability to create, change, or remove an index defined within a table. |
| TRIGGER || This privilege allows the grantee to govern the ability to create triggers associated with the table. |
| REFERENCES || This privilege allows the grantee to grant limited access to any table referenced by a foreign key constraint. For example, say you’re securing a table named transactions that has a foreign key constraint or reference to a table named customers. Granting REFERENCES to table transactions also grants limited access to table customers. |
| UNMASKED || This privilege grants access to masked data stored in a table and allows the grantee to query the table or view and view the actual data stored within. |

**Table 8.2**    Privileges That Can Be Granted to Catalog Tables

#### Catalog Views

[Table 8.3](#08_001.html#t8.3) lists the frequently used SQL actions related to catalog views. These actions can be granted to a user or roles. In [Table 8.3](#08_001.html#t8.3), we briefly describe how each action relates to the view and the objects referenced by the view.

 
| Grantable Privileges for Catalog Views || Description of SQL Action |
| --- | --- |
| ALTER || This privilege allows the grantee to make changes to the definition of a view. |
| --- | --- |
| DROP || This privilege allows the view to be deleted or dropped from the system. |
| SELECT || This privilege allows the grantee to use SQL SELECT statements against a view. Note that objects referenced within the definition of the view are granted as well. |
| INSERT || This privilege allows data to be inserted into the view’s underlying table. There are limitations to the types of catalog views that support these operations. Based on our testing, you can only INSERT data into a view if that view references a single table and if no formulas or functions are applied to the columns defined within the view. |
| UPDATE || This privilege allows data to be updated within the view’s underlying table. There are limitations to the types of catalog views that support these operations. Based on our testing, you can only UPDATE data into a view if that view references a single table and if no formulas or functions are applied to the columns defined within the view. |
| DELETE || This privilege allows data to be deleted within the view’s underlying table. There are limitations to the types of catalog views that support these operations. Based on our testing, you can only DELETE data from a view if that view references a single table. |
| UNMASKED || This privilege grants access to masked data stored in a table and allows the grantee to query the table or view and view the actual data stored within. |

**Table 8.3**    Privileges That Can Be Granted to Catalog Views

#### Catalog Stored Procedures and Functions

[Table 8.4](#08_001.html#t8.4) lists the frequently used SQL actions related to catalog stored procedures and to functions. Because these two catalog objects have the same privileges and related actions, we’ve combined them into a single table. These actions can be granted to a user or role. In [Table 8.4](#08_001.html#t8.4), we briefly describe how each action relates to the stored procedure or function and the objects referenced by each.

 
| Grantable Privileges for Procedures or Functions || Description of SQL Action |
| --- | --- |
| ALTER || This privilege allows for changes to the definition of the stored procedure or function using the ALTER SQL syntax. |
| --- | --- |
| DROP || This privilege allows the stored procedure or function to be deleted or dropped from the system. |
| EXECUTE || This privilege allows the stored procedure or function to be executed. Actions that can be executed directly depend on the SQL or SQLScript code defined within the procedure or function.In definer mode, objects referenced within the definition of the stored procedure or function don’t need to be explicitly granted to the user executing the stored procedure or function. Those objects are accessible by the creator of the procedure or function. However, objects referenced with the invoker mode enabled must be explicitly granted to the user executing the procedure or function. |
| DEBUG || This privilege allows for the debugging of the stored procedure or function. |

**Table 8.4**    Privileges That Can Be Granted to Catalog Stored Procedures or Catalog Functions

#### Remote Sources

Remote sources are a unique type of catalog object. They’re virtual tables that reference RDBMS tables through SAP HANA smart data access, a mechanism built into SAP HANA that supports data federation from a third-party or remote RDBMS. Using SAP HANA smart data access, you can treat a remote table as though it were a local table within the SAP HANA database catalog. When this table is queried within SAP HANA, the system will fetch the requested data from the remote table in real time. Because of its unique nature, special privileges are available within SAP HANA to accommodate interactions with remote sources and virtual tables. [Table 8.5](#08_001.html#t8.5) lists the available privileges by name and describes their behavior related to remote sources.

 
| Grantable Privileges for Remote Sources || Description of SQL Action |
| --- | --- |
| CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE || This privilege grants the ability to create a virtual table within an authorized schema. The user must also have the CREATE ANY privilege or own the schema in which the virtual table is placed. |
| --- | --- |
