| DROP || This privilege grants the ability to delete or drop a virtual table from the system. |
| CREATE VIRTUAL FUNCTION || This privilege grants the ability to create a function. |
| CREATE VIRTUAL PROCEDURE || This privilege grants the ability to create a virtual procedure. |
| PROCESS REMOTE SUBSCRIPTION EXCEPTION || This privilege allows processing exceptions for a remote subscription. |
| CREATE REMOTE SUBSCRIPTION || This privilege allows for the creation of subscriptions for capturing changed data from a virtual source. |
| ALTER || This privilege allows for the modification of an existing remote source configuration. |

**Table 8.5**    Privileges That Can Be Assigned for Working with Remote Sources

#### Catalog Sequences

You can use sequences to define the behavior of automatically incrementing number sequences. For example, you can define a primary key column in a table and call a sequence to retrieve the next or previously available value within the sequence. [Table 8.6](#08_001.html#t8.6) lists the available privileges by name and describes their behavior related to sequences.

 
| Grantable Privileges for Sequences || Description of SQL Action |
| --- | --- |
| Drop || This privilege allows for a sequence to be deleted or dropped from the system. |
| --- | --- |
| Select || This privilege allows the sequence to be queried, for example, to retrieve the next number in the sequence. |

**Table 8.6**    Privileges That Can Be Assigned for Working with Sequences

### 8.1.2    Security Considerations for Catalog Objects

Let’s take a moment to discuss a few critical security considerations when dealing with catalog objects. We discussed some of these items in [Chapter 2](#02_001.html#h2), but we feel that reiterating them in this chapter is important. When designing a security model, you’ll need to consider the Grantable to Others authorization, object ownership, schema-level privileges, object-level privileges, authorizations for catalog views, authorizations for stored procedures, authorizations for functions, and repository objects.

#### Grantable to Others Authorization

In addition to the SQL privileges outlined in the tables in [Section 8.1](#08_001.html#h8.1), you also must consider the authorizations required to grant privileges to other users. In most cases, a security administrator will need both a SQL privilege and the Grantable to Others authorization for that privilege to establish a security model. SAP HANA won’t allow just any user account to grant other users access to an object. If the user is the owner of the objects, he can grant rights to other users.

However, most security administrators aren’t the owners of all objects; each object has only one owner, and often, you’ll need multiple security administrators. Therefore, security administrators require both SQL access to an object and the ability to grant those same privileges to other users.

When you establish privileges for a user and a role using the SAP HANA cockpit, notice that to the right of each privilege are Yes and No indicators in a column labeled Grantable to Others. When the Yes option is selected, the grantee can grant the same privilege to a different grantee.

#### Object Ownership

Recall that the individual that creates an object is the owner of that object. She inherently has full control of the privileges for that catalog object. Depending on the setup of your security model, each time an object is created, you’ll probably need to grant privileges to other users and roles for that object. However, authorizing privileges at the schema level might simplify this requirement, which we’ll discuss in the next subsection.

Object ownership is also important in relation to the user account that creates the object. If a user account is used to create a catalog object, that user account should never be deleted because deleting the account also deletes any catalog objects and granted privileges established by that user account. Thus, special technical accounts are often created for users that create catalog objects and manage security. Hopefully, an established policy ensures that technical user accounts are never deleted. As we’ll discuss shortly, alternatively, you can create most objects as repository objects. These objects are owned by the \_SYS\_REPO system account and won’t be deleted when a developer’s account is deleted.

#### Authorizations at the Schema Level

When securing catalog objects, you can establish authorizations either at the schema level or, in some cases, for each individual object. Simply establishing the privileges at the schema level is much easier; when privileges are established at the individual object level, the security model must be adjusted each time a new object is created. The owner of the object or a security administrator will then need to update existing roles to accommodate each new object. These tasks can become tedious and are often overlooked if objects are created frequently. To simplify the security model, privileges can be established at the schema level. In this way, all objects with a schema automatically inherit the privileges assigned to the schema.

#### Authorizations at the Catalog Object Level

Although establishing privileges at the schema level is easier, this approach can be less secure. If you determine that using schema-level privileges is acceptable, be aware that all current and future objects in that schema will be accessible for the assigned users or roles. No mechanisms exist for denying privileges in SAP HANA. Therefore, if your security requirements call for two catalog tables in the same schema, each with different privileges assigned to different roles, you’ll have to establish privileges at the individual table level and forgo the use of schema-level privileges. While this approach is more tedious, it provides more granular control of the privileges for objects within the same schema.

#### Considerations for Catalog Views

As discussed in [Chapter 2](#02_001.html#h2), catalog views reference other catalog views or tables within their definitions. When a user queries a catalog view, he only needs the SELECT privilege on that catalog view. The system doesn’t validate the privileges against objects referenced within the view.

However, the developer creating the catalog view must have the SELECT privilege and the authority to give this privilege to other users. The developer won’t be able to activate the view unless he is the owner of all referenced objects or has the SELECT privilege and Grantable to Others privilege for each referenced object. In our experience, this concept is most often not understood and implemented poorly within most security models. If your organization plans to develop catalog database views to support access to data, make sure that your developers have the appropriate privileges to activate catalog views.

#### Considerations for Catalog Stored Procedures and Functions

As discussed in [Chapter 2](#02_001.html#h2), you can choose between two security options when defining stored procedures or functions. You can establish the SQL security in definer or invoker mode.

In definer mode, the developer must have privileges to perform all SQL actions defined within the stored procedure or function. In addition, he must have the Grantable to Others privilege for each associated SQL privilege. In this way, the definer is effectively delegating those privileges to the user or role that’s been granted the EXECUTE privilege against the stored procedure or function. In most cases, this approach is the least restrictive way to manage access to the activities performed by the stored procedure or function.

In invoker mode, the user or role with EXECUTE privileges against the stored procedure or function must also have the appropriate privileges to support the defined actions against each referenced catalog object. For example, if the stored procedure adds data to a table, the user first would need the EXECUTE privilege for the stored procedure. Second, he would need the INSERT privilege against the referenced catalog table. In most cases, this approach is the most restrictive way to manage access to the activities performed by the stored procedure or function.

#### Schemas, Tables, Procedures, and Views as Repository Objects

One of the most important concepts in SAP HANA security is the ability to understand the difference between catalog objects created using a SQL CREATE statement and catalog objects created using development artifacts within the SAP HANA development repository. Objects created within the SAP HANA repository are often called repository objects. The key differentiator between the two object types lies in the ownership of the objects, as we’ll discuss next.

When a user executes a CREATE SQL statement to define an object, he becomes the sole owner of the object. In most cases, he must then grant privileges to other users or roles for them to access the object he created. If the owner’s user account is deleted from the system, any objects he created or privileges he granted are also removed from the system. In addition, if an organization has multiple SAP HANA environments to support proper lifecycle management, these CREATE statements must be manually executed in each environment. These situations should be avoided when establishing a security model because the model should be able to be transported easily between SAP HANA environments.

When an object is created as a development artifact in the SAP HANA repository, the object isn’t owned by the developer. Instead, the object is owned by a special system account called \_SYS\_REPO. This account can’t be deleted from the system and exists in all SAP HANA systems. Therefore, if needed, you can easily transport the definition of catalog objects or a security model between two or more SAP HANA systems; it already exists in each environment and therefore can easily take ownership of these objects in each.

As discussed in [Chapter 3](#03_001.html#h3) and [Chapter 6](#06_001.html#h6), \_SYS\_REPO is responsible for activating repository-based roles, SAP HANA information views, and a few other security-sensitive objects. In an ideal security model, almost all catalog objects would be created as development artifacts specifically to ensure that \_SYS\_REPO is the owner of the object. When \_SYS\_REPO owns most objects, establishing, transporting, and maintaining a security model within an SAP HANA landscape is much easier.

## 8.2    Granting Object Privileges with SQL

In this section, we’ll review the different ways to grant object privileges to users or roles using SQL statements.

### 8.2.1    Securing Schemas with SQL

When you secure catalog objects, you’re essentially granting SQL privileges to users, roles, or both. In [Section 8.1](#08_001.html#h8.1), we outlined many of the privileges that you grant based on the type of catalog objects you’re working with. In this section, we’ll demonstrate the actual process of granting those privileges to users or roles using SQL statements.

In [Chapter 3](#03_001.html#h3), we outlined the process for creating catalog schemas. Once a schema is created, the owner of the schema will likely need to access the SAP HANA cockpit and grant other administrator users or security administration roles full privileges that are grantable to others on the schema. Once this process is complete, the security administrators will be able to establish a security model based on the schema and its objects. Keep in mind that the schema might also be associated with a service account and not an actual human user. For example, if you set up an SAP HANA service account to manage table replication between SAP ERP and SAP HANA using SAP Landscape Transformation Replication Server, then additional security settings in SAP HANA will need to be maintained. This approach assumes that users will interact with the replicated data. Once an SAP Landscape Transformation Replication Server mass data transfer configuration is established, you’ll need to log on to SAP HANA using the service account credentials and grant others access to the schema used by SAP Landscape Transformation Replication Server. Remember, only the owner of the schema can grant this access.

One way a user can grant or revoke privileges to its schema is by issuing SQL statements, which can be executed within the SQL console. The basic syntax of the SQL script that grants privileges is as follows:

```
GRANT <PRIVILEGE1, PRIVILEGE2,…> ON SCHEMA <SCHEMA> TO <SOME_USER or 
SOME_ROLE> WITH GRANT OPTION;
```

In this syntax, the items inside the angle brackets (<>) are variables that you can adjust based on the privilege, schema, user, or role. The GRANT command means that you’re allowing the action. A comma-separated array of privileges can also be specified after the GRANT statement. If only one privilege is required, you don’t need an array; simply specify a single privilege by name without commas. Include ON SCHEMA followed by the schema name to identify the schema catalog object. Then, include TO followed by a user or role to identify who is receiving the granted privileges.

For example, to grant the ADMIN\_SEC user account the SELECT privilege on a user’s schema, log on as the user that owns the schema, access the SQL console, and execute the following statement (assuming that the account that owns the schema is named TEST\_USER and that the schema name is the same):

```
GRANT SELECT on SCHEMA TEST_USER to ADMIN_SEC WITH GRANT OPTION;
```

Adding the WITH GRANT OPTION syntax is critical in this case because you need to grant the security administrator full access to a user’s schema. The user must include this statement to grant the security administrator the ability to grant the same privilege to other users or roles.

As an alternative, the schema owner can also grant privileges to existing roles. We typically recommend that the schema owner grant the privileges to existing roles because roles can be assigned to multiple security administrator user accounts. To grant the SEC\_ADMINS role SELECT rights for a user’s schema, log on as the user that owns the schema, access the SQL console, and execute the following statement. In our example, we are assuming that the account that owns the schema is named TEST\_USER and that the SEC\_ADMINS role is assigned to all security administration accounts; you can assume that this schema is a user schema because the user name and schema name are the same:

```
GRANT SELECT on SCHEMA TEST_USER to SEC_ADMINS WITH GRANT OPTION;
```

Now, let’s say that you need to give the SEC\_ADMIN role full privileges for a user schema named TEST\_USER. Issuing the statement shown in [Listing 8.1](#08_002.html#l8.1) will grant all privileges to that role.

```
GRANT 
ALTER, SELECT, CREATE ANY, DEBUG, 
DELETE, DROP, EXECUTE, INDEX, 
INSERT, UPDATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER,
SELECT CDS METADATA, SELECT METADATA,
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE, CREATE VIRTUAL FUNCTION PACKAGE
ON SCHEMA TEST_USER TO ADMIN_SEC WITH GRANT OPTION;
```

**Listing 8.1**    SQL Code to Grant Multiple Schema Privileges

Notice how you can specify multiple SQL privileges separated by commas in a single statement. To remove privileges, you’ll need to issue a REVOKE statement, as follows:

```
REVOKE <PRIVILEGE1, PRIVILEGE2,…> ON SCHEMA <SCHEMA> FROM <SOME_USER or 
SOME_ROLE>
```

In this syntax, the items inside the angle brackets (<>) are variables that you can adjust based on the privilege, schema, user, or role. The REVOKE command means that you’re removing the action. A comma-separated array of privileges can also be specified after the REVOKE statement. Include ON SCHEMA followed by the schema name to identify the schema catalog object. Then, include FROM followed by a user or role to identify from whom we’re removing privileges.

To remove all privileges assigned to a role for a given schema, execute the SQL statement shown in [Listing 8.2](#08_002.html#l8.2) as the schema owner.

```
REVOKE
ALTER, SELECT, CREATE ANY, DEBUG, 
DELETE, DROP, EXECUTE, INDEX, 
INSERT, UPDATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER,
SELECT CDS METADATA, SELECT METADATA,
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE, CREATE VIRTUAL FUNCTION PACKAGE
ON SCHEMA TEST_USER FROM ADMIN_SEC;
```

**Listing 8.2**    SQL Code to Revoke Multiple Schema Privileges

Note that the GRANT and REVOKE SQL statements can be issued against a user or role even if the listed privileges are already granted or not already revoked. This option is helpful when you’re programmatically granting or revoking privileges because you won’t need to first identify which privileges are missing or which privileges are absent before executing commands; they’ll execute regardless.

### 8.2.2    Securing Individual Catalog Objects with SQL

Tables and other catalog objects within a schema can be secured individually. We identified these other catalog objects in [Section 8.1.1](#08_001.html#h8.1.1). In these cases, privileges are granted not at the schema level but at the individual object level. For example, let’s assume that user account JH2345 has been granted the SELECT privilege on schema CORPORATE. Another user account, GR4555, has the CREATE ANY privilege on schema COPORATE. GR4555 creates a table named CUSTOMERS in schema CORPORATE. At this point, GR4555 has all privileges on table CUSTOMERS because the account owns the table. However, JH2345 also has SELECT privileges on the table because he was granted that privilege on schema CORPORATE.

Always consider this relationship between schema privileges and individual object privileges. Granting too many privileges on a schema can expose security risks for objects created within that schema. Granting too many privileges on individual objects can lead to difficulties in maintaining the security model. Therefore, security administers often must carefully balance their use of schema privileges and individual object privileges.

Now, let’s walk through the process of granting and revoking privileges for a catalog table, one of many different types of catalog objects that can be secured. However, the SQL statements and processes for securing each item is the same as the code used to secure tables. The syntax for granting privileges to a table is as follows:

```
GRANT <PRIVILEGE1, PRIVILEGE2,…> ON <CATALOG OBJECT> TO <SOME_USER or SOME_ROLE> WITH GRANT OPTION;
```

As with the syntax used for schemas, you can specify one or more privileges in a comma-separated array. The privileges that can be granted are specific to the object listed after the ON clause. [Section 8.1.1](#08_001.html#h8.1.1) contains a list of the privileges that can be granted based on the object type. After the ON clause, you’ll then specify the catalog object. After the TO clause, you’ll list the users or roles to which you want to grant privileges.

For example, to grant SELECT on table CUSTOMERS, created in the CORP schema, to the role named QUERY\_USERS, you’d issue the following SQL statement:

```
GRANT SELECT ON CORP.CUSTOMERS TO QUERY_USERS;
```

Notice that we prefixed the catalog table with the schema name. This prefix is often required so that the system knows the exact table you’re referencing.

Now, let’s look at how an object owner would delegate all privileges to the security administrator group. Keep in mind that they’ll likely need to delegate these privileges to other users in the future. To grant all privileges to the security administrator role named SEC\_ADMIN, you’d use the following SQL statement:

```
GRANT ALTER, DROP, SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, INDEX, TRIGGER, REFERENCES ON CORP.CUSTOMERS TO SEC_ADMIN WITH GRANT OPTION;
```

Note that we included WITH GRANT OPTION, which is required to allow the grantee to grant these privileges to other users or roles. In most cases, you’ll only specify this option if the grantee will be responsible for establishing security within the SAP HANA system.

In some instances, you’ll also need to revoke privileges, that is, remove privileges granted to a user or role. Use the following syntax to revoke catalog object privileges from a user or role:

```
REVOKE <PRIVILEGE1, PRIVILEGE2,…> ON <Catalog Object> FROM <SOME_USER or 
SOME_ROLE>
```

As with schemas, the statement starts with REVOKE followed by a list of privileges. After the ON clause, you’ll specify the catalog object. After the FROM clause, you’ll include the user or role to remove the privilege from.

Now, let’s look at how an object owner would remove all privileges from the security administrator group, in this case named SEC\_ADMIN. Use the following SQL statement:

```
REVOKE ALTER, DROP, SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, INDEX, TRIGGER, REFERENCES ON CORP.CUSTOMERS FROM SEC_ADMIN;
```

Except for schemas, the syntax you use to either GRANT or REVOKE privileges for a given catalog object applies to all individual catalog object types. You can grant or revoke privileges for tables, views, procedures, functions, and sequences. Now, let’s look at how to use the SAP HANA cockpit to grant or revoke privileges for catalog objects.

## 8.3    Granting Object Privileges with the SAP HANA Cockpit

Let’s review the workflows necessary to grant and revoke catalog object privileges with the SAP HANA cockpit. As an alternative to using SQL statements, you can use the SAP HANA cockpit options called Assign Privileges or Manage Roles. Each interface allows you to both grant and revoke object privileges for a given user account or for a given role. Most users will find using the SAP HANA cockpit easier than memorizing and entering in SQL statements.

To access the Assign Privileges or Manage Roles interfaces, start at the SAP HANA cockpit Home screen, locate an SAP HANA system in the resource directory. Connect to the desired tenant database or SYSTEMDB, which will take you to the System Overview window. Using the Filter by Area dropdown list, choose the option Security. Locate the Assign Privileges or Manage Roles in the User & Role Management tile.

[Figure 8.1](#08_003.html#f8.1) shows the Assign Privileges interface within the SAP HANA cockpit for the TEST\_01 user account. In this windows, you’ll see several tabs for the various privilege categories, such as the System Privileges, Object Privileges, Analytic Privileges, Application Privileges, Package Privileges, and Privileges on Users tabs. You’ll find a similar interface when working with roles. However, the Role Details GUI has an additional link called Roles where you can grant existing roles to the selected role.

[![Managing Privileges Assigned to User Account in the SAP HANA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein08_001.png)](img-f8.1.html) 

**Figure 8.1**    Managing Privileges Assigned to User Account in the SAP HANA Cockpit

The second tab in the Assign Privileges window is named Object Privileges. Use this tab to list, grant, or revoke object privileges for a given grantee.

The privileges listed in this interface are already granted to the grantee. If the list is blank, nothing is currently granted. To grant an object privilege, click the Edit button located on the far-right side of the interface near the Search field. Click the Edit button to enable edit mode, and new buttons labeled Cancel, Add Object, Change Privileges, and Remove Object will appear. Click the Add Object button to open the Select Objects popup window. Within this window, you’ll see a search bar and a list of catalog objects.

Use the search bar to filter the list based on the entered text. The search allows for multiple words, allowing you to enter the object name and type. For example, you can enter the text “\_SYS\_BIC schema” to filter objects with that name and of a catalog object type. Scroll through the list and highlight the catalog object you want to assign privileges too. Once you click the desired catalog object, the Add Object with Privileges window will appear, as shown in [Figure 8.2](#08_003.html#f8.2). In this window, you’ll see a list of possible object privileges that can be assigned. Select the checkbox beside each privilege you want to grant.

[![Assigning Object Privileges to a Grantee Using the SAP HANA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein08_002.png)](img-f8.2.html) 

**Figure 8.2**    Assigning Object Privileges to a Grantee Using the SAP HANA Cockpit

To assign the Grantable to Others privilege, locate an object privilege in the same list. To the right, you’ll see a slider button move to Yes allowing the grantee to grant the same privilege to another user or role. Repeat this process for each object privilege in the list. Once you’ve maintained all the desired object privileges in the list, click the OK button to return to the list of granted object privileges. Your selected object and object privileges should now appear in the list.

Unlike the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench and SAP HANA Studio, the SAP HANA cockpit GUI does not support repository-based catalog objects and schemas with SAP HANA extended application services, classic model (SAP HANA XS). Therefore, you cannot grant privileges to design-time objects nor their runtime objects in the catalog. In short, the SAP HANA cockpit is not designed to work with SAP HANA XS repository objects that are owned by the \_SYS\_REPO account. Why SAP chose not to support this functionality is not clear; the most likely explanation is that future versions of SAP HANA will not support the SAP HANA XS development architecture.

To revoke an object privilege, click an assigned object and its assigned privilege from the list and then click the Remove Object button to revoke the privilege. To make the changes active, click the Save button or continue making other changes if necessary. Note that, once the Save button is clicked, you’ll be returned to the list of privileges and be required to click the Edit button again to make further changes.

To change assigned object privileges, while in Edit mode click an assigned object and its assigned privilege from the list and then click the Change Privileges button to open a new popup window with the title Change Privileges of concatenated with the name of the object. A list of assigned and unassigned privileges for the object will appear. Select the checkbox to grant the privilege or deselect the checkbox to revoke the privilege. Use the Yes/No slider under Grantable to Others to manage the grantable to others privilege. Click the OK button at the bottom right of the window to apply your changes. Again, to make the changes active, click the Save button or continue making other changes if necessary until you’re ready to activate all changes.

## 8.4    Granting Object Privileges with the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, hosted within the XS engine, provides an interface that you can use to create users, create roles, or manage security for standard roles. This interface provides a web-based alternative to SAP HANA Studio and serves as an alternative to issues GRANT and REVOKE statement with SQL.

You can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench via a supported Internet browser. The following URLs can be customized to match the details of your environment:

*   http://sap-hana.myhost.com:8000/sap/hana/ide/security
    
*   http://<sap\_hana\_host>:80<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/security
    

In the last example, replace <sap\_hana\_host> with the host name of the SAP HANA system in your environment and <instance\_number> with the two-digit instance number corresponding to your SAP HANA system.

For secure access, the following examples should help you construct the correct URL:

*   https://<sap\_hana\_host>:43<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/security
    
*   https://sap-hana.myhost.com:4300/sap/hana/ide/security
    

Once you have access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, expand the Security node on the right. Expand Roles to reveal a list of standard roles defined in the system. Double-click a role to open the management interface for the given role. With the selected role management window open, you can begin granting and revoking privileges.

###### Note

To perform the same action for an individual user account, expand the Users node and double-click the desired user account.

Recall that we recommend you use repository-based roles to support an SAP HANA security model. However, in this section, we’ll simply highlight the basic workflow if you chose to manage security with standard roles or directly on individual user accounts.

With the GUI management interface open for a given grantee, you can add an object privilege under the Object Privileges tab. Click the plus sign (+) to add and search for the desired object privilege. The Find Catalog Object window appears allowing you to search for a specific database object. Select the desired objects and click OK to add them to the list. With the selected catalog object now in the list, highlight the object to reveal a frame to the right where you can select specific object privileges to be granted or revoked for that object. Select the checkbox beside each privilege you intend to grant. Choose Grantable to Other Users and Roles radio options Yes or No to the right of each listed system privilege as needed.

To save your changes, press (Ctrl)+(S) or click the disk icon at the top left to save and activate the privilege. To revoke or change an object privilege, select the object in the list. If you want to remove the object from the grantee and revoke all its privileges, click the red X and save. If you want to change the current privileges assignments, select or deselect the desired privileges listed in the frame to the right of the selected object. Once again, save the changes to make them active within the database system.

If any activation issues arise, warning messages will appear in the status frame at the bottom of the user management window. The status frame has a dark background color. Error messages will appear in red text. Errors are only generated during an attempted activation or saving of changes.

## 8.5    Granting Object Privileges with Repository Roles

In [Chapter 6](#06_001.html#h6), we introduced you to repository roles and described the process for managing and creating them. Remember that repository roles can be defined and managed using the role script language within an .hdbrole development artifact. Repository roles can also be defined and managed in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor using either the GUI or text editor. In this section, we’ll dive more deeply into the text editor syntax and show you processes specific to catalog object privileges using repository roles.

### 8.5.1    Script-Based Repository Roles

In [Chapter 6](#06_001.html#h6), we outlined the steps and procedures necessary for creating an .hdbrole repository artifact. Within that script, you can define catalog object privileges for both individual catalog objects and for schemas. The script supports referencing both runtime and design-time catalog objects. Runtime objects are objects that only exist in the SAP HANA database. Design-time objects are objects active in the development repository.

The syntax for defining privileges against individual runtime catalog objects is as follows:

```
catalog sql object <schema>.<object>: <array of privileges> ;
```

The statement starts with catalog sql object and is case sensitive. This term is followed by a fully qualified catalog object name, including the schema name. After the catalog object, you’ll include a colon, followed by a comma-separated array of privileges identified by name. The statement concludes with a semicolon.

For example, to grant the role access to execute a system stored procedure, use the following syntax:

```
catalog sql object "SYS"."REPOSITORY_REST": EXECUTE;
```

To grant privileges to multiple individual catalog objects, simply repeat the syntax for each catalog object. Each line will need to end with a semicolon, which tells the system that the statement is complete. [Listing 8.3](#08_005.html#l8.3) shows the syntax to grant privileges for three different catalog objects.

```
catalog sql object "dev_tables"."MyTable": SELECT, DELETE;
catalog sql object "dev_tables"."MyStoredProc": SELECT, EXECUTE, DROP, ALTER;
catalog sql object "dev_tables"."MyUDFunction": SELECT, EXECUTE, DROP, ALTER;
```

**Listing 8.3**    Repository Role Script Granting Privileges to Three Different Catalog Objects

Now, let’s look at the syntax used when privileges need to be assigned to an entire runtime schema, as follows:

```
catalog schema <schema name>: <array of privileges>;
```

This syntax is similar to the syntax used to grant individual catalog objects, but you’ll start the statement with catalog schema followed by the name of the schema. For example, to grant multiple privileges for the schema named demo\_schema, use the following syntax within the .hdbrole development script:

```
catalog schema "demo_schema": ALTER, SELECT, EXECUTE, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, 
CREATE ANY, DROP, DEBUG, TRIGGER, INDEX;
```

To grant privileges to multiple runtime catalog schemas, simply repeat the syntax for each schema. Remember to conclude each line with a semicolon, as shown in [Listing 8.4](#08_005.html#l8.4).

```
catalog schema "dev_tables": SELECT, EXECUTE;
catalog schema "ECCDATA": SELECT, EXECUTE;
catalog schema "_SYS_BIC": SELECT, EXECUTE;
catalog schema "SLT_ECC_ECP": SELECT, UPDATE, ALTER, DROP;
catalog schema "ECC76DATA": SELECT;
```

**Listing 8.4**    Repository Role Script Granting Privileges to Five Different Schemas

For design-time objects, you’ll use a slightly different syntax. Notice that with runtime objects, you’ll use the phrase catalog sql object and catalog schema before referencing the runtime objects in the SAP HANA catalog. With design time objects, you’ll simply begin with the phrase schema or sql object. In addition, when referencing design-time catalog objects, you’ll need to use their fully qualified design-time name. This fully qualified design-time name is a combination of the package hierarchy, a colon, and then the design-time file name. For example, to grant SELECT and EXECUTE on the design-time schema SalesMart stored in the Security.Schemas package, you would use the following syntax:

```
schema Security.Schemas:SalesMart.hdbschema: SELECT, EXECUTE;
```

Notice that the schema was stored in the package Security.Schemas and that the name of the schema file was SalesMart.hdbscema. For the fully qualified name of a schema, you’ll use the naming convention of package name separated by a colon (:) and finally the design-time object name.

For other catalog objects like tables, you’ll use a similar syntax. For example, to grant SELECT and DELETE on the design-time table adusers stored in the package Security.Tables, you would use the following syntax:

```
sql object Security.Tables::adusers: SELECT, DELETE;
```

Note that, with table objects, you did not reference their design-time script file extension.hdbtable. While schema objects require the extension .hdbschema, references to design-time catalog objects do not require the repository file extension reference. Notice also that, in the fully qualified name of a design-time table, a double colon (::) separates the package name and the catalog object name. You’ll find that this convention is the norm for all design-time catalog objects except for repository-based schemas.

Be aware that, when these privileges are activated in an .hdbrole script, the grantee will be the system managed user \_SYS\_REPO. However, before the system will allow these privileges to be activated, the owner of the catalog object must ensure that the \_SYS\_REPO account has complete access to the objects, including the ability to grant the privileges to other users. This requirement is only applicable if the object itself is a standard catalog object owned by a standard user account. However, if the catalog object is repository-based, that object is already owned by the \_SYS\_REPO account, so you don’t need to grant any additional privileges to the \_SYS\_REPO user. As mentioned earlier, this arrangement is one reason we recommend developers create catalog objects via the repository-based development process.

### 8.5.2    SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench GUI

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor, hosted within the XS engine, provides an interface that you can use to build and test development artifacts. From a security perspective, you can use this interface to create and manage repository-based roles. This interface helps you manage repository roles with a GUI or to view and edit their underlying scripting language with the built-in text editor. This flexibility allows security administrators to manage repository roles in a single interface.

You can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor via a supported Internet browser. The following URLs can be customized to match the details of your environment:

*   http://sap-hana.myhost.com:8000/sap/hana/ide/editor
    
*   http://<sap\_hana\_host>:80<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/editor
    

Replace <sap\_hana\_host> with the host name of the SAP HANA system in your environment and <instance\_number> with the two-digit instance number corresponding to your SAP HANA system.

For secure access, the following examples should help you construct the correct URL:

*   https://<sap\_hana\_host>:43<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/editor
    
*   https://sap-hana.myhost.com:4300/sap/hana/ide/editor
    

To use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench and define a role, the user account first will need to be granted one of the roles listed in [Table 8.7](#08_005.html#t8.7). Users only need one of the two roles to use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench.

 
| Role Name || Summary |
| --- | --- |
| sap.hana.ide.roles::EditorDeveloper || Within the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench, users will only have access to the editor. Within the editor, users can view, edit, create, delete, or activate a repository-based role or other repository-based development artifacts found in development packages or the development repository. A user must have package privileges in addition to this role to properly access and activate the repository role or other development artifacts. |
| --- | --- |
| sap.hana.ide.roles::Developer || This role grants a higher level of privileges for users that need full access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench. This role grants access to the editor, catalog, and security interfaces and can be considered the parent to the sap.hana.ide.roles::EditorDeveloper role. |

**Table 8.7**    Roles Required to the Use SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor

###### Package Privileges Required for the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor

In addition to the roles listed in [Table 8.7](#08_005.html#t8.7), users will also need the appropriate package privileges on the package in which they plan to edit, create, or activate repository roles. For example, they’ll need the following package privileges to create a repository role using the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor interface:

*   REPO.READ
    
*   REPO.EDIT\_NATIVE\_OBJECTS
    
*   REPO.ACTIVATE\_NATIVE\_OBJECTS
    

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor organizes design-time objects into packages. [Figure 8.3](#08_005.html#f8.3) shows the editor; on the left, you’ll see a Content folder, which contains the package hierarchy.

[![View of the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor and an Example Package Hierarchy](bilderklein/klein08_003.png)](img-f8.3.html) 

**Figure 8.3**    View of the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor and an Example Package Hierarchy

As you expand the package hierarchy nodes, you’ll probably see development artifacts, depending on what’s available within your environment. To create a repository role, right-click the package where you want to store the role and choose New • Role. A small window will appear asking for the Role Name. After entering the name, click OK, and a new tab-based window will appear on the right, as shown in [Figure 8.4](#08_005.html#f8.4). Click the Object Packages tab to manage object privileges.

[![The Object Privileges Tab in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor](bilderklein/klein08_004.png)](img-f8.4.html) 

**Figure 8.4**    The Object Privileges Tab in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor

Select or add a catalog object to manage its privileges by clicking the plus sign (+). Once you click the plus sign, the Select Object Privileges window will appear where you can search for catalog objects within SAP HANA. As demonstrated in [Section 8.5.1](#08_005.html#h8.5.1), within .hdbrole scripting, you can reference either design-time or runtime catalog objects. As shown in [Figure 8.5](#08_005.html#f8.5), the first two radio buttons in the Select Object Privileges window provides the options to filter for Design-time or Run-time objects. We highly recommend that you use design-time objects when defining repository roles. The use of design-time objects helps the internal dependency checkers used within the SAP HANA development and SAP HANA application lifecycle management. Select an object and click OK to continue, which will return you to the list of catalog objects and their privileges.

Once an object is selected, you’re now ready to grant object privileges to that objects. As shown earlier in [Figure 8.4](#08_005.html#f8.4), to the right of a selected object, you’ll see a frame called Privileges with various object privileges listed. Note that the privileges listed here are specific to the type catalog object selected. To grant these privileges, select the checkbox next to each privilege name. When finished, click the Save All icon to save and activate the repository role.

[![Repository Role and Select Object Privilege GUI with Various Filtering Options](bilderklein/klein08_005.png)](img-f8.5.html) 

**Figure 8.5**    Repository Role and Select Object Privilege GUI with Various Filtering Options

By avoiding the need for SQL or repository role scripts to define a security model with repository roles, users will find this GUI to be an efficient alternative. The GUI is easy to use and alleviates the need for security developers to memorize SQL statements or script syntax.

So far, we’ve reviewed the process for granting catalog object privileges using SQL statements, the SAP HANA cockpit, script-based repository roles, and now GUI-based repository roles. In the next section, we’ll walk you through a case study to provide a real-world example of how to use catalog object privileges within a security model based on repository roles.

## 8.6    Case Study: Updating Repository Roles to Access Information Views

E-Corporation is in the processing of defining its security model using repository roles. Its security consultant directs the company to define a few necessary catalog object privileges within its base-level repository roles. Three repository roles will need to be updated: the consumer, power user, and developer roles. In the next three subsections, we’ll provide an overview of each role and the catalog object privileges required. We’ll also provide the repository role scripts that make up each of the repository roles.

### 8.6.1    Consumer

E-Corporation is building several SAP HANA information views to provide analytical query access to the data hosted in the SAP HANA system. When an information view is activated, its runtime catalog column view object is generated in the \_SYS\_BIC schema. For users to query these information views, they’ll need both catalog object and analytic privileges.

The security consultant explains that E-Corporation should simply provide the SELECT and EXECUTE catalog object privileges to the design-time versions of each calculation view and runtime SELECT access to the entire \_SYS\_BI schema. In SAP HANA terminology, a calculation view is the design-time name of an SAP HANA model, but the runtime name of that same model is called a column view. Also, the \_SYS\_BI schema contains a few non-sensitive date- and time-based tables that users might need SELECT access to.

Because total information view access is a component of both SELECT catalog object privileges on column views and granted analytics privileges, E-Corporation can provide data security via dynamic analytic privileges and SELECT access via catalog object privileges. E-Corporation has also chosen to restrict access to individual column views within the \_SYS\_BIC schema so that users only see the column views (or models) that they have corresponding analytic privilege access to.

The consumer role will be created within the Security.Roles package hierarchy. The security consultant recommends that the consumer role be set up based on the script shown in [Listing 8.5](#08_006.html#l8.5).

```
role Security.Roles::CONSUMER extends role sap.hana.xs.formLogin.profile::ProfileOwner, sap.bc.ina.service.v2.userRole::INA_USER
{
catalog schema "_SYS_BI": SELECT, EXECUTE;
sql object e-corp.sales.models::SCV_CUSTOMER_SALES: SELECT;
analytic privilege : Security.AP:AP_CUSTOMER_SALES.analyticprivilege;

}
```

**Listing 8.5**    Consumer Repository Role Syntax

E-Corporation’s security developers decide to use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor to develop and activate their script-based repository roles. [Figure 8.6](#08_006.html#f8.6) shows an example script in the package hierarchy on the left and open in the script editor window on the right.

[![View of the Consumer Role Script in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Text Editor](bilderklein/klein08_006.png)](img-f8.6.html) 

**Figure 8.6**    View of the Consumer Role Script in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Text Editor

### 8.6.2    Power User

The power user role will need all the privileges assigned to the consumer role, plus the ability to query the sales data mart tables and staging tables. Power users have also requested the ability to view the definition of information views defined in the e-corp package.

To facilitate these requirements, the security consultant recommends that the power user repository role script use the syntax shown in [Listing 8.6](#08_006.html#l8.6).

```
role Security.Roles::POWERUSERS extends role Security.Roles::CONSUMER
{
catalog sql object "SYS"."REPOSITORY_REST": EXECUTE;
schema Security.Schemas:SalesMart.hdbschema: SELECT, EXECUTE;
schema Security.Schemas:StagingMart.hdbschema: SELECT, EXECUTE;
package e-corp: REPO.READ;
}
```

**Listing 8.6**    Power User Repository Role Syntax

This role grants SELECT access to the SalesMart and StagingMart schemas while also granting access to the REPOSITORY\_REST system stored procedure. These users require EXECUTE access to this system procedure to view and navigate the SAP HANA package hierarchy using SAP HANA Studio or other tools that provide similar access. In addition to the catalog object privileges, power users will need READ access to the top-level e-corp package node. To include the privileges assigned to the consumer role, the syntax includes the extends role Security.Roles::consumer syntax, as shown in [Listing 8.5](#08_006.html#l8.5). Thus, the power user role also has the privileges found in the consumer role.

### 8.6.3    Developer

The developer repository role will contain several types of privileges. For this case study, we’ll focus on privileges related to catalog objects.

The security consultant has identified that developers will require a high level of access to all catalog objects associated with the SalesMart and StagingMart schemas. Developers need the ability to create catalog objects and to load data into these objects. [Listing 8.7](#08_006.html#l8.7) contains an excerpt of the script that grants the appropriate catalog schema privileges to the developer repository role.

```
role Security.Roles::DEVELOPER extends role Security.Roles::POWERUSERS, 
sap.hana.ide.roles::CatalogDeveloper, sap.hana.ide.roles::EditorDeveloper
{
catalog sql object "SYS"."REPOSITORY_REST": EXECUTE;
schema Security.Schemas:SalesMart.hdbschema: ALTER, DROP, DELETE, UPDATE, INSERT, INDEX, TRIGGER;
schema Security.Schemas:StagingMart.hdbschema: ALTER, DROP, DELETE, UPDATE, INSERT, INDEX, TRIGGER;
package e-corp: REPO.READ;
}
```

**Listing 8.7**    Excerpt from Developer Repository Role Syntax

Notice that the developer role is an extension of the power user role. Thus, you don’t need to include the privileges granted to the consumer and power user roles. (Recall that the power user role extends the consumer role.) In this way, you can cascade the granting of role privileges from the consumer role, through the power user role, to the developer role. This cascading technique minimizes the duplication of code for each repository role.

## 8.7    Summary

In this chapter, you learned about different catalog objects and their privileges. We also discussed a variety of ways you can grant catalog object privileges to users and roles. Because of the numerous benefits of repository roles, we reviewed a case study in which catalog object roles were granted.

# 9    Package Privileges

In this chapter, we’ll explore the different package privileges that you can grant to a package hierarchy and the processes you’ll use for granting them.

SAP HANA is a development platform, in addition to many of its other data management qualities. To facilitate application development, application code storage, security, and application lifecycle management, SAP HANA provides a repository. This repository is used to store design-time objects used by both the database system and the SAP HANA extended application services, classic model (SAP HANA XS). The hierarchy of this repository is organized into packages and their subpackages. Each package contains design-time development artifacts. To govern access to both packages and development artifacts, SAP HANA package privileges can be assigned to users and roles.

To understand package privileges thoroughly, you must understand the makeup of the SAP HANA development repository. In this chapter, we’ll start by discussing the SAP HANA development repository. We’ll then review the various privileges that can be granted for packages and show you how they’re granted. Let’s first discuss how the development repository is organized and managed.

## 9.1    What Is the SAP HANA Development Repository?

The SAP HANA development repository is organized into major node structures called packages. In this section, we’ll explore the hierarchical structure of this package-based repository, and we’ll explain the process for creating packages. Finally, we’ll explain the process for creating delivery units.

### 9.1.1    Structure of the Development Repository

The development repository consists of packages, logical organizational units that begin with the root node, followed by the top-level nodes, then optionally a hierarchy of subpackage nodes. [Figure 9.1](#09_001.html#f9.1) shows an example package hierarchy as viewed in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor.

[![Package and Development Artifact Hierarchy in SAP HANA Repository](bilderklein/klein09_001.png)](img-f9.1.html) 

**Figure 9.1**    Package and Development Artifact Hierarchy in SAP HANA Repository

As shown in [Figure 9.1](#09_001.html#f9.1), the root of all the packages is at the top, with the Content folder. This folder is a logical location, but privileges can be applied at this level. The logical root node is named .REPO\_PACKAGE\_ROOT; you’ll reference that name when assigning root package privileges in graphical user interfaces (GUIs) and via SQL commands. However, only top-level packages can exist under the root level. You can’t create development artifacts directly under the root node. Beneath the root are several top-level packages, for example, the package named e-corp shown in [Figure 9.1](#09_001.html#f9.1). Top-level packages can contain either subpackages or development artifacts. Several development artifacts are stored below or within the package named Roles also shown in [Figure 9.1](#09_001.html#f9.1). Package privileges can only be applied at the package level; development artifacts effectively inherit privileges from their parent or grandparent package nodes.

With this structure in mind, let’s review the process for creating packages and subpackages.

### 9.1.2    Creating Packages and Subpackages

Using the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor, you can create packages within the hierarchy. To create a top-level package, right-click the Content folder and choose New • Package. To create a subpackage within a top-level package, right-click an existing package and choose New • Package. You can also use the keyboard shortcut (Ctrl)+(Alt)+(Shift)+(N) as an alternative to the right-click menu to launch the package creation process. Once you start the process, the Create Package popup window will appear. [Figure 9.2](#09_001.html#f9.2) shows an example of the window that will appear where you can define the package.

[![Naming Your Package in the Create Package Popup Window](bilderklein/klein09_002.png)](img-f9.2.html) 

**Figure 9.2**    Naming Your Package in the Create Package Popup Window

Enter the Package Name in the provided field. Enter a text description to help others identify the purpose of the package in the Description field. The remaining Responsible and Original Language fields are additional, optional metadata fields. Click the Create button, and a new package will appear in the hierarchy below the node where you started the creation process. You can repeat this process for each new top-level node or subpackage that is required to secure and organize your development artifacts.

### 9.1.3    Overview of Delivery Units

Delivery units play a role in the lifecycle management of packages. Before you can export content to a file or transport development content from one SAP HANA system to another, you must first assign a package or package hierarchy to a delivery unit. A delivery unit should contain package and development artifacts that are associated with each other. For example, a web-based application developed in the XS engine and its associated package hierarchy can be assigned to a single delivery unit. Using a delivery unit allows the content to be transported in an organized and consistent manner.

Once content is organized into a delivery unit, you can export the delivery unit to a compressed file, which then can be imported into another SAP HANA system for the purposes of transporting the code. Using SAP HANA application lifecycle management, you can also transport delivery units between systems. A delivery unit can also serve as an external code backup and can be imported back into the originating SAP HANA system if content needs to be restored.

Note that an administrator must define the vendor ID or content vendor within the system configuration before content can be assigned to a delivery unit. This vendor definition is configured in the indexserver.ini file under the repository option and content\_vendor key. Specify a value that will identify your organization’s name; for example, you could enter a domain name, such as “e-corp.com.”

The user creating the delivery unit must have privileges similar to those assigned to the default role sap.hana.xs.lm.roles::Administrator. Note that the INIFILE admin system privilege, found in this default role, is only necessary for defining the content vendor. A custom role should be created for developers that create delivery units to avoid granting them access to make configuration changes to the SAP HANA system.

###### Additional Information about Delivery Units

For additional information pertaining to the creation and management of delivery units, refer to the SAP HANA Application Lifecycle Management Guide, available at [http://s-prs.co/v498206](http://s-prs.co/v498206).

## 9.2    What Are Package Privileges?

Package privileges are organized into two broad categories: native package privileges and imported package privileges. Native package privileges refer to packages and their child development artifacts developed from scratch in an SAP HANA system. You should expect to create and edit native content in a development system. Imported package privileges represent packages and their child development artifacts that are imported into a system. These objects are created in a remote system, exported, and then imported into a different system.

As noted earlier, packages are nodes organized in a parent-child relationship. Together, these nodes make up the SAP HANA repository. Each package contains a subpackage or one or more development artifacts. Package privileges are assigned for a package node; development artifacts can’t be granted privileges individually or explicitly. However, development artifacts do inherit the privileges assigned to their parent and grandparent package nodes.

Inheritance can simplify the design of a security model. For example, you can establish privileges for a top-level package and assume that all child objects will inherit the same privileges. You won’t need to explicitly configure privileges for each child package or subpackage within the repository. Inheritance simplifies the design of repository roles because you won’t need to address package privileges each time a new package or development artifact is created.

In addition to its benefits, inheritance also introduces some risks, depending on the placement of critical development artifacts such as repository roles. For example, repository roles must be stored in an isolated location to prevent privilege elevation by users that don’t manage roles or the assignment of privileges. Stored procedures used to provision users must also be stored in an isolated location for the same reasons. Therefore, inheritance can also present challenges to a security model that leverages development artifacts.

When the system validates access to a development artifact, it first checks the privileges assigned to the direct parent package. If no privileges have been assigned to the direct parent, the system will continue to traverse up the hierarchy, checking each grandparent node until it can validate the requested action. If no parent or grandparent node has assigned privileges for that user, the user fails authorization and is considered not authorized to perform the requested action.

Development artifacts use a bottom-up approach to authorization validation. Therefore, you don’t have to explicitly assign privileges to each parent and grandparent package node; you only need to grant privileges to its closest desired parent or grandparent package, and no privileges need to be established specifically for a given user at each level of the package hierarchy. Be sure you understand this point because experienced security professionals might assume that development artifacts use a top-down approach based on inheritance and might then overengineer the security model.

Native package privileges apply to objects that are directly created, maintained, and activated within a particular originating environment. For example, if you create a repository role within a development system, that role will always remain a native object within that system. The native package privileges are as follows:

*   REPO.READ  
    This package privilege grants read access to a package and its child objects. This privilege applies to both native and imported objects.
    
*   REPO.EDIT\_NATIVE\_OBJECTS  
    This package privilege grants edit privileges to design-time objects within a package. This privilege only applies to native objects or those created within an originating system.
    
*   REPO.ACTIVATE\_NATIVE\_OBJECTS  
    This package privilege grants the ability to create, activate, or reactivate design-time objects within a package. This privilege only applies to native objects or those created within an originating system.
    
*   REPO.MAINTAIN\_NATIVE\_PACKAGES  
    This package privilege grants the ability to edit and create packages and subpackages. This privilege only applies to native packages or those created within an originating system.
    

Imported package privileges are as follows:

*   REPO.EDIT\_IMPORTED\_OBJECTS  
    This package privilege grants edit privileges to design-time objects within a package. This privilege only applies to imported objects or those imported from a delivery unit.
    
*   REPO.ACTIVATE\_IMPORTED \_OBJECTS  
    This package grants that ability to create, activate or reactivate design-time objects within a package. This privilege only applies to imported objects or those imported from a delivery unit.
    
*   REPO.MAINTAIN\_IMPORTED\_PACKAGES  
    This package privilege grants the ability to edit and create packages and subpackages. This privilege only applies to imported packages or those imported from a delivery unit.
    

## 9.3    Granting Package Privileges

In this section, we’ll review four options available for granting package privileges: via SQL commands, the SAP HANA cockpit, the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, and repository-based role scripts/the repository-based role editor.

### 9.3.1    Granting Package Privileges with SQL

Using the SQL console, you can grant access to a package in the SAP HANA repository using the following SQL syntax:

```
GRANT <PACKAGE_PRIVILEGE> ON <"package.subpackage"> TO <GRANTEE> WITH GRANT 
OPTION;
```

The <PACKAGE\_PRIVILEGE> variable can be replaced with a comma-separated array of package privileges. The <"package.subpackage"> variable can be replaced by the case-sensitive name of the package and subpackage hierarchy. When constructing a complete package name, each node of the package hierarchy should be separated by a period. The WITH GRANT OPTION allows the grantee to grant the same privileges to other users. The <GRANTEE> can either be a role or a user account. For example, you can use the following SQL statement:

```
GRANT REPO.READ, REPO.EDIT_NATIVE_OBJECTS ON "e-corp" TO JONATHAN WITH GRANT 
OPTION;
```

To remove package privileges, use the REVOKE SQL statement. The following SQL statement will remove the privileges specified in the <PACKAGE\_PRIVILEGES> variable array:

```
REVOKE <PACKAGE_PRIVILEGE> ON <"package.subpackage"> FROM <GRANTEE>;
```

The following statement is a more concrete example:

```
REVOKE REPO.EDIT_NATIVE_OBJECTS ON "e-corp" FROM JONATHAN;
```

### 9.3.2    Granting Package Privileges with the SAP HANA Cockpit

Let’s review the workflows necessary to grant and revoke package privileges with the SAP HANA cockpit. As an alternative to using SQL statements, you can use the SAP HANA cockpit options called Assign Privileges or Manage Roles. Each interface allows you to both grant and revoke package privileges for a given user account or for a given role. Most users will find using the SAP HANA cockpit easier than memorizing and entering in SQL statements.

To access the Assign Privileges or Manage Roles interfaces, start at the SAP HANA cockpit Home screen, locate an SAP HANA system in the Resource Directory. Connect to the desired tenant database or SYSTEMDB, which will take you to the System Overview window. Using the Filter by Area dropdown list, choose the option Security. Locate the Assign Privileges or Manage Roles in the User & Role Management tile.

[Section 9.3](#09_003.html#h9.3) shows the Assign Privileges interface within the SAP HANA cockpit for the TEST\_01 user account. In the windows, you’ll see several tabs representing privilege categories, such as the System Privileges, Object Privileges, Analytic Privileges, Application Privileges, Package Privileges, and Privileges on Users tabs. You’ll find a similar interface when working with roles. However, the Role Details GUI has an additional link labeled Roles where you can grant existing roles to the selected role.

[![Managing Package Privileges Assigned to a User Account in the SAP HANA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein09_003.png)](img-f9.3.html) 

**Figure 9.3**    Managing Package Privileges Assigned to a User Account in the SAP HANA Cockpit

The fifth tab in the Assign Privileges window is named Package Privileges. Use this tab to list, grant, or revoke package privileges for a given grantee. As shown in [Section 9.3](#09_003.html#h9.3), the packages and privileges listed in this interface have already been granted to the grantee. If the list is blank, nothing is currently granted. To grant a Package Privilege, click the Edit button located on the far-right side of the interface near the Search field. Once you click the Edit button, new buttons labeled Cancel, add Package, Change Privileges, and Remove Package will appear. Click the Add Package button to open the Select Packages popup window. Within this window, you’ll see a search bar and a list of existing packages within the repository. Use the search bar to filter the list based on the entered text. Then, scroll through the list and select the package you want to configure.

Click the desired package, and the Add Package with Privileges window will appear. In this window, you’ll see a list of possible package privileges that can be assigned. Select the checkbox beside each privilege you want to grant. In addition, for each privilege, you can use the Yes/No Grantable to Others slider to allow the privilege to be granted to other users. Click the OK button located at the bottom right of the interface to continue.

You should now see the selected packages and the privileges you assigned listed in the Package Privileges tab, as shown in [Section 9.3](#09_003.html#h9.3).

To revoke a package privilege, click an assigned package and its assigned privilege from the list and then click the Remove Package button to revoke the privilege. To make the changes active, click the Save button or continue making other changes if necessary. Note that, once the Save button is clicked, you’ll be returned to the list of privileges and be required to click the Edit button again to make further changes.

To change assigned package privileges, while in Edit mode, click an assigned object and its assigned privilege from the list and then click the Change Privileges button to open a new popup window with the title Change Privileges of concatenated with the name of the package. A list of assigned and unassigned privileges for the package will appear. Select the checkbox to grant the privilege or deselect the checkbox to revoke the privilege. Use the Yes/No Grantable to Others slider button to manage the grantable to others privilege. Click the OK button at the bottom right of the window to apply your changes. Again, to make these changes active, click the Save button or continue making other changes if necessary until you’re ready to activate all changes.

### 9.3.3    Granting Package Privileges with the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, hosted within the XS engine, provides an interface that you can use to create users, create roles, or manage security for standard roles. This interface provides another web-based alternative to the SAP HANA cockpit and also serves as an alternative to issuing GRANT and REVOKE statements with SQL.

You can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench via a supported Internet browser. The following two URLs can be customized to match the details of your environment:

*   http://sap-hana.myhost.com:8000/sap/hana/ide/security
    
*   http://<sap\_hana\_host>:80<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/security
    

In the last example, replace <sap\_hana\_host> with the host name of the SAP HANA system in your environment. Replace <instance\_number> with the two-digit instance number corresponding to your SAP HANA system.

For secure access, the following examples should help you construct the correct URL:

*   https://<sap\_hana\_host>:43<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/security
    
*   https://sap-hana.myhost.com:4300/sap/hana/ide/security
    

Once you have access to the security manager, expand the Security node on the right. Expand Users to reveal a list of user accounts or expand Roles to reveal a list of roles. Double-click a grantee to open the management interface for the given item. With the selected grantee management window open, you can begin granting and revoking package privileges. [Figure 9.4](#09_003.html#f9.4) shows the Package Privileges management tab.

[![Managing Package Privileges in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Security Manager](bilderklein/klein09_004.png)](img-f9.4.html) 

**Figure 9.4**    Managing Package Privileges in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Security Manager

To add a package and configure its privileges, click the plus sign (+) and search for the desired package hierarchy level. The Find Package search interface window will appear where you can search for and select one or more package levels. Select the packages you want to secure and click the OK button to return to the previous screen where you can grant the desired package privileges. Again, [Figure 9.4](#09_003.html#f9.4) shows an example of the Package Privileges interface where you can assign packages and grant privileges.

To save your changes, press (Ctrl)+(S) or click the disk icon to save and activate the privilege. To revoke a package privilege or make changes, select the package hierarchy level from the list and click the red X to remove the package from the grantee and revoke all its privileges. To make changes, highlight the package in the list to reveal the Privileges for frame to its right. Select or deselect the checkboxes for each privilege to achieve your desired result. Once again, click Save to activate the changes in the database.

If any activation issues arise, warning messages will appear in the status frame at the bottom of the user management window. The status frame has a dark background. Error messages will appear in red text.

### 9.3.4    Granting Package Privileges within Repository-Based Roles

In [Chapter 6](#06_001.html#h6), we discussed the importance of using repository-based roles as the foundation for your security model. We also thoroughly discussed the workflows for creating repository-based roles. For a complete review of repository roles, refer to [Chapter 6](#06_001.html#h6). In this section, we’ll provide a summary of the workflows used to grant or revoke package privileges within repository-based roles, either via design-time scripts or via the role management options in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench repository.

#### Granting and Revoking Privileges with Design-Time Scripts

When defining package privileges within repository-based role scripts, you must start the line with the term package, then include the name of the package hierarchy node. After the package name, include a single colon. After the colon, include a comma-separated list of package privileges. At the end of the statement, include a semicolon to finish the line.

The following example is a single line of code that grants multiple privileges to the e-corp.sales package:

```
Package e-corp.sales: REPO.READ, REPO.ACTIVATE_NATIVE_OBJECTS, REPO.MAINTAIN_NATIVE_PACKAGES, REPO.EDIT_IMPORTED_OBJECTS;
```

The following example is a single line of code that grants a single privilege to a single package:

```
Package e-corp.sales: REPO.READ;
```

To grant the root package privilege, use the system-defined package name value, .REPO\_PACKAGE\_ROOT, to represent privileges that will be applied to all packages, as in the following statement:

```
package .REPO_PACKAGE_ROOT: REPO.READ;
```

#### Using the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench GUI

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor, hosted within the XS engine, provides an interface to manage and create repository roles. The interface looks a lot like the standard role management options in SAP HANA Studio, but the role objects it creates are profoundly different: The editor creates repository-based roles. The objects created in the editor also can be opened in the SAP HANA Studio developer perspective, which means that you can use either the SAP HANA Studio interface or the script editor to manage repository roles.

You can access SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench via a supported Internet browser. The following two URLs can be customized to match the details of your environment:

*   http://sap-hana.myhost.com:8000/sap/hana/ide/editor
    
*   http://<sap\_hana\_host>:80<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/editor
    

In the last example, replace <sap\_hana\_host> with the host name of the SAP HANA system in your environment and <instance\_number> with the two-digit instance number corresponding to your SAP HANA system.

For secure access, the following examples should help you construct the correct URL:

*   https://<sap\_hana\_host>:43<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/editor
    
*   https://sap-hana.myhost.com:4300/sap/hana/ide/editor
    

Once you have access to the editor, expand the Content node on the right, then expand Packages to reveal a list of packages defined in the system. You’ll typically create a top-level package named Security to host such objects.

To create a repository role, right-click the package in which you want to store it. From the context menu, choose New • Role, as shown in [Figure 9.5](#09_003.html#f9.5).

A small window named New Role will appear. Enter the desired name of the role and click Create. A new tabbed window will appear in the large frame on the right. The tab’s label should match the provided name of the repository role. The new window will contain a series of subtabs: Granted Roles, System Privileges, Object Privileges, Analytic Privileges, Package Privileges, and Application Privileges. Each tab allows security administrators define privileges specific to that tab. Let’s now take a closer look at the process required for configuring the Package Privileges tab.

[![Navigating the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor and Creating a Repository Role](bilderklein/klein09_005.png)](img-f9.5.html) 

**Figure 9.5**    Navigating the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor and Creating a Repository Role

Click the Package Privileges tab to reveal an interface via which you can add or remove package privileges. To add a package, click the large plus sign (+) on the subtab header. The Select Package window will appear, as shown in [Figure 9.6](#09_003.html#f9.6).

[![Selecting and Assigning Package Privileges in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench](bilderklein/klein09_006.png)](img-f9.6.html) 

**Figure 9.6**    Selecting and Assigning Package Privileges in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

Within the window, a search box will appear. In the search box, enter a portion of the package name to narrow the results. Alternatively, you can scroll through the unfiltered list to locate the desired package by its complete hierarchical name. Select one or more objects within the list, holding down the (Ctrl) key while clicking to select multiple items. The selected items are highlighted with a light blue color. Click the OK button at the bottom of the window to finalize the selection. The selected packages will now appear in the Package Privileges tab, as shown in [Figure 9.7](#09_003.html#f9.7).

[![Selected Packages and Their Privileges Listed in Package Privileges Tab](bilderklein/klein09_007.png)](img-f9.7.html) 

**Figure 9.7**    Selected Packages and Their Privileges Listed in Package Privileges Tab

With the objects listed, you’ll now need to assign the various package privileges to each selected package. To specify the privileges for an individual package, select and highlight the package within the list on the left. To the right of the selected package, a series of privileges and corresponding checkboxes will appear, as shown on the right of [Figure 9.7](#09_003.html#f9.7).

Select the checkbox beside each privilege to assign the selected privilege to the selected package. Repeat the process for all packages. To remove the privilege, simply deselect the checkbox beside the privilege you want to remove.

To remove an assigned package and all its privileges, select an object from the list on the left, then click the large minus sign (–) above the list to remove the package. Items in the list must be deleted one at a time.

Once you’ve configured the desired list of packages and established their privileges, click the Save All button at the top left, which looks like three stacked floppy disks.

If any issues arise when saving and activating the repository role, messages will appear in red text within the console window just below the opened Repository Roles tab. The console window has a dark background and is located at the bottom of the open tab. Affirmative messages will appear in white text, and error messages will appear in red text.

To close the Repository Roles tab, click the small X to the right of the tab.

## 9.4    Case Study: Preventing Content Developers from Elevating Their Privileges

E-Corporation has several developers using the SAP HANA system to create information views and custom applications within the SAP HANA XS engine. The company also relies heavily on the use of repository-based roles to support its security model. Because developers and security administrators both require access to the same repository, E-Corporation management is concerned that developers might have access to the repository roles. If developers were to gain access, they could edit the repository roles and grant their assigned roles additional privileges. In the following sections, we’ll look at E-Corporation’s current security model before discussing some changes the company can make to improve it.

### 9.4.1    Assessing the Current Configuration

E-Corporation requests that the company’s security consultant review the security model and repository structure to make sure the company has properly secured access to its repository-based roles. To properly assess the current design, the security consultant creates a diagram to outline the current package hierarchy, as shown in [Figure 9.8](#09_004.html#f9.8).

[![Current E-Corporation Package Hierarchy](bilderklein/klein09_008.png)](img-f9.8.html) 

**Figure 9.8**    Current E-Corporation Package Hierarchy

E-Corporation currently stores all security-related artifacts, including repository roles, in the E-corp.Admins.Security package. The parent package, E-corp.Admins, contains system administration-related development artifacts. The E-corp package is configured as a structural package, which prevents development artifacts from being created directly under the E-corp top-level package.

In addition to assessing the package hierarchy, the consultant requests a listing of all roles that are assigned package privileges for the ROOT, E-corp, E-corp.Admins, and E-corp.Admins.Security nodes. [Table 9.1](#09_004.html#t9.1) outlines the role types and package privileges assigned for each package node.

 
| Role Type || Package Node || Assigned Package Privileges |
| --- | --- | --- |
| System administrators || ROOT || All |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Developers || E-corp || REPO.READ |
| System administrators || E-corp.Admins || All |
| Role managers || E-corp.Admins.Security || All |

**Table 9.1**    Roles with Access to ROOT, Administration, and Security Packages at E‐Corporation
