Based on the provided information, system administrators have full access to all packages in E-Corporation’s SAP HANA system. Developers can review all content created under the top-level E-corp node, system administrators are again granted full access to the E-corp.Admins node, and role managers are granted full package access to the E-corp.Admins.Security node. With this information, the security consultant determines that several changes could be implemented to improve the overall security of the environment, as we’ll discuss next.

### 9.4.2    Recommendations

The consultant recommends changes to both the package hierarchy and the package privileges that are assigned the role types at E-Corporation. The predominant recommendation is that only security managers should have access to elevate the privileges assigned within repository roles. System administrators should not have access to create or edit existing repository roles because of the need for the separation of duties at E-Corporation. To achieve this separation, changes related to the package hierarchy and the package privileges assigned to roles are needed.

#### Changes to the Package Hierarchy

E-Corporation’s current package hierarchy places repository roles in the E-corp.Admins.Security package. This design allows repository roles to reside in a dedicated package but complicates the design of the security model. Recall that you can’t explicitly deny privileges in SAP HANA, and packages inherit the privileges assigned to parent and grandparent nodes. If a role is assigned privileges at a parent or grandparent node, child nodes will inherit those privileges. You have no option to break this inheritance or to explicitly deny a privilege on a child node. The current design grants full access to the system administrators, even though they were not explicitly granted full access on the E-corp.Admins.Security node. This problem is due to the inheritance of privileges assigned at the ROOT and E-corp.Admins nodes. The design also grants REPO.READ access to all developers. Although read access for developers is not a significant concern, it does highlight the importance of calculating the risk of accidental privilege inheritance within the package hierarchy. For example, the security team might accidently grant the REPO.EDIT\_NATIVE\_OBJECTS developer role to the E-corp package node, which would grant developers edit access to the repository roles via inheritance.

The security consultant recommends a simple change to the hierarchy. Given the significance of inheritance and the likelihood of accidental privilege elevation through inheritance, he recommends that the Security package node move to the top level of the hierarchy. In this way, only ROOT\-level package privileges will present a challenge to the security model design. Furthermore, the security consultant recommends that the Security.Roles, Security.UserProvisioning, and Security.Schemas packages be created to better organize and potentially restrict security-related development artifacts. [Figure 9.9](#09_004.html#f9.9) shows an example of the recommended package hierarchy for E-Corporation.

[![Recommended E-Corporation Package Hierarchy](bilderklein/klein09_009.png)](img-f9.9.html) 

**Figure 9.9**    Recommended E-Corporation Package Hierarchy

#### Role Types and Changes to Their Package Privileges

With the Security package configured as a top-level package, several changes to the roles will need to be implemented, as listed in [Table 9.2](#09_004.html#t9.2).

 
| Role Type || Package Node || Assigned Package Privileges |
| --- | --- | --- |
| System administrators || ROOT || REPO.READ, REPO\_MAINTAIN\_NATIVE\_PACKAGES, REPO\_MAINTAIN\_IMPORTED\_PACKAGES |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Developers || E-corp || None |
| Developers || E-corp.Sales || All |
| System administrators || E-corp.Admins || All |
| Role managers || Security || All |

**Table 9.2**    Recommended Role Types and Package Privileges for E-Corporation

Starting with the system administrators, the consultant recommends that their ROOT\-level package privileges be limited to REPO.READ, REPO, REPO\_MAINTAIN\_NATIVE\_PACKAGES, and REPO\_MAINTAIN\_IMPORTED\_PACKAGES, which will allow them to add package nodes at any level without automatically being granted privileges to activate or modify existing development artifacts within existing packages. The Grantable to Others or WITH GRANT option must not be assigned to the system administrators role type, to prevent them from assigning their package privileges to other users or standard roles. System administrators can be granted full access to the E-corp.Admins package because it contains their development-related artifacts. This package should be the only area in which system administrators can activate or modify content.

Unless justified, developer’s role should not receive REPO.READ privileges on the top-level E-corp package node. Developers should only be granted privileges on the nodes containing their development artifacts. For example, for the E-corp.sales package node, they might have full access to create SAP HANA information views. Developers don’t require REPO.READ on parent or grandparent nodes to work within their designated packages. Recall that package privileges are evaluated from the bottom up; therefore, you won’t need to grant REPO.READ access for each parent or grandparent level of the package hierarchy. Developers will be able to navigate the package hierarchy because of this bottom-up evaluation.

The managers role should be granted full access to the top-level package security. This top-level package is where role managers will create development artifacts used for the security model.

Overall, the recommended changes will create a more secure environment. Moving the security package to the top level will reduce the likelihood of both accidental and deliberate privilege elevation within the environment. Adding a few additional subpackages within the Security node helps better organize security-related development artifacts. By preventing system administrators from having full access at the ROOT node, E-Corporation can better ensure that only role managers are able to manage repository roles within the environment.

## 9.5    Summary

Securing the package hierarchy plays an important role in any security model. Package privileges are divided into two broad categories: privileges for native content and privileges for imported content. When repository-based roles are used within the model, you must ensure that only role managers can modify repository roles. In addition, you must establish the appropriate security to support development activities within the environment. Inheritance can be both beneficial and risky when leveraged to implement package privileges.

# 10    Analytic Privileges

In this chapter, we’ll explore analytic privileges and describe how you can use these privileges to secure access to SAP HANA information views and data.

Analytic privileges grant or restrict access to data hosted within the SAP HANA system. These privileges provide two levels of access. First, they provide read-only access to information views. Assuming that the information view requires an analytics privilege check, to query an information view, you must have an associated analytic privilege; in other words, users can’t query an information view unless they’re granted an analytic privilege referencing that information view or an analytic privilege that applies to all information views. Second, analytic privileges can be configured to restrict the data that an information view returns when queried. At a high level, this data restriction is achieved by filtering the attribute data during query execution. When using analytic privileges to filter data, each user accessing an information view will require his own unique user account, which becomes the basis for filtering the data.

In this chapter, we’ll provide an overview of analytic privileges and discuss the differences between static and dynamic analytic privileges. We’ll also discuss how classic XML-based analytic privileges are being replaced with the new SQL-based analytic privileges, and we’ll explain how to manage and create static and dynamic privileges. Finally, we’ll review the process used to troubleshoot a grantee’s effective analytic privileges and discuss the processes available to grant analytic privileges.

However, before we can begin discussing analytic privileges, first you’ll need understand a few basics about SAP HANA information views, which we’ll discuss next.

## 10.1    What Are SAP HANA Information Views?

Information view is a generic term describing any of the components used to create metadata-rich, multidimensional models within the SAP HANA system. In addition to SAP HANA’s ability to store data in columnar tables, you can also create information views to consolidate the complex relationships between tables and data elements. Information views are typically used to produce analytical models that aggregate quantifiable data elements by various attributes. For example, an information view for Controlling and Profitability Analysis (CO-PA) in SAP ERP can be created to generate analytics for gross margin by time, material, customer, market, and region, attributes that become the basis for restricting the data using analytic privileges.

Three main types of information views exist in SAP HANA: attribute views, analytic views, and calculation views. In this section, we’ll briefly discuss these three view types and how they relate to analytic privileges.

### 10.1.1    Attribute Views

Attribute views are models created to produce views of master data. For example, a customer attribute view would generate columns such as customer ID, customer name, customer address line 1, customer region, customer sales region, and many more customer-related attributes. Attribute views are objects that help associated attributes with measures within analytic views. These reusable objects can be associated with multiple analytic views. On their own, attribute views don’t create a complete multidimensional model. They simply model the master data that will be used within a multidimensional model. Each column within an attribute view is a candidate for filtering through an analytic privilege. For example, you can limit the customers returned in a query based on the sales region attribute column.

Starting with SAP HANA 1.0 SPS 07, SAP replaced attribute views with a new type of calculation view: dimensional calculation views. Dimensional calculation views are defined when you initially create the calculation view within the various graphical user interfaces (GUIs). When creating the view, you’ll notice the Dimension option when defining the view’s Data Category. Dimensional calculation views support more advanced transformations like the use of ranking and unions, which is appealing from a modeling standpoint. These views also allow SAP to maintain a single user interface for all calculation view types. Another main difference with a dimensional calculation view is that their final transformation node is always a projection node, meaning the view will produce a flat dataset without aggregating the results.

###### Differences between SAP HANA 1.0 and SAP HANA 2.0

With SAP HANA 1.0 through SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, attribute views can only be created using SAP HANA Studio and cannot be created using the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor. In addition, as SAP has transitioned SAP HANA extended application services, classic model (SAP HANA XS) to SAP HANA extended application services, advanced model (SAP HANA XSA), SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA can be used for creating SAP HANA dimensional calculation views.

### 10.1.2    Analytic Views

Analytic views are models that connect one or more attribute views to quantifiable transactions. Within analytic views, you can define measure objects to aggregate values within specific tables. The combination of attribute views and analytic views create a complete multidimensional model. These views can answer analytic questions, such as the following: What are my sales by region? Which are my top 10 customers by gross margin? What quantity did we sell in January of 2016? What is the current balance of the expense account?

Starting with SAP HANA 1.0 SPS 07, SAP replaced analytics views with a new type of calculation view: star join calculation views. Star join calculation views are calculation views with unique settings and a specific composition. When creating the view, you’ll notice the option Cube under the Data Category dropdown list and the additional With Star Join setting checkbox. If these options are selected properly, you’ll find a unique star join transformation node within the definition of the calculation view.

Star join calculation views support more advanced transformations like the use of ranking, measures from multiple tables, and unions before the star join node, which is appealing from a modeling standpoint. These views also allowed SAP to maintain a single user interface for all calculation view types. Another main difference with a star join calculation view is that their final transformation node is always a star join node followed by an aggregation node. Another unique aspect of the star join is that it is designed to join dimensional calculi on views only. In this way, a star join calculation view is almost identical to the legacy analytics view.

Nonaggregate columns within analytic views or star join calculation views can be filtered using analytic privileges. With both analytic views and star join calculation views, the attribute views or dimensional calculation views within each play a role in the analytic privilege evaluation. In general terms, a user must have access directly to the analytic view or star join views as well as their constituent attribute views or dimensional calculation views.

###### Differences between SAP HANA 1.0 and SAP HANA 2.0

With SAP HANA 1.0 through SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, analytic views can only be created using SAP HANA Studio and cannot be created using the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor. In addition, as SAP has transitioned the SAP HANA XS to the SAP HANA XSA platform, SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA can be used for creating SAP HANA star join calculation views.

### 10.1.3    Calculation Views

Historically, standard calculation views were the third type of information view available within SAP HANA. You could use these views to perform complex calculations, scripted calculations, and complex denormalizations of data. Given the advent of dimensional calculation views and star join calculation views, determining exactly when to use a standard calculation view can be confusing. However, without going into too much detail, the use of standard calculation views has not evolved recently.

Standard calculation views are defined with the Data Category option Cube only. The With Star Join option should not be configured in this case. In many cases, you’ll use these views to merge multiple star join calculation views or to create user-specific query type models to accommodate user demand and requirements. However, from the perspective of analytic privileges, they can also be secured like all other types of information views. Attribute columns within the final semantic node of the view can be leveraged with static or dynamic filter conditions to secure access to the data.

## 10.2    What Are Analytic Privileges?

Analytic privileges govern access to data made available through SAP HANA’s information views. Two types of analytic privileges exist: classic XML-based and SQL-based. XML-based analytic privileges are a legacy type of analytic privilege. These privileges manage access to information views and provide both simple and dynamic filtering capabilities. SQL-based analytic privileges offer the ability to govern access to both information views and catalog database views. These privileges also offer the ability to implement more complex filter logic using subquery statements, which overcomes some of the limitations associated with the filter logic available with XML-based analytic privileges.

### 10.2.1    XML-Based Analytic Privileges

Like all analytic privileges, XML-based analytic privileges provide a twofold level of access. First, XML-based analytic privileges grant read access to the information views associated with the analytic privilege. Within the SAP HANA, we refer to them as secured models. In most security models, every information view will be associated with at least one analytic privilege, which will then be assigned to a role. When an analytic privilege is assigned to a role, grantees of that role will have read access to the information views.

Second, data restrictions can be applied within analytic privileges to statically or dynamically filter the data based on specified filter criteria. In the world of business intelligence, we call this row-level security. Rows of data are strategically filtered to restrict a user’s access to specific rows of data. For example, if the security administrator needs to restrict data so that regional managers can only see records associated with their region, he’d use analytic privileges to do so.

XML-based analytic privileges provide two different types of restriction to filter data. You can define static analytic privileges using static filter conditions or dynamic analytic privileges that will dynamically look up filter conditions on a user-by-user basis. Let’s look at these options in more detail.

#### Static Analytic Privileges

The methodology behind static analytic privileges dictates that an analytic privilege object be created for each unique filter scenario. For example, if your organization wanted to filter its information views for 10 different regions, you would need to define 10 different analytic privilege objects within the repository. You would probably define 10 different roles for each analytic privilege and assign user accounts one or more corresponding roles for matching filter conditions. [Figure 10.1](#10_002.html#f10.1) shows how the mapping between static analytic privileges and roles/users typically would be set up.

[![Static Analytic Privileges Mapped to Roles and Users](bilderklein/klein10_001.png)](img-f10.1.html) 

**Figure 10.1**    Static Analytic Privileges Mapped to Roles and Users

Let’s assume that each analytic privilege filters the sales region attribute column within each assigned information view. For example, the attribute column SALES\_REGION = 'NORTH' would be applied to the analytic privilege AP\_STATIC\_REGION\_NORTH, and the SALES\_REGION = 'SOUTH EAST' condition would be applied to the analytic privilege AP\_STATIC\_REGION\_SOUTH\_EAST. As shown in [Figure 10.1](#10_002.html#f10.1), each filter condition would require an analytic privilege, and each analytic privilege would require a role. Each user can be granted one or more roles.

Each analytic privilege can be assigned one or more filter conditions or restrictions. When multiple conditions are configured within the same analytic privilege, they’re executed using an AND condition, which means that all filter conditions or restrictions must be true. For example, if you configured an analytic privilege with the conditions SALES\_REGION = 'NORTH' AND SELLING\_PLANT = 'Chicago North', only data records that fulfill both conditions would be returned when queried.

When a user is assigned one or more analytic privileges, the overall filter condition is executed using an OR condition, which means that either of the restrictions in each individual analytic privilege can be true. For example, a user is granted two roles, each with its own unique analytic privileges. The first role’s analytic privilege requires the SALES\_REGION = 'NORTH' restriction, and the second role’s analytic privilege requires the SALES\_REGION = 'SOUTH\_EAST' restriction. When the user queries the assigned information view, the query would result in records with SALES\_REGION of either NORTH or SOUTH\_EAST.

Static analytic privileges are effective at providing data-level security. However, as shown in [Figure 10.1](#10_002.html#f10.1), each unique filter condition requires an analytic privilege object and role. If your organization requires a large quantity of restrictions on a variety of different attribute columns, you’ll need to create and maintain a significant number of objects. This proliferation of objects can produce management issues in most SAP HANA systems. Let’s look at how dynamic analytic privileges can help to solve this problem.

#### Dynamic Analytic Privileges

The methodology behind dynamic analytic privileges allows a single analytic privilege object to dynamically look up restrictions based on one or more data elements. Dynamic analytic privileges significantly reduce the number of objects required to support a large and diverse set of restrictions. [Figure 10.2](#10_002.html#f10.2) shows an overview of the objects required to implement dynamic analytic privileges.

Dynamic analytic privileges work by retrieving the filter criteria from a catalog table within the SAP HANA system. The catalog table, at a minimum, must map each SAP HANA user account to a specific data element. For example, each user account is mapped to one or more regions within a table. Users with multiple data element assignments will have multiple rows defined in the table, and each row will map the user account name to a unique data element. These data elements will be dynamically generated and applied to the analytic privilege when an associated information view is queried.

The major benefit of dynamic analytic privileges is that they reduce the number of analytic privilege and role objects required to facilitate data restrictions. For example, in the previous region-based example, using dynamic analytic privileges would require only a single analytic privilege and role. You wouldn’t need to create an analytic privilege and role for each filter condition. However, the catalog table containing the user-to-region mapping still must be maintained. In an ideal scenario, this mapping could be programmatically derived and refreshed from an external source.

[![Dynamic Analytic Privilege Mapping to Roles and Users](bilderklein/klein10_002.png)](img-f10.2.html) 

**Figure 10.2**    Dynamic Analytic Privilege Mapping to Roles and Users

### 10.2.2    SQL-Based Analytic Privileges

SQL-based analytic privileges grant access to either information views or catalog views. In this chapter, we’ll only discuss the options for restricting information views using the analytic privilege objects stored in the SAP HANA repository. Note that SQL-based analytic privileges are a type of structured privilege. Typically, when we refer to SQL-based analytic privileges, we’re referring to the graphical analytic privilege objects created in the SAP HANA repository. When working with catalog views, you’ll typically create structured privileges or refer to the restrictions as structured privileges.

Before an information view can use SQL-based analytic privileges, the view must be registered for an authorization check. When defining an information view, the option to support an analytic privilege check must be selected. This option is found under the View Properties tab of the semantics node, in the Apply Privileges dropdown list. [Figure 10.3](#10_002.html#f10.3) shows this option within an information view. Notice the View Properties tab and the Apply Privileges dropdown list with three options: SQL Analytic Privileges, Analytic Privilege, and <blank> options. You’ll find the same options when working with all calculation view types. Note that the Analytic Privilege option only applies to XML-based analytic privileges, and the blank option means that an analytic privilege check will not be performed on the information view.

[![Setting SQL Analytic Privileges Option in Information View](bilderklein/klein10_003.png)](img-f10.3.html) 

**Figure 10.3**    Setting SQL Analytic Privileges Option in Information View

SQL analytic privileges also offer you the ability to define both simple and complex data restrictions using complex SQL filter logic. They support three options for defining restrictions: static, dynamic, and SQL expression.

#### Static Analytic Privileges

Static SQL-based analytic privileges are like their XML counterparts, and they too can lead to scalability issues if your organization requires a diverse allotment of filter conditions. You can assume that all the benefits and issues associated with static XML-based privileges also apply to static SQL-based analytic privileges.

#### Dynamic Analytic Privileges

Dynamic SQL-based analytic privileges are also like their XML-based counterparts. However, SQL-based analytic privileges look up filter conditions as opposed to filter values. For example, dynamic XML-based analytic privileges will look up and return an array of values such as 10, 100, 300, 400, and 900. Dynamic SQL-based analytic privileges will look up and return a single string value, such as (CUSTOMER IN (10, 100, 300, 400, 900)). This string value can become the syntax for a condition used to filter an information view. Dynamic SQL-based analytic privileges also support more complex conditions, such as (( CUSTOMER = 900 ) or ( PLANT = 1000)). We’ll explore dynamic analytic privileges further in [Section 10.5.2](#10_005.html#h10.5.2).

#### SQL Expression Analytic Privileges

Dynamic expression-based SQL analytic privileges are unique and don’t have an XML-based counterpart. These types of analytic privileges are dynamic, but they don’t require the use of stored procedures to look up filter conditions; the filter conditions are manually crafted into a filter expression. Filter expressions support the use of subqueries and other complex operators in their definition. For example, you can use a complex subquery expression to dynamically filter data for a given user, for example, in the following example code:

```
"CUSTOMERKEY" IN     
(SELECT DISTINCT CUSTOMERKEY     
FROM "SECURITY"."Security.ap::RLS_CUSTOMER_ACCESS"    
WHERE USERNAME = SESSION_USER)
```

Expressions can be even more complex than this example, and they support a wide variety of solutions. We’ll explore expressions further in [Section 10.6](#10_006.html#h10.6).

## 10.3    \_SYS\_BI\_CP\_ALL: A System-Generated Analytic Privilege

Only one system-generated analytic privilege is included with SAP HANA by default: The system-generated analytic privilege \_SYS\_BI\_CP\_ALL is a special analytic privilege that provides access to all information views and all data produced by an information view configured using classic XML-based analytic privileges. When a grantee is granted this analytic privilege, this privilege will override the restrictions of other classic XML-based analytic privileges that have been assigned to the same grantee; therefore, this privilege should only be granted to grantees that do not require any analytic privileges.

Based on testing and research, the \_SYS\_BI\_CP\_ALL analytic privilege doesn’t override SQL-based analytic privileges. When using SQL-based analytic privileges, all users require at least one custom analytic privilege referencing each information view they want to query. To grant full access to an information view, simply reference the information view without any defined restrictions. This approach will grant such grantees full data access to the referenced information view, even if other SQL-based analytic privileges are granted to the same user. Now, let’s look at the processes for creating analytic privileges.

## 10.4    Managing Static Analytic Privileges

You can create two types of static analytic privileges: XML-based or SQL-based. Both options are nearly identical, with a few exceptions. SAP has not officially deprecated the classic XML-based option as of SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, but the documentation indicates that SAP will deprecate this option in the future. Some user interfaces (UIs) also refer to XML-based analytic privileges as the classic option. Therefore, we recommend that all new developments be based on SQL analytic privilege workflows. In this section, we’ll provide instructions for creating both types.

### 10.4.1    Creating Static XML-Based Analytic Privileges

Analytic privileges are development artifacts and, as such, are created and stored in the SAP HANA repository. Typically, they’re stored in a package with limited access. For example, the same package structure that stores repository roles would be an ideal location. This package structure should already be set up so that only role administrators have the proper package privileges. Developers must have the appropriate package privileges to create and activate these development artifacts.

To create an analytic privilege, open the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor. Within the content repository, locate a package in a secure location. Right-click the package and choose New • Analytic Privilege…. A popup window will appear labeled New Analytic Privilege, as shown in [Figure 10.4](#10_004.html#f10.4).

In this window, specify the technical name of the analytic privilege in the Name\* field. The name can only contain the characters Aa–Zz and the underscore (\_) special character. In the Label field, enter a description for the analytic privilege. In the Type dropdown list, choose the appropriate option based on the referenced information views. For example, select the Classical analytic privilege option for referenced information views configured to use classical XML-based analytic privileges. Click Create to continue.

[![New XML-Based Analytic Privilege Window](bilderklein/klein10_004.png)](img-f10.4.html) 

**Figure 10.4**    New XML-Based Analytic Privilege Window

The classic XML-based or classic analytic privilege management window is organized into four main sections, as shown in [Figure 10.5](#10_004.html#f10.5).

[![XML-Based Analytic Privilege Management Window](bilderklein/klein10_005.png)](img-f10.5.html) 

**Figure 10.5**    XML-Based Analytic Privilege Management Window

The General section (top left) provides the option of updating the Label field. Just below this field is a second option, the Apply to all information models checkbox. When the Apply to all information models checkbox is selected, all XML-based information views will be subject to the analytic privilege restrictions. For example, if 12 information views have been activated in the system and each information view has an attribute column with a technical name of CUSTOMER\_REGION, the restrictions defined within this analytic privilege will apply even if they aren’t explicitly referenced within the analytic privilege.

The Secured Models section (bottom left) provides the option to add or remove referenced information models. If the Apply to all information models option isn’t selected, information views will be within the scope of the analytics privileges access and applied restrictions. Remove an information view by selecting it in the list and then clicking the Remove button.

In the Privilege Validity section (top right), you can define a validity period for the restrictions. To define a validity period, click the Add… button, then choose an Operator to define the date range. Maintain the From and To date fields to define the date based on the chosen operator. When validity is defined, the analytic privileges will only be applied within the date range specified. If no validity is defined, the privilege will be valid all the time. To remove the validity, select it in the list and click the Remove button.

In the Associated Attribute Restrictions section (bottom right of [Figure 10.5](#10_004.html#f10.5)), you can select the attribute columns that will be subject to the filter restrictions. Click the Add… button to select an attribute column from an information view referenced in the Secured Models section. If the attribute column is derived from a dimensional calculation view or attribute view, the checkbox in the column labeled Shared will be selected. To remove the attribute column, select it in the list and click the Remove button.

Once you’ve added a column, click the \+ Restrictions button within the restriction type column. You can use this interface to define the filter conditions or restrictions for each column specified in the Associated Attribute Restrictions section. When you click the \+ Restrictions button, a row will be inserted below the column. You can add multiple rows to define multiple restrictions for a given column. In each case, the restriction conditions will be listed in a row below the attribute column. To define the filter condition, for static analytic privileges, choose the Fixed value option. Select an Operator in the column to its right from the dropdown list to define part of the filter condition. For example, choose Equal if the filter condition requires that the attribute column value equal the static value specified in the Value field. Alternatively, choose GreaterEqual if the value must be greater than or equal to the static value specified. The Value column contains the static value used in the filter condition. You can click the icon in the corner of this field to see a list of possible values in the attribute column.

Filter conditions in the static XML-based analytic privileges support the use of the Between, ContainsPattern, Equal, GreaterEqual, GreaterThan, Is Not Null, IsNull, LessEqual, and LessThan operators. If multiple restrictions are applied to the same attribute column, all filter conditions will be executed as true or executed using an AND condition. [Figure 10.6](#10_004.html#f10.6) shows static restrictions configured for the example attribute TYPE. The filter conditions of EQUEL CHAR30 are applied in the example.

[![Example Restrictions Applied in an Analytic Privilege](bilderklein/klein10_006.png)](img-f10.6.html) 

**Figure 10.6**    Example Restrictions Applied in an Analytic Privilege

Note that the Count column and the Associated Attribute Restrictions section shown in [Figure 10.6](#10_004.html#f10.6) indicate that one restriction has been applied to the attribute column. Expect the count to increase each time you add an additional restriction for a given attribute column.

When you’ve finished defining the analytic privilege, click the save icon (floppy disk) in the top left to save and activate the analytic privilege. Clicking the save icon will both save the analytic privilege within the repository and deploy it to the system for use within a role.

Once the analytic privileges are activated, their restrictions won’t apply until the analytic privileges are granted to existing roles or users. If no competing analytic privileges are also applied to the grantee, queries to the referenced information views will be limited based on the defined filter conditions or restrictions.

### 10.4.2    Creating Static SQL-Based Analytic Privileges

The process for creating static SQL-based analytic privileges is nearly identical to that of its classic XML-based counterpart. To create a static SQL-based analytic privilege, open the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor. Within the repository, locate a package in a secure location. Right-click the package and choose New • Analytic Privilege…. A popup window will appear labeled New Analytic Privilege, as shown in [Figure 10.7](#10_004.html#f10.7).

[![New SQL-Based Analytic Privilege Window](bilderklein/klein10_007.png)](img-f10.7.html) 

**Figure 10.7**    New SQL-Based Analytic Privilege Window

To specify the use of SQL analytic privileges, the Type dropdown list must be set to SQL. Other than this difference, the process is identical to what we outlined in [Section 10.4.1](#10_004.html#h10.4.1). In the New Analytic Privilege window, specify the technical name of the analytic privilege in the Name field. The name can only contain the characters A–Z, a–z, and the underscore (\_) special character. In the Label field, enter a description. In the Type dropdown list, choose the appropriate option based on the referenced information views. For example, select the SQL option for referenced information views configured to use SQL analytic privileges. Click Create to continue.

The SQL-based analytic privilege management window is almost identical to the window used to manage XML-based analytic privileges. One key difference is that the SQL-based analytic privilege windows has three additional radio button options, shown in [Figure 10.8](#10_004.html#f10.8) just above the Privilege Validity section. The three options are Attributes, SQL Editor, and Dynamic.

[![SQL-Based Analytic Privileges Management Window](bilderklein/klein10_008.png)](img-f10.8.html) 

**Figure 10.8**    SQL-Based Analytic Privileges Management Window

To configure a static analytic privilege, the Attributes option must be selected. Later in this chapter, we’ll explore the use of the remaining two options: Dynamic ([Section 10.5.2](#10_005.html#h10.5.2)) and SQL Editor ([Section 10.6](#10_006.html#h10.6)).

With the Attributes option selected, the configuration for the Secured Models, Associated Attribute Restrictions, and Privilege Validity sections is identical to the steps we provided in [Section 10.4.1](#10_004.html#h10.4.1).

Note that, if you reference an information view in the Secure Models section and fail to define any restrictions, roles granted this analytic privilege will have full query access to the referenced information view and any data it governs. This rule is true even when the grantee has multiple contradicting SQL-based analytic privileges also granted for the same information view. Based on testing, in such cases, the filter condition 1 = 1 is effectively derived and applied as a restriction. All other restrictions are effectively ignored because 1 = 1 is true for all records.

## 10.5    Managing Dynamic Analytic Privileges

You can create either XML-based or SQL-based dynamic analytic privileges. The options are similar but have a few major differences. Note that SAP documentation indicates XML-based analytic privileges will be replaced in the future by SQL-based analytic privileges, so we recommend that all new developments be based on the SQL analytic privilege workflows. In this section, we’ll first provide a brief overview of XML-based analytic privileges. Then, because SQL-based analytic privileges are the recommended approach going forward, we’ll provide a more through discussion covering their end-to-end creation process.

### 10.5.1    Dynamic XML-Based Analytic Privileges

Dynamic XML-based analytic privileges are set up within the same interface used to define static XML-based analytic privileges ([Section 10.4.1](#10_004.html#h10.4.1)). However, to configure the analytic privileges as dynamic, you must select different options within the Assign Restrictions section of the management interface. Within this section, you must change the value of the Restriction Type column from Fixed to Catalog Procedure or to Repository Procedure. The Operator column should contain an operator that facilitates the results of the stored procedure selected in the Value column. In most cases, you’ll choose the IN operator because the procedure will return an array of values.

Before we discuss the configuration of the stored procedure, let’s review how XML-based dynamic privileges are structured. These analytic privileges are essentially configured to perform lookups in catalog tables to retrieve an array of filter values for a given user. The lookup is based on user name, which is derived from the SAP HANA user account querying a referenced information view. The table that stores the mapping data requires a minimum of two columns: The first column will contain the user name, and the second column will contain the filter value. [Table 10.1](#10_005.html#t10.1) shows an example of how this table is structured and includes some example data.

 
| USER\_NAME || FILTER\_VALUE |
| --- | --- |
| SHODGE01 || North Central |
| --- | --- |
| CBESSLER04 || South West |
| WTRAN05 || North Central |
| WTRAN05 || South Central |

**Table 10.1**    Mapping to Facilitate XML-Based Dynamic Analytic Privileges

The stored procedure selected for use with the analytic privilege must be configured to return a single value or an array of values from this table. Therefore, the stored procedure’s output variable must be configured as a table type. Table types are catalog objects that act as a kind of virtual table and are most often used to temporarily define the tabular output of a stored procedure. For example, you can use the following SQL code to define the table type required to accommodate the output of this stored procedure:

```
CREATE TYPE "SECURITY"."CUSTOMER_ACCESS" AS TABLE ( "CUSTOMERKEY" int);
```

The procedure itself is defined to output one or more records based on the table containing the user-to-value mappings. The SAP HANA-specific SQLScript shown in [Listing 10.1](#10_005.html#l10.1) will create a procedure that accommodates these requirements.

```
CREATE PROCEDURE "SECURITY"."SP_RLS_CUSTOMER" ( OUT VAL     "SECURITY"."CUSTOMER_ACCESS" )        
LANGUAGE SQLSCRIPT     
SQL SECURITY DEFINER     
READS SQL DATA AS    
BEGIN
      VAL = SELECT FILTER_VALUE FROM "SECURITY"."RLS_CUSTOMER_ACCESS”  
WHERE USER_NAME = SESSION_USER;    
END;
```

**Listing 10.1**    Stored Procedure Used with XML-Based Dynamic Analytic Privileges

In the SQLScript code, note the line that begins VAL = SELECT FILTER\_VALUE FROM. The SELECT statement in this line queries the table and uses the WHERE clause of USER\_NAME = SESSION\_USER to refine the values returned. The SESSION\_USER variable is known to the SAP HANA system and is replaced at runtime with the user name assigned this analytic privilege.

For example, assume that the user account WTRAN05 is used to authenticate with SAP HANA when querying an information view. This user account is granted an XML-based dynamic analytic privilege. When WTRAN05 queries an information view referenced by the dynamic analytic privilege, the filter condition within the stored procedure is changed from USER\_NAME = SESSION\_USER to USER\_NAME = WTRAN05. All values in the table associated with WTRAN05 are returned by the table type output variable. The array of values is then passed to the execution engine and used to filter the information view. Based on [Table 10.1](#10_005.html#t10.1), the values North Central and South Central will be used as the filter condition.

You should now have a basic understanding of the structure of an XML-based dynamic analytic privilege. Remember that this type of analytic privilege will be replaced by SQL-based dynamic analytic privileges. In the next section, we’ll review the process for creating SQL-based dynamic analytic privileges in detail.

### 10.5.2    Dynamic SQL-Based Analytic Privileges

Dynamic SQL-based analytic privileges offer the ability to perform programmatic lookups of filter conditions based on a mapping between user names and filter conditions. XML-based dynamic analytic privileges require individual data values, but SQL-based dynamic analytic privileges require filter conditions, similar to a filter within a SQL WHERE clause. The use of filter conditions supports complex and diverse filters that are dynamically generated for a given user. For example, you can reference multiple attribute columns and filter operator types in the same condition clause. In contrast, each XML-based dynamic analytic privilege restriction is limited to a single attribute column and array of filter values.

To accommodate the lookups, a table must exist that maps each user account to one or more filter conditions. [Table 10.2](#10_005.html#t10.2) shows a basic example of how this table and its data should be structured. The table can be more complex but, at a minimum, must adhere to this structure.

 
| User Name || Filter Condition |
| --- | --- |
| JHARRIS01 || ("REGION" = ' North Central') |
| --- | --- |
| TTIM03 || ("REGION" = ' South West') |
| WTRAN05 || ("REGION" = ' North Central') |
| TIMG05 || ("REGION" = ' South Central') |

**Table 10.2**    Example Mapping Used with SQL-Based Dynamic Analytic Privileges

In the table, the left column contains the user name. User name values should exactly match configured SAP HANA user account names. The column on the right provides the filter conditions, which will be retrieved and added to the execution of the information view. These conditions should be constructed in such a way that matches an attribute column to a data value. Again, this construction is similar to a filter within a SQL WHERE clause. The following syntax represents the construction of a basic single column filter condition:

```
( <"COLUMN"> operator <'VALUE'> )
```

Parentheses are recommended around the entire condition statement. Attribute columns should use double quotes. The supported operators are \=, <=, <, \>=, \>, LIKE, BETWEEN, and IN. The value should use single quotes if a string value. Single quotes are not required for number type values. Note that subquery filter conditions aren’t supported in this mode.

Unlike XML-based analytic privileges, the stored procedure that returns these conditions must only support a single-valued string output variable. If multiple rows for a given user are stored in the table, the stored procedure code will need to condense these rows into a single value. Alternatively, the condition you store in the table can be quite complex, using a mixture of columns and operators and eliminating the need to store multiple values for a given user. For example, the following condition is also supported for a given user:

```
((REGION IN ('NE','NW','SW','NC') ) or (PLANT IN ('1001','1005','1006')))
```

Again, to accommodate the lookup of the values from within the table, you’ll need to create a stored procedure. Ideally, you’d create a repository-based stored procedure, but catalog stored procedures are supported as well. Keep in mind that the \_SYS\_REPO system account will require access to the table and stored procedure. Therefore, creating these objects within the repository for which \_SYS\_REPO will be the owner with full access is best. The objects will also be transportable within a delivery unit when they’re created within the repository.

The structure of the stored procedure must comply with a few conditions. First, the stored procedure must be configured as a DEFINER\-based procedure. In other words, the creator of the procedure will be used for validation when executed. Second, the procedure must be considered read-only and should only return values without executing any Data Manipulation Language (DML) statements. Third, the stored procedure can’t contain any input parameters. Fourth, the procedure can only contain a single-value output parameter with a data type of VARCHAR or NVARCHAR. Finally, the \_SYS\_REPO must have full access to the procedure and any tables it references.

To better understand the process, let’s walk through the three main steps required to implement a dynamic analytic privilege. First, you must create a table to host the user and data element mappings. Second, you must create a stored procedure to perform the lookups of the values. Finally, you’ll construct a SQL-based dynamic analytic privilege.

#### Creating a Repository-Based Security Table

To simplify the design, you’ll create a repository-based table. You can create this table using the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor. Locate a secure package location to host the repository-based table. Right-click the desired package node and choose New • File. A window titled Create File will appear. In the File Name field, enter the name of the repository-based table. For example, enter “RLS\_CUSTOMERKEY\_ACCESS.hdbtable.” Click Create to define the table. [Figure 10.9](#10_005.html#f10.9) shows an example of the script you can use to define this table.

[![Example Repository-Based Table Definition Script](bilderklein/klein10_009.png)](img-f10.9.html) 

**Figure 10.9**    Example Repository-Based Table Definition Script

The example table is configured with two columns. The first column contains the filter conditions; in our example, the CUSTOMER\_FILTERS column was used, which contains the conditions for filtering the CUSTOMER\_REGION in the data. The second column is USER\_NAME and will be filtered based on the SESSION\_USER variable.

With the table created, you must now populate the table with the mapping data. Multiple options exist for populating this table. You can import data from a file, insert records manually using SQL, or use supported tools to extract the data from other sources and load it into the security table. [Figure 10.10](#10_005.html#f10.10) shows sample data within the table.

[Listing 10.2](#10_005.html#l10.2) shows an example of how the data can be populated in the example table using SQL insert statements. Notice that you must use two consecutive single quotes around the CUSTOMER\_REGION data values, not double quotes. In SAP HANA, a single quote is an escape character. When inserting static values into a table, you have to “escape” the inserted single quote with another single quote so that the table values only store a single quote, as shown in [Figure 10.10](#10_005.html#f10.10).

```
INSERT INTO "security_tables"."Security.Tables::RLS_CUSTOMERKEY_ACCESS"
VALUES ('JHARRIS01', '("CUSTOMER_REGION" = ''North Central'')');
INSERT INTO "security_tables"."Security.Tables::RLS_CUSTOMERKEY_ACCESS"
VALUES ('TTIM03', '("CUSTOMER_REGION" = ''South West'')');
INSERT INTO "security_tables"."Security.Tables::RLS_CUSTOMERKEY_ACCESS"
VALUES ('WTRAN05', '("CUSTOMER_REGION" in (''South West'',''North Central''))');
INSERT INTO "security_tables"."Security.Tables::RLS_CUSTOMERKEY_ACCESS"
VALUES ('TIMG05', '("CUSTOMER_REGION" in (''South Central'',''North Central''))');
INSERT INTO "security_tables"."Security.Tables::RLS_CUSTOMERKEY_ACCESS"
VALUES ('TIMG05', '("CUSTOMER_REGION" = (''South Central''))');
INSERT INTO  "security_tables"."Security.Tables::RLS_CUSTOMERKEY_ACCESS"
VALUES ('SYSTEM', '_ALL');
```

**Listing 10.2**    A Series of Six SQL INSERT Statements Used to Populate the Example Table

[![Example Filter Conditions in Security Table](bilderklein/klein10_010.png)](img-f10.10.html) 

**Figure 10.10**    Example Filter Conditions in Security Table

#### Creating a Repository-Based Stored Procedure

To simplify the design, we’ll create a repository-based stored procedure. You can create this table using the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor. Locate a secure package location to host the repository-based stored procedure. Right-click the desired package node and choose New • HDB Procedure. A window titled New HDB Procedure will appear. In that window, type the name of the stored procedure in the File Name field. In the Schema field, choose an existing schema where the procedure will reside. Click Create to continue.

A table titled with the name of your procedure will appear. Within the tab, you’ll see a preconfigured, text-based template of the stored procedure script. You can modify the script to suit your requirements. [Figure 10.11](#10_005.html#f10.11) shows an example of the complete stored procedure code required to facilitate a dynamic SQL-based analytic privilege security value lookup.

[![Example Stored Procedure Used with SQL-Based Dynamic Analytic Privileges](bilderklein/klein10_011.png)](img-f10.11.html) 

**Figure 10.11**    Example Stored Procedure Used with SQL-Based Dynamic Analytic Privileges

This example is programmed to retrieve the filter conditions from the security mapping table. If no records are found for a given user, a filter condition of CUSTOMER\_REGION = ’’ is returned. Because all customer regions are populated with values, this condition simply returns no data. If the value \_ALL is found in the table, the condition (1=1) is returned, resulting in all records being returned. For users with a single condition or multiple conditions in the table, the procedure uses a cursor loop to concatenate multiple condition lines together, using an OR operator to divide them. Based on the example data, [Figure 10.12](#10_005.html#f10.12) shows the output when the example user TIMG05 executes the stored procedure. The output is on line 1 under the Resutls1 tab.

[![Example Stored Procedure Output When Executed by User TIMG05](bilderklein/klein10_012.png)](img-f10.12.html) 

**Figure 10.12**    Example Stored Procedure Output When Executed by User TIMG05

Notice that, in the results, the two different filter conditions are concatenated together using an OR operator. This design is an optional feature for this example. You could have simply stored this exact condition in the table and avoided the need to construct a stored procedure. However, this example illustrates the need to return only a single string for each user.

Also, within the example, notice that the cursor v\_Cursor is based on a SQL SELECT statement that uses the SESSION\_USER system variable in the WHERE clause to dynamically filter the security table based on the user name querying the information view. At runtime, SESSION\_USER is replaced with the user accessing the information view. This step is critical to the functionality of the dynamic analytic privileges.

When you’ve completed programming the stored procedure, save and activate the stored procedure.

#### Defining a SQL-Based Dynamic Analytic Privilege

To create a SQL-based dynamic analytic privilege, you can use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor. Within the editor, locate a secure package location to host the analytic privileges. Within the repository, locate a package in a secure location. Right-click the package and choose New • Analytic Privilege…. A popup window will appear labeled New Analytic Privilege, as shown in [Figure 10.13](#10_005.html#f10.13).

In this window, specify the technical name of the analytic privilege in the field labeled Name. The name can only contain the characters A–Z, a–z, and the underscore special character. In the Label field, specify a description for the analytic privilege. The Type dropdown list must have the SQL option selected because the information views are configured to use SQL analytic privileges. Click Create to continue.

[![New SQL-Based Analytic Privilege Window](bilderklein/klein10_013.png)](img-f10.13.html) 

**Figure 10.13**    New SQL-Based Analytic Privilege Window

A new tab should appear where you can configure the analytic privilege. Just above the Privilege Validity section, you’ll see three radio buttons, Attributes, SQL Editor, and Dynamic, as shown in [Figure 10.14](#10_005.html#f10.14). Choose Dynamic to configure a stored procedure-based dynamic SQL-based analytic privilege.

As shown in [Figure 10.14](#10_005.html#f10.14), the SQL-based dynamic analytic privileges management window is divided into three main sections: General, Dynamic, and Secured Models.

[![SQL-Based Dynamic Analytic Privileges Management Window](bilderklein/klein10_014.png)](img-f10.14.html) 

**Figure 10.14**    SQL-Based Dynamic Analytic Privileges Management Window

The first section, General, located in the top left corner, contains fields for the Name, Label, and Type of analytic privileges. The Label field can be updated at any time; Name and Type filed are read-only at this point in the process.

The Secured Models section, located in the bottom left corner, provides an interface to add or remove additional referenced information views. To add information views, click the Add… button and search for the desired information views. To remove an information view, highlight it in the list and click the Remove button.

The large section on the top right titled Dynamic is where you’ll configure the procedure that will drive the dynamic filtering of conditions. The dropdown list next to the Procedure field contains two options: Repository Procedure and Catalog Procedure. Select Repository Procedure to leverage a design-time stored procedure. Select the option Catalog Procedure to use a runtime procedure. Click the stacked squares icon in the right corner of the empty field below the procedure type to search for a stored procedure by name. The assumption at this point is that the stored procedure will return a string value containing an information view column, operator, and filter condition. The information view column in the string must match a column name in the output of the referenced information view in the Secured Models section.

Once the analytic privileges are activated, their restrictions won’t apply until the analytic privileges are granted to an existing role or user. If no competing analytic privileges are also applied to the grantee, queries to the referenced information views will be limited based on the defined filter conditions or restrictions.

SQL-based dynamic analytic privileges can accommodate a variety of complex filter conditions and filter condition operators and thus offer more flexibility than the legacy XML-based options. In the next section, we’ll review options that enable you to construct even more complex dynamic filter conditions through the use of SQL expressions, including the use of subqueries.

## 10.6    Managing Dynamic Expression-Based SQL Analytic Privileges

SQL-based analytic privileges offer a third option for defining filter expressions. This option allows you to use custom SQL expressions to define a WHERE clause generated by the analytic privileges. When mixed with the use of filter values in a catalog table and the SESSION\_USER system variable, they are both dynamic and flexible.

Unlike dynamic analytic privileges, expression-based SQL analytic privileges don’t require a stored procedure to accommodate the dynamic lookup of the filter conditions or values. You can directly define the lookup within the SQL editor provided within the interface. In some ways, this approach is a more simplistic way to support complex filter conditions within SQL-based analytic privileges.

Although a stored procedure is not required, the use of a catalog table to store the mappings between user accounts and filter values is required. The structure of this table is different from that of the dynamic SQL-based analytic privileges, which requires the mapping of filter conditions to users. In fact, the structure is similar to the structure required to support dynamic XML-based analytic privileges. [Table 10.3](#10_006.html#t10.3) provides an example of the structure and data found in such a table.

 
| USER\_NAME || FILTER\_VALUE |
| --- | --- |
| JHARRIS01 || 1000 |
| --- | --- |
| TTIM03 || 2000 |
| WTRAN05 || 2000 |
| WTRAN05 || 3000 |

**Table 10.3**    Example Mapping Used to Facilitate Dynamic Expression-Based SQL Analytic Privileges

The USER\_NAME column must contain values that match user accounts defined in the SAP HANA system. The FILTER\_VALUE column must contain individual values. This table will become the source of your subqueries defined in the SQL editor.

Based on our testing, the SQL editor supports a variety of different SQL expressions. The supported syntax seems to match anything that can be used in a SQL statement WHERE clause. However, some limitations may exist that we were unable to identify during testing and validation.

In the following statement, you can define a static filter condition. Assume that the information view has an attribute column named CUSTOMERKEY. You’ll use the IN clause and a static string array of values, as in the following example:

```
("CUSTOMERKEY" in (1000,2000,3000,4000,5000))
```

In the following statement, you can reference two different columns in the expression. Assume that all referenced information views have attribute columns with names CUSTOMERKEY and PLANT. You’ll use two different operators in the expression—an IN operator for CUSTOMERKEY and an \= operator for PLANT:

```
("CUSTOMERKEY" in (1000,2000,3000,4000,5000)) and ("PLANT" = 1000)
```

As shown in [Listing 10.3](#10_006.html#l10.3), you can reference two different columns in the expressions. Assume that all referenced information views have attribute columns with names CUSTOMERKEY and PLANT. However, as opposed to the static list of filter values, you’ll use a subquery to look up filter values from two different catalog tables. You’ll also use the SESSION\_USER system variable to dynamically reference the user account column USER\_NAME within the table.

```
 ("CUSTOMERKEY" in (SELECT DISTINCT "FILTER_VALUE" FROM "SECURITY".
"RLS_CUSTOMER_ACCESS" WHERE USER_NAME = SESSION_USER))
AND 
("PLANT" in (SELECT DISTINCT "FILTER_VALUE" FROM "SECURITY".
"RLS_PLANT_ACCESS" WHERE USER_NAME = SESSION_USER) )
```

**Listing 10.3**    SQL Expression for Dynamically Filtering Data

In these examples, notice that you can use a variety of attribute columns, operators, and even subqueries to define filter expressions. To better illustrate dynamic expression-based SQL-based analytic privileges, let’s walk through the process of defining them.

To create a SQL-based dynamic analytic privilege, you can use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor. Within the editor, locate a secure package location to host the analytic privileges. Within the repository, locate a package in a secure location. Right-click the package and choose New • Analytic Privilege…. A popup window will appear labeled New Analytic Privilege.

In this window, specify the technical name of the analytic privilege in the Name field. The name can only contain the characters A–Z, a–z, and the underscore special character. In the Label field, specify a description for the analytic privilege. The Type dropdown list must contain have the SQL option selected because these information views are configured to use SQL analytic privileges. Click Create to continue.

A new SQL-based dynamic analytic privileges management tab will appear titled with the name of the analytic privilege. Just above the Privilege Validity section, you’ll see three radio buttons: Attributes, SQL Editor, and Dynamic. Choose the SQL Editor option to continue. The tab layout will again update, and a new section titled SQL Editor will appear. As shown in [Figure 10.15](#10_006.html#f10.15), the new layout window is divided into three main sections: General, Secured Models, and Sql Editor.

The first section, General, located in the top left corner, contains fields for the Name, Label, and Type of the analytic privileges. The Label field can be updated at any time. The Name and Type fields are read-only at this point in the process.

[![Dynamic Expression-Based SQL Analytic Privileges Management Window](bilderklein/klein10_015.png)](img-f10.15.html) 

**Figure 10.15**    Dynamic Expression-Based SQL Analytic Privileges Management Window

The Secured Models section, located on the bottom left corner, provides an interface to add or remove additional referenced information views. To add additional information views, click the Add button and search for the desired information view. To remove an information view, highlight it in the list and click the Remove button. The large section on the right named SQL Editor, is where you can type the desired SQL filter expression.

Let’s assume that the SQL expression must support a subquery lookup based on the security table values shown in [Table 10.3](#10_006.html#t10.3). To accommodate this, we’ll use a subquery to look up an array of filter value from the FILTER\_VALUES column. Based on this requirement, we’ll use the expression shown in [Listing 10.4](#10_006.html#l10.4).

```
 "CUSTOMERKEY" IN 
    (SELECT "CUSTOMERKEY"
    FROM "security_tables"."Security.Tables::RLS_CUSTOMER_ACC"
    WHERE "USER_NAME" = SESSION_USER)
```

**Listing 10.4**    Example Complex SQL Filter Expression

In effect, you can look up filter values and apply these values to the filter expression using the SESSION\_USER variable at runtime. You can do this even without the use of a stored procedure, which simplifies the solution by reducing the number of design-time objects required.

Click the save icon when you’re ready to deploy the analytic privileges, which will both save an analytic privilege within the repository and deploy it to the system for use within a role. Once an analytic privilege is activated, its restrictions won’t apply until the analytic privilege is granted to an existing role or user. If no competing analytic privileges have also been applied to the grantee, queries to the referenced information views will be limited based on the defined filter conditions or restrictions.

## 10.7    Troubleshooting Effective Analytic Privileges and Filter Conditions

The easiest method of troubleshooting the net effect of analytic privileges for a given user and information view is to query the SYS.EFFECTIVE\_STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGES system view.

When querying this system view, three filter conditions within the WHERE clause must be satisfied before the query will execute. The USER\_NAME, ROOT\_SCHEMA\_NAME, and ROOT\_OBJECT\_NAME columns must all be specified in the WHERE clause as filter conditions. The SQL code shown in [Listing 10.5](#10_007.html#l10.5) will check for the effective analytic privileges applied to the WTRAN05 user for the e-corp.sales.models/SCV\_CUSTOMER\_SALES information view.

```
SELECT *
FROM "SYS"."EFFECTIVE_STRUCTURED_PRIVILEGES" 
WHERE
"USER_NAME" = 'WTRAN05' AND 
"ROOT_SCHEMA_NAME" = '_SYS_BIC' AND
"ROOT_OBJECT_NAME" = 'e-corp.sales.models/SCV_CUSTOMER_SALES'
```

**Listing 10.5**    SQL Statement for Querying EFFECTIVE\_STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGES System View

The output of the query provides some important information. The EFFECTIVE\_FILTER output column will indicate the total filters applied from all restrictions. If multiple restrictions are applied, this column will have the same output value for all rows.

The STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGE\_NAME output column will indicate the source of the restriction. A unique row will exist for each unique analytic privilege.

The STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGE\_FILTER output column will indicate the syntax of the restriction in relation to the analytic privileges that produced the restriction. A unique row will exist for each unique analytic privilege.

The STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGE\_STATUS output column will contain the value APPLIED when a restriction is found and applied. If the value NOT AUTHORIZED is returned, then the user doesn’t have any analytic privileges assigned. Other values, such as NOT GRANTED, NO MATCHING ATTRIBUTE, and NO FILTER VALUES FOUND, are also possible depending on the type of structured privilege referenced.

## 10.8    Granting Analytic Privileges

In this section, we’ll review the options available for granting analytic privileges to and revoking analytic privileges from grantees: SQL commands, the SAP HANA cockpit, the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, and repository-based role scripts or repository-based role editor options.

### 10.8.1    Granting Analytic Privileges with SQL

When you create an analytic privilege, that privilege is owned by the system user \_SYS\_REPO. Analytic privileges are a type of structured privilege, but you can’t use the standard GRANT and REVOKE SQL syntax to assign analytic privileges to a grantee. Instead, you must use a specific stored procedure to grant and another to revoke analytic privileges for a grantee.

To grant an analytic privilege to a grantee, you must execute the GRANT\_ACTIVATED\_ANALYTIC\_PRIVILEGE stored procedure in the \_SYS\_REPO schema. To use this procedure, the security administrator must have the EXECUTE object privilege on the stored procedure. The procedure provides two input parameters. The first parameter should contain the name of the analytic privilege, and the second input parameter should contain the name of the grantee. Use the following SQL syntax to execute the stored procedure and assign the analytic privilege:

```
CALL "_SYS_REPO"."GRANT_ACTIVATED_ANALYTICAL_PRIVILEGE"
('<ANALLYTIC_PRIVILEGE_NAME>','<GRANTEE>');
```

Following is another example, using an actual analytic privilege and role:

```
CALL "_SYS_REPO"."GRANT_ACTIVATED_ANALYTICAL_PRIVILEGE"
('"e-corp.sales.security/ap_sales_reporting_region"','ROLE_REGION');
```

To revoke an analytic privilege from a grantee, you must execute the REVOKE\_ACTIVATED\_ANALYTIC\_PRIVILEGE stored procedure in the \_SYS\_REPO schema. This stored procedure uses the same two input parameters. Use the following syntax to execute the stored procedure:

```
CALL "_SYS_REPO"."REVOKE_ACTIVATED_ANALYTICAL_PRIVILEGE"
('<ANALLYTIC_PRIVILEGE_NAME>','<GRANTEE>');
```

The following example uses an actual analytic privilege and role:

```
CALL "_SYS_REPO"."REVOKE_ACTIVATED_ANALYTICAL_PRIVILEGE"
('"e-corp.sales.security/ap_sales_reporting_region"','ROLE_REGION' );
```

### 10.8.2    Granting Analytic Privileges with the SAP HANA Cockpit

Let’s review the workflows necessary to grant and revoke analytic privileges with the SAP HANA cockpit. As an alternative to using SQL statements, you can use the SAP HANA cockpit options called Assign Privileges or Manage Roles. Each interface allows you to both grant and revoke analytic privileges for a given user account or for a given role. Most users will find using the SAP HANA cockpit easier than memorizing and entering in SQL statements.

To access the Assign Privileges or Manage Roles interfaces, start at the SAP HANA cockpit Home screen, locate an SAP HANA system in the Resource Directory. Connect to the desired tenant database or SYSTEMDB, which will take you to the System Overview window. Using the Filter by Area dropdown list, choose the option Security. Locate the Assign Privileges or Manage Roles in the User & Role Management tile.

[Figure 10.16](#10_008.html#f10.16) shows the Assign Privileges interface within the SAP HANA cockpit for the TEST\_01 user account. In the windows, you’ll see several tabs for various privilege categories starting with the System Privileges, Object Privileges, Analytic Privileges, Application Privileges, Package Privileges, and Privileges on Users tabs. You’ll find a similar interface when working with roles. However, the Role Details GUI has an additional link called Roles where you can grant existing roles to the selected role.

The third tab in the Assign Privileges window is named Analytic Privileges. Click this tab to list, grant, or revoke analytic privileges for a given grantee.

The privileges listed in this interface have already been granted to the user or role. If the list is blank, nothing is currently granted. To grant an analytic privilege, click the Edit button located on the far-right side of the interface near the Search field. Once you click the Edit button, new buttons labeled Save, Cancel, Add, and Remove will appear. Click the Add button to open the Select Analytic Privileges popup window. Within this window, you’ll see a search bar and a list of analytic privileges with checkboxes. Use the search bar to filter the list based on the entered text. Then, scroll through the list and select the checkbox beside the analytic privilege you want to grant. With one or more analytic privileges checked, click the OK button to add the desired items to the user. Your selected analytic privileges should now appear in the Analytic Privileges section.

[![Managing Privileges Assigned to User Accounts in the SAP HANA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein10_016.png)](img-f10.16.html) 

**Figure 10.16**    Managing Privileges Assigned to User Accounts in the SAP HANA Cockpit

To assign the Grantable to Others privilege, locate an analytic privilege in the list. To the right, you’ll see a slider button to move to Yes, thus allowing the user to grant the same privilege to another user or role. Repeat this process for each analytic privilege in the list. Once you’ve added all the desired analytic privileges to the list, click the Save button to grant the privileges. Note that most analytic privileges are owned by the system user \_SYS\_REPO and cannot be configured as grantable to others. However, generic structured privileges, like the runtime catalog object type, can be configured with this option.

To revoke an analytic privilege, start by clicking the Edit button again, then select the checkbox beside each analytic privilege in the list, and click the Remove button to revoke the privileges. Repeat the process for each analytic privilege you want to revoke. Once you’ve removed all the desired analytic privileges, click the Save button. The removed privileges will be revoked, and the user object will be updated.

During the process of adding or removing privileges, you can click the Cancel button to discard any unsaved changes. Clicking the Cancel button will deactivate the Add, Cancel, and Remove buttons and return you to a read-only list of currently granted analytic privileges.

### 10.8.3    Granting Analytic Privileges with the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, hosted within the XS engine, provides an interface that you can use to create users, create roles, or manage security for standard roles. This interface provides a web-based alternative to SAP HANA Studio and also serves as an alternative to issues GRANT and REVOKE statement with SQL.

You can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench via a supported Internet browser. The following URLs can be customized to match the details of your environment:

*   http://sap-hana.myhost.com:8000/sap/hana/ide/security
    
*   http://<sap\_hana\_host>:80<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/security
    

In the last example, replace <sap\_hana\_host> with the host name of the SAP HANA system in your environment and <instance\_number> with the two-digit instance number corresponding to your SAP HANA system.

For secure access, the following examples should help you construct the correct URL:

*   https://<sap\_hana\_host>:43<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/security
    
*   https://sap-hana.myhost.com:4300/sap/hana/ide/security
    

Once you have access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, expand the Security node on the right. Expand Roles to reveal a list of standard roles defined in the system. Double-click a role to open the management interface for the given role. With the selected role management window open, you can begin granting and revoking privileges.

###### Note

To perform the same action for an individual user account, expand the Users node and double-click the desired user account.

As mentioned earlier, we recommend you use repository-based roles to support an SAP HANA security model. However, in this section, we’ll simply highlight the basic workflow if you chose to manage security with standard roles or directly on individual user accounts.

With the GUI management interface open for a given grantee, you can add an analytic privilege in the following way. Click the Analytic Privileges tab. Click the plus sign (+) button, which will open the Find Analytic Privileges window where you can search for a specific analytic privilege. Select the desired analytic privileges and click OK to add them to the list.

To save your changes, press (Ctrl)+(S), or click the disk icon at the top left to save and activate the privilege. To revoke an analytic privilege, select it in the list and click the red X. Once again, save the changes to make them active within the database system.

If any activation issues arise, warning messages will appear in the status frame at the bottom of the user management window. The status frame has a dark background. Error messages will appear in red text. Errors are only generated during an attempted activation or saving of changes.

### 10.8.4    Granting Analytic Privileges with Repository Roles

When SAP HANA was initially released, assigning analytic privileges to standard roles was the best available option. Multiple GUIs and SQL statements were created to help organizations manage granting and revoking privileges to standard role. As SAP HANA evolved, repository roles were introduced to aid in application development. Because of their numerous benefits, we highly recommend that repository roles be used to generate a security model. Now, let’s review the process for granting analytic privileges to and revoking analytic privileges from repository-based roles.

#### Script-Based Repository Roles

In [Chapter 6](#06_001.html#h6), we introduced you to repository roles and outlined the workflows required to create and manage repository roles. In this section, we’ll again review the syntax necessary to assign analytic privileges to design-time repository-based role scripts. If you require more information about this process, please see [Chapter 6](#06_001.html#h6).

When defining analytic privileges within design-time repository-based role scripts, you must start each line with analytic privilege:. After the colon, you can provide a comma-separated list of analytic privileges. At the end of the list, include a semicolon to finish the line. If you don’t want to include a comma-separated list, you can explicitly list each privilege on its own line, with each line beginning with analytic privilege:.

The following example grants the ap\_sales\_reporting\_region analytic privilege, stored in the e-corp.sales.security package. Remember that repository package and object names are case sensitive:

```
analytic privilege:     
  e-corp.security:ap_sales_reporting_region.analyticprivilege;
```

In a final example, we’ll grant the \_SYS\_BI\_CP\_ALL system analytic privilege. This special catalog analytic privilege, when granted, gives full access to all information views defined within the repository:

```
catalog analytic privilege : "_SYS_BI_CP_ALL";
```

#### SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor, hosted within the XS engine, provides an interface that you can use to build and test development artifacts. From a security perspective, you can use this interface to create and manage repository-based roles. This interface offers all the advantages of repository-based roles without the need to use scripts and SAP HANA domain-specific language to create these roles. However, you can use this same interface to either edit the role via a GUI or open the role file in the text editor.

You can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor via a supported Internet browser. The following URLs can be customized to match the details of your environment:

*   http://sap-hana.myhost.com:8000/sap/hana/ide/editor
    
*   http://<sap\_hana\_host>:80<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/editor
    

Replace <sap\_hana\_host> with the host name of the SAP HANA system in your environment. Replace <instance\_number> with the two-digit instance corresponding to your SAP HANA system.

For secure access, the following examples should help you construct the correct URL:

*   https://<sap\_hana\_host>:43<instance\_number>/sap/hana/ide/editor
    
*   https://sap-hana.myhost.com:4300/sap/hana/ide/editor
    

To use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench and define a repository role, the user account first will need to be granted one of the roles listed in [Table 10.4](#10_008.html#t10.4). Users only need one of the two roles to use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench.

 
| Role Name || Summary |
| --- | --- |
