The pink eraser icon deletes audit events from the audit log. The final icon is a table with a green gear overlay. You can use this icon to open the SQL console where you can query the audit log table or execute SQL commands.

To define a new audit policy, click the plus icon (+). A new row will appear in the audit policy table. To begin the process, enter a unique name for the policy within the Policy column using the Enter Name cell. In the Policy Status column, click the down arrow within the cell and select Enable from the options. In the Audited Actions column, click the icon within the cell that contains two stacked boxes to open a new window, Edit Actions Audited by Policy. In this window, you can choose from some of the available audit actions by category. Select the actions that need to be audited; remember that the selected actions must be from the same category. When finished, click the OK button located at the bottom right.

Within the Audited Actions Status column, click the down arrow located to the right of the cell. Choose Successful, Unsuccessful, or All. Within the Audit Level column, click the down arrow located to the right of the cell. Choose Emergency, Critical, Alert, Warning, or Info.

In the Users column, click the two stacked boxes icon within the cell. The Select Users window will appear. Use the options in the window to search for one or more existing users. Once users are located, click the Add button located between the Matching Items list and Selected Items list to add the selected users to the right side of the window. Choose Include Selected Users in policy or Exclude Selected Users from policy above the Selected Items area. Click OK once you’ve selected users to include or exclude. Note that most actions don’t require that you select a user. When this field is left blank, the system assumes that the policy should be applied to all users. If the policy won’t activate without a user, you can assume that the policy action requires a referenced user.

If the audit policy uses actions from the data query and manipulation and procedure execution categories, you must also choose a target object. Within the Target Object cell, click the two stacked boxes icon. The Target Object window will appear. Within the search box, enter the name of the catalog object that will serve as the target for the audit policy. Click the OK button found in the bottom right once you’ve completed your selections.

If you want to define specific audit targets for the audit policy, use the cells in the Audit Trail Target column to define additional targets. Within the Audit Trail Target cell, click the two stacked boxes icon. The Select Targets window will appear. Select the checkbox for each audit target location. Click the OK button to continue.

Once the audit policy is defined, to save the audit policy settings, click the large disk icon on the main icon bar to save the changes or press (Ctrl)+(S).

In addition to defining audit policies this way, you can also use SQL commands, as we’ll discuss in the next section.

### 15.3.3    Managing Audit Policies with SQL

You can also use SQL statements to define SAP HANA audit policies. Using SQL isn’t as easy, but this scripting option can help you apply a consistent audit policy throughout your SAP HANA landscape. SQL script can be executed with the SQL console found in most management tools in SAP HANA. We’ve found that the GUI-based tools are at inconsistent times and don’t always support all audit policy options, but the SQL options support all possible audit configurations.

When creating an audit policy, use the generic SQL syntax shown in [Listing 15.2](#15_003.html#l15.2).

```
CREATE AUDIT POLICY <POLICY NAME> 
AUDITING <STATUS> <ACTIONS>
ON <CATALOG OBJECTS>
FOR | EXCEP FOR <USER LIST>
LEVEL <LEVEL> 
TRAIL TYPE <TRAIL>;
```

**Listing 15.2**    SQL Template for Defining an Audit Policy

The <POLICY NAME> variable will be replaced with the name of the policy. The <STATUS> variable should be replaced with SUCCESSFUL, UNSUCCESSFUL, or ALL. The <ACTIONS> variable should be replaced with the syntax specific to the action being audited; for example, you can specify one or more actions, such as CREATE USER, ALTER USER, or ALTER ROLE.

###### Note

The syntax of all possible actions is quite extensive and can be found in the SAP HANA SQL and System View Reference Guide, in the “CREATE AUDIT POLICY Statement reference” section.

You can download the guide from [http://s-prs.co/v498219](http://s-prs.co/v498219).

The ON clause and the <CATALOG OBJECTS> variable are required for data manipulation actions. The <CATALOG OBJECTS> variable should be replaced with the fully qualified name of the catalog object.

The <USER LIST> variable can contain a comma-separated list of user accounts in the system. The FOR and EXCEPT FOR syntax is optional for most audit actions. The <LEVEL> variable can be replaced with EMERGENCY, ALERT, CRITICAL, WARNING, or INFO. The <TRAIL> variable can be replaced with TABLE, SYSLOG, or CSV.

To better understand the SQL syntax, let’s review a few complete SQL examples. To audit the management of standard roles, you can create an audit policy titled MANAGE ROLE with the following code:

```
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "MANAGE ROLE" 
AUDITING ALL CREATE ROLE, ALTER ROLE, DROP ROLE
LEVEL INFO;
```

To audit the management of user accounts, you can create an audit policy titled MANAGE USER with the following code:

```
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "MANAGE USER" 
AUDITING ALL CREATE USER, ALTER USER, DROP USER
LEVEL INFO;
```

To monitor instances in which the stored procedures in the \_SYS\_REPO schema are executed, you can create an audit policy using the SQL code shown in [Listing 15.3](#15_003.html#l15.3).

```
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "GRANT OR REVOKE REPOSITORY OBJECTS" 
AUDITING ALL 
EXECUTE ON 
"_SYS_REPO"."*"
LEVEL INFO;
```

**Listing 15.3**    Creating a Policy Named GRANT OR REVOKE REPOSITORY OBJECTS

To monitor all unsuccessful actions for all users except system account users, you can create a policy using the SQL code shown in [Listing 15.4](#15_003.html#l15.4).

```
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "ALL ACTIONS" 
AUDITING UNSUCCESSFUL ACTIONS 
EXCEPT FOR 
_SYS_DI, _SYS_AFL, _SYS_XB, _SYS_WORKLOAD_REPLAY, 
_SYS_TASK, _SYS_STATISTICS, _SYS_SQL_ANALYZER, 
_SYS_REPO, _SYS_ES, _SYS_EPM, _SYS_DI_TO, _SYS_DI_SU, 
_SYS_DI_SEARCH_CATALOG, _SYS_DI_CDS_CATALOG, _SYS_DI_CATALOG, 
_SYS_DI_BI_CATALOG 
LEVEL INFO;
```

**Listing 15.4**    Creating a Policy Named ALL ACTIONS

When an audit policy is created using SQL, the audit policy disabled by default. To activate the policy, you’ll need to issue an ALTER AUDIT POLICY SQL statement. For example, you can issue the following SQL statement to enable an audit policy named ALL ACTIONS:

```
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "ALL ACTIONS" ENABLE;
```

To disable an audit policy, you can issue the following SQL statement:

```
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "ALL ACTIONS" DISABLE;
```

To delete an audit policy, you must use a DROP AUDIT POLICY SQL statement. For example, you can delete the ALL ACTIONS policy as follows:

```
DROP AUDIT POLICY "ALL ACTIONS";
```

###### SAP HANA SQL and System View Reference Guide

The complete syntax used to drop and alter audit policies can be found online in the SAP HANA SQL and System View Reference Guide. Look for the “ALTER AUDIT POLICY Statement (Access Control)” and “DROP AUDIT POLICY Statement (Access Control) sections.

The complete syntax used to create audit policies can be also be found in this guide. Look for the “CREATE AUDIT POLICY Statement (Access Control)” section.

Using SQL to define and manage audit policies is helpful for applying a consistent audit policy through the SAP HANA landscape. In the next section, we’ll briefly review how audit policies can be created in the SAP HANA cockpit.

### 15.3.4    Creating Policies with the SAP HANA Cockpit

The SAP HANA cockpit provides a GUI interface where you can manage auditing in an SAP HANA database. To access the security manager, log on to your SAP HANA cockpit and connect to the desired database. Click the Auditing tile. Within this tile, click the Auditing header to access the Auditing interface.

In the Auditing interface, look for the Audit Policies tab, as shown in [Figure 15.6](#15_003.html#f15.6).

To define a new audit policy, click the Create Audit Policy link located above the list of defined audit policies. A new interface will appear with a two-step option that will eventually morph into a four-step process. In the first step, 1\. Name, enter the name of the audit policy in the provided file, and a new button labeled Step 2 will appear. Click the Step 2 button to proceed to the next step.

[![Audit Policy Area in the SAP HANA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein15_006.png)](img-f15.6.html) 

**Figure 15.6**    Audit Policy Area in the SAP HANA Cockpit

The next step, 2\. Audited Actions and Action Status, will appear, as shown in [Figure 15.7](#15_003.html#f15.7). On this page, you can configure the Audited Action Status and the specific audit action by category for the policy. Notice that you can search for a category or action using the Search box located over the listed audit events. Once an action is selected, the Step 3 button will appear. Click this button to proceed to the next step.

[![Configuring the Audit Action Status and Audit Policy Action within the SAP HANA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein15_007.png)](img-f15.7.html) 

**Figure 15.7**    Configuring the Audit Action Status and Audit Policy Action within the SAP HANA Cockpit

The next step, 3\. Audited Users, will appear, as shown in [Figure 15.8](#15_003.html#f15.8). Select an option for the under Select the users to be audited by the policy section. If you need to audit a specific user or several users, search for the user in the provided list and select the checkbox for each user to be audited. Click the Step 4 button below the list to proceed.

[![Configuring Audit Policy Target Users within the SAP HANA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein15_008.png)](img-f15.8.html) 

**Figure 15.8**    Configuring Audit Policy Target Users within the SAP HANA Cockpit

The next step, 4\. Audit Trail, will appear, as shown in [Figure 15.9](#15_003.html#f15.9). In this step, you’ll configure the Audit Level setting for the policy.

[![Configuring the Audit Policy Audit Trail in the SAP HANA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein15_009.png)](img-f15.9.html) 

**Figure 15.9**    Configuring the Audit Policy Audit Trail in the SAP HANA Cockpit

For a system database, you can configure one or more audit trail targets. For a tenant database, you can only choose the default trail target configured for the database. Click the Step 5 button to continue.

The final step, 5\. Policy Status, allows you to choose to Enable or Disable the policy when saving, as shown in [Figure 15.10](#15_003.html#f15.10). Click the Review button to go to a summary screen and review each individual setting and then click the Save button at the bottom once you’re ready to activate the policy.

[![Configuring the Audit Policy Status in the SAP HANA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein15_010.png)](img-f15.10.html) 

**Figure 15.10**    Configuring the Audit Policy Status in the SAP HANA Cockpit

Once saved, you should now see the policy listed in the audit interface of the SAP HANA cockpit. To edit the policy after creation, click on the policy name in the list to option the policy details. Click the Edit button on the top right of the overview screen. With edit mode enabled, you can change the Policy Status, Audited Action Status, and Audit Trail Target options. In the Audited Actions section, as shown in [Figure 15.11](#15_003.html#f15.11), you can delete actions by clicking the X within a circle icon to the right of each action. You can add additional actions by clicking the Add Actions button located on the top right side.

[![Interface for Modifying an Existing Audit Policy in the SAP HANA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein15_011.png)](img-f15.11.html) 

**Figure 15.11**    Interface for Modifying an Existing Audit Policy in the SAP HANA Cockpit

You’ll follow a similar process when modifying Audited Objects and Users Included in Policy section. Once your changes are completed, click the save button at the bottom right of the window.

You should now have a strong understanding of the components that make up an audit policy. In addition, you should have a strong understanding of how policies are configured using the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security console, the SAP HANA cockpit, and SQL statements. In the next section, we’ll review various system views that contain audit-specific data.

## 15.4    Querying Audit Data

You can query three main system views that are related to audit data and the auditing configuration within SAP HANA. These views are useful for a variety of purposes. The three views are AUDIT\_ACTIONS, AUDIT\_LOG, and AUDIT\_POLICIES and are all located in the SYS schema.

###### Note

For more information on each of these views, refer to the SAP HANA SQL and System View Reference Guide, available at [http://s-prs.co/v498219](http://s-prs.co/v498219).

*   AUDIT\_ACTIONS  
    The audit actions view provides access to a listing of all possible auditable actions within the SAP HANA system. This view provides a listing of audit actions and flags to indicate actions that require a user or catalog object reference. This view is useful when you need to see a listing of supported audit actions. To query the view, issue the following SQL statement:
    
    ```
    SELECT * FROM SYS.AUDIT_ACTIONS;
    ```
    
*   AUDIT\_LOG  
    The audit log view provides access to all recorded actions based on enabled audit policies. When an audit policy is enabled, events are written to the hidden system table \_SYS\_AUDIT.CS\_AUDIT\_LOG\_. The audit log view references this system table. Administrators can create a variety of audit-related queries referencing this system view, and the view contains several columns. To query the view, issue the following SQL statement:
    
    ```
    SELECT * FROM SYS.AUDIT_LOG;
    ```
    
*   AUDIT\_POLICIES  
    The audit policies view provides a complete listing of all audit policies defined within the system. This view can be queried to determine the quantity and scope of audit policies defined within the SAP HANA system. Note that a single policy might have multiple records within the view; each record represents a unique configuration option. For example, if you reference multiple users in the policy, a record for each user will be represented in this view. To query the view, issue the following SQL statement:
    
    ```
    SELECT * FROM SYS.AUDIT_POLICIES;
    ```
    

The views listed in this section are useful when your organization needs to examine the data that is collected from auditing and the configuration of the auditing mechanism itself. In the next section, we’ll walk you through a case study that outlines the decision-making process E-Corporation used when defining its audit policies. We’ll also show you the SQL the company used to define its audit policies.

## 15.5    Case Study: Defining Audit Policies

E-Corporation recently enabled auditing within the SAP HANA landscape. Its internal audit group determined that capturing audit events for the purposes of regulatory compliance and best practices was necessary. E-Corporation contacted its SAP HANA security consultant and requested help reviewing and implementing proposed audit policies. Thus, E-Corporation listed its requirements followed by its consultant’s recommendations, which we’ll review in the following sections. The consultant will use SQL statements to define the exact policy recommended.

E-Corporation requires that the audit policy be configured to facilitate proactive event monitoring, audit reporting, authentication actions, unauthorized access, system change, security management, and super user events. Let’s look at each requirement in detail.

### 15.5.1    Proactive Event Monitoring

#### Requirements

E-Corporation requires that the SAP HANA audit system support external tools that can proactively mine the system’s audit logs. These tools will require Open Database Connectivity (ODBC) and Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) access to the audit log tables.

#### Solution

Audit policies should be configured to support events that can be proactively monitored. These events include, but are not limited to, failed logon events, unauthorized actions, excessive query access to the system, and other activities. In addition, events will need to be recorded to the internal SAP HANA database table to allow these events to be available via JDBC or ODBC connections and via SQL queries. Most monitoring tools support this type of access.

### 15.5.2    Audit Reporting

#### Requirements

E-Corporation requires that all audit log data be accessible using the ODBC and JDBC protocols.

#### Solution

Audit events must be recorded to the internal SAP HANA database table, which will allow these events to be available via JDBC or ODBC connections and via SQL queries. Most reporting tools support this type of access.

### 15.5.3    Authentication Auditing

#### Requirements

E-Corporation requires that all connection and disconnection attempts are recorded within the audit logs. However, E-Corporation doesn’t want to record authentication attempts made by internal system accounts.

#### Solution

The security consultant recommends that an audit policy be created to record these activities to table AUDIT\_LOG within SAP HANA. An audit policy titled USER CONNECT AND DISCONNECT will be created to monitor all SUCCESSFUL connections and subsequent disconnection actions performed by standard users. Unsuccessful attempts won’t be recorded in this policy because they’ll be captured in a subsequent audit policy. The policy won’t record events for system-generated accounts.

The policy will be defined using the SQL code shown in [Listing 15.5](#15_005.html#l15.5).

```
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "USER CONNECT AND DISCONNECT" 
AUDITING SUCCESSFUL CONNECT, DISCONNECT SESSION 
EXCEPT FOR 
     _SYS_AFL,
     _SYS_DI,
     _SYS_DI_BI_CATALOG,
     _SYS_DI_CATALOG,
     _SYS_DI_CDS_CATALOG,
     _SYS_DI_SEARCH_CATALOG,
     _SYS_DI_SU,
     _SYS_DI_TO,
     _SYS_EPM,
     _SYS_ES,
     _SYS_REPO,
     _SYS_SQL_ANALYZER,
     _SYS_STATISTICS,
     _SYS_TASK,
     _SYS_WORKLOAD_REPLAY,
     _SYS_XB,
     SYS_XS_SBSS 
LEVEL INFO;
```

**Listing 15.5**    SQL Code to Create Policy Named USER CONNECT AND DISCONNECT

To activate the policy, the following SQL statement must be executed:

```
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "USER CONNECT AND DISCONNECT" ENABLE;
```

### 15.5.4    Unauthorized Action Auditing

#### Requirements

E-Corporation requires that all unsuccessful actions be recorded to the audit logs. Users with a high number of unsuccessful actions within a given day are to be questioned immediately. A high number of unsuccessful actions often indicates that someone is trying to compromise the system’s security using their own account or someone else’s account.

#### Solution

The security consultant recommends that an audit policy named ALL FAILED ACTIONS be created to record this activity to table AUDIT\_LOG within SAP HANA. The policy will be configured to record all UNSUCCESSFUL actions performed within the system.

The policy will be defined using the SQL code shown in [Listing 15.6](#15_005.html#l15.6).

```
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "ALL FAILED ACTIONS" 
AUDITING UNSUCCESSFUL ACTIONS 
EXCEPT FOR 
_SYS_DI, _SYS_AFL, _SYS_XB, _SYS_WORKLOAD_REPLAY, 
_SYS_TASK, _SYS_STATISTICS, _SYS_SQL_ANALYZER, 
_SYS_REPO, _SYS_ES, _SYS_EPM, _SYS_DI_TO, _SYS_DI_SU, 
_SYS_DI_SEARCH_CATALOG, _SYS_DI_CDS_CATALOG, _SYS_DI_CATALOG, 
_SYS_DI_BI_CATALOG 
LEVEL INFO;
```

**Listing 15.6**    SQL Code to Create Policy Named ALL FAILED ACTIONS

To activate the policy, the following SQL statement must be executed:

```
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "ALL FAILED ACTIONS" ENABLE;
```

### 15.5.5    System Change Auditing

#### Requirements

E-Corporation requires that all system configuration changes be recorded to the audit logs. These events should also be set up using the EMERGENCY level so that they’re easily identified within the audit logs. In addition, these events should be written to a CSV file stored in a secure directory in the operating system.

#### Solution

The security consultant recommends that an audit policy titled ALTER SYSTEM be created to record this activity to table AUDIT\_LOG table and a CSV file within SAP HANA. The policy will be defined using the following SQL code:

```
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "ALTER SYSTEM" 
AUDITING ALL SYSTEM CONFIGURATION CHANGE 
LEVEL EMERGENCY
TRAIL TYPE CSV, TABLE;
```

Note that the SQL code uses a LEVEL of EMERGENCY and a TRAIL TYPE of both CSV and TABLE. To activate the policy, the following SQL statement must be executed:

```
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "ALTER SYSTEM" ENABLE;
```

Because the policy will record such events to a CSV file, the system needs to be configured with a new default audit trail CSV file path. A directory was created within the path /usr/sap/HB5/HDB00/auditlog/, which will store audit trail files containing system configuration changes. No other audit rules within the system will use the CSV file option. To configure the CSV file path within SAP HANA, the following SQL statement must be executed:

```
ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini', 'SYSTEM') 
   SET ('auditing configuration', 'default_audit_trail_path') = 
'/usr/sap/HB5/HDB00/auditlog/' WITH RECONFIGURE ;
```

### 15.5.6    Security Management Task Auditing

#### Requirements

E-Corporation requires that all security-related activities be recorded to the audit log, including the management of users, roles, and repository roles, as well as granting and revoking of privileges and roles to other users.

#### Solution

The security consultant recommends that a series of audit policies be created to record this activity to table AUDIT\_LOG within SAP HANA. The audit policies MANAGE ROLE, MANAGE USER, GRANT OR REVOKE REPOSITORY OBJECTS, GRANT OR REVOKE PRIVILEGES, ANALYTIC PRIVILEGES, and ACTIVATE REPOSITORY OBJECTS will be created.

The MANAGE ROLE policy will record all attempts to create, alter, or drop roles within the SAP HANA system. E-Corporation’s standard policy is to create repository-based roles, and such roles would not be covered using this policy. However, this policy will identify security administrators that are not following policy. In addition, their actions related to standard roles will be recorded. To create the policy, the following SQL code must be executed:

```
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "MANAGE ROLE" 
AUDITING ALL CREATE ROLE, ALTER ROLE, DROP ROLE
LEVEL INFO;
```

The MANAGE USER policy will record all attempts to create, alter, or drop users within the SAP HANA system. E-Corporation allows security administrators to create users within the system. To create the policy, the following SQL code must be executed:

```
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "MANAGE USER" 
AUDITING ALL CREATE USER, ALTER USER, DROP USER
LEVEL INFO;
```

The GRANT OR REVOKE REPOSITORY OBJECTS policy is designed to record the use of stored procedures within the \_SYS\_REPO schema. These procedures are used by security administrators and give them the ability to grant privileges to repository-based objects, including repository-based roles. These procedures should be closely monitored because repository object privileges are always granted by \_SYS\_REPO regardless of the user executing these procedures. To create the policy, the SQL code shown in [Listing 15.7](#15_005.html#l15.7) must be executed.

```
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "GRANT OR REVOKE REPOSITORY OBJECTS" 
AUDITING ALL 
EXECUTE ON 
"_SYS_REPO"."*"
LEVEL INFO;
```

**Listing 15.7**    SQL Code to Create Policy Named GRANT OR REVOKE REPOSITORY OBJECTS

The GRANT OR REVOKE PRIVILEGES policy will record all attempts to grant or revoke privileges within the SAP HANA system. E-Corporation’s standard policy is to create repository-based roles, and privileges within repository-based roles are granted or revoked by the system account \_SYS\_REPO. However, this policy will identify security administrators that are not following policy. In addition, their actions related to the granting and revoking of privileges will be recorded. To create the policy, the following SQL code must be executed:

```
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "GRANT OR REVOKE PRIVILEGES" 
AUDITING ALL GRANT ANY, REVOKE ANY 
LEVEL INFO;
```

The ANALYTIC PRIVILEGES policy will record any attempts to create, alter, or drop structured privileges within the SAP HANA system. Because these privileges provide data-level security, auditing these privileges is important. Note that classic repository-based analytic privileges will be created, altered, and dropped by the system account \_SYS\_REPO. To create the policy, the SQL code shown in [Listing 15.8](#15_005.html#l15.8) must be executed.

```
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "ANALYTIC PRIVILEGES" 
AUDITING ALL 
ALTER STRUCTURED PRIVILEGE, 
CREATE STRUCTURED PRIVILEGE, 
DROP STRUCTURED PRIVILEGE 
LEVEL INFO;
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "ACTIVATE REPOSITORY OBJECTS" 
AUDITING ALL ACTIVATE REPOSITORY CONTENT 
LEVEL INFO;
```

**Listing 15.8**    Two SQL Statements to Create ACTIVATE REPOSITORY OBJECTS and ANALYTIC PRIVILEGES Policies

The ACTIVATE REPOSITORY OBJECTS policy is required to capture the true source of changes related to repository roles and other repository-based objects. When a repository object is activated, many auditing events will record that the \_SYS\_REPO user performed a series of actions. To properly correlate those actions to an actual user, you must ensure that all repository activations are also audited. In this way, you can know the identity of the user that initiated the actions carried out by the \_SYS\_REPO user. To create the policy, the following SQL code must be executed:

```
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "ACTIVATE REPOSITORY OBJECTS" 
AUDITING ALL ACTIVATE REPOSITORY CONTENT 
LEVEL INFO;
```

Once created, the policies will need to be activated. To activate these policies, the SQL shown in [Listing 15.9](#15_005.html#l15.9) must be executed.

```
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "MANAGE ROLE" ENABLE;
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "ANALYTIC PRIVILEGES" ENABLE;
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "ACTIVATE REPOSITORY OBJECTS" ENABLE;
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "GRANT OR REVOKE PRIVILEGES" ENABLE;
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "MANAGE USER" ENABLE;
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "GRANT OR REVOKE REPOSITORY OBJECTS" ENABLE;
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "ACTIVATE REPOSITORY OBJECTS" ENABLE;
```

**Listing 15.9**    Seven SQL Statements to Activate Seven Audit Policies

### 15.5.7    Super User Event Auditing

#### Requirements

E-Corporation requires that all users with elevated privileges have all their actions recorded. Super users at E-Corporation have user names prefixed with ADMIN\_. Every month, the audit team will query the audit logs to make sure that super user activities fall within the acceptable usage requirements for their given responsibilities.

In addition to super users, E-Corporation requests that all actions performed using the SYSTEM user account be recorded. This account is typically disabled and only used when necessary.

#### Solution

The SUPER USER AUDIT policy is required to record the SUCCESSFUL actions of all super users set up within the SAP HANA system. UNSUCCESSFUL actions will be recorded by the ALL FAILED ACTIONS policy. To create the policy, the following SQL code must be executed:

```
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "SUPER USER AUDIT" 
AUDITING SUCCESSFUL ACTIONS 
FOR SYSTEM, ADMIN_JHAUN, ADMIN_PETER, ADMIN_BOB
LEVEL INFO;
```

Once the policy is created, the following SQL must be executed to activate the policy:

```
ALTER AUDIT POLICY " SUPER USER AUDIT " ENABLE;
```

The policies recommended by the SAP HANA security consultant will grant E-Corporation better insight into the critical actions that take place within its SAP HANA system, help E-Corporation remain compliant with many regulations, and help E-Corporation manage compliance with its own internal policies.

## 15.6    Summary

A critical component of any SAP HANA security model, auditing allows your organization keep users accountable to policies and procedures related to security and system changes. Auditing can help your organization proactively identify unauthorized access attempts. Finally, auditing can help your organization reconstruct events after a security breach has occurred.

Within an SAP HANA landscape, auditing should be enabled, and specific audit policies should be implemented to protect the security and stability of the system.

# 16    Security Tracing and Troubleshooting

Implementing a security model can be a complex endeavor, and security administrators often find gaps within their security models. In this chapter, we’ll discuss security tracing and effective privileges views, which can help a security administrator identify these gaps.

In the real world, most security models are quite complex. When traversing the complex lineage of roles and their privileges is difficult, SAP HANA offers a security trace option that will capture and list many of the privileges missing from users attempting to interact with SAP HANA. This chapter will outline the steps required to enable a security-related authorization trace and review the trace file results.

In addition to security tracing, we’ll also review the various system views that provide details about the effective rights granted to individual users, and we’ll provide example queries to help bolster your understanding of how these system views can be leveraged.

## 16.1    Authorization Tracing

An authorization trace is a type of user-specific trace that’s limited to tracing detailed actions conducted by an individual user account. You can configure user-specific traces to record detailed information about a variety of activities within the SAP HANA system. Just about every component of SAP HANA can be traced, and trace information can be leveraged to provide specific information related to an activity within the SAP HANA system. Security administrators can use this trace mechanism to focus on the authorization component of an activity.

Tracing the authorization component provides detailed information related to actions that are both allowed and denied for a given user. For example, an authorization trace will record instances in which a user is not authorized to perform an action. In addition, the authorization trace often records the privileges a user is missing when attempting to conduct an unauthorized action.

Tracing is different from auditing (discussed in [Chapter 15](#15_001.html#h15)). Tracing provides significantly more detail concerning the internal processing of a user’s actions. Because of this level of detail, tracing should only be enabled for a short time and should be coordinated only with troubleshooting activities. An authorization trace not only records the actions of a user but also in many cases provides suggestions on the permissions required when actions are denied. Tracing activities are also recorded only to trace files; the information recorded to the trace file is semistructured and not easily recorded to a database table. Therefore, querying the trace data is difficult.

In contrast, auditing records the specific actions performed, including the action status. Audit data can be queried easily when recorded to a database table but doesn’t provide the same level of detail that tracing can provide. In addition, audit policies typically remain active all the time and aren’t intended to troubleshoot security-related gaps.

In general, you can enable a security trace for an individual user in two ways: The SAP HANA cockpit provides a graphical user interface (GUI) in which an authorization trace can be enabled, and administrators can also use ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION SQL statements to configure and enable an authorization trace. In the following sections, we’ll explore these options in detail.

### 16.1.1    Enabling Tracing with the SAP HANA Cockpit

Within the SAP HANA cockpit, you can use the SAP HANA database explorer to configure trace settings and view trace log output. To access the SAP HANA database explorer in the SAP HANA cockpit, log on and click the Browse Database Objects tile on the Home screen, which will launch the SAP HANA database explorer interface, as shown in [Figure 16.1](#16_001.html#f16.1).

On the top right of the SAP HANA database explorer, you’ll see connected databases similar to what’s shown in [Figure 16.1](#16_001.html#f16.1). However, if no databases are listed, you’ll need to add one. To add an SAP HANA database system, click the large plus sign (+) on the right side of that section, which will launch the Add Databases popup window. The easiest way to add a system is by selecting one from the Cockpit Resources. This shortcut will take the registered system information from the SAP HANA cockpit manager and quickly add a database to the interface. Alternatively, you can add a nonregistered SAP HANA database using the Database Type dropdown list.

Once you have a database connected, right-click the database and click the Trace Configuration option. A new tab titled Trace Configuration will appear to the right of the database systems list, as shown in [Figure 16.2](#16_001.html#f16.2).

[![SAP HANA Database Explorer in the SAP HANA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein16_001.png)](img-f16.1.html) 

**Figure 16.1**    SAP HANA Database Explorer in the SAP HANA Cockpit

[![Trace Configuration Found in the SAP HANA Database Explorer of the SAP HANA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein16_002.png)](img-f16.2.html) 

**Figure 16.2**    Trace Configuration Found in the SAP HANA Database Explorer of the SAP HANA Cockpit

Locate the section within the Trace Configuration tab called User-Specific Trace. On the right side of this section, you’ll see an Add button. Click this button to configure the trace settings. The User Specific Trace Configuration window will appear, as shown in [Figure 16.3](#16_001.html#f16.3).

[![User-Specific Trace Configuration Tab in SAP HANA Database Explorer of the SAP HANA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein16_003.png)](img-f16.3.html) 

**Figure 16.3**    User-Specific Trace Configuration Tab in SAP HANA Database Explorer of the SAP HANA Cockpit

Within the trace configuration window, you’ll need to configure several options to enable the user-specific trace. In the Context Name field, enter the custom name you want to use for a portion of the trace file that will be generated, for example, “USERAUTHTRACE.” In the Database User field, enter the name of a single database user within the system. Maintaining the Application User field isn’t necessary when performing an authorization trace. Use the Connection ID field to limit the trace to a specific connection ID; otherwise, keep this field blank.

To configure the trace as an authorization trace, set the trace level for authorization. In the section below the Hide components with default tracing option, you’ll see a table with three columns: Component, Default Trace Level, and System Trace Level, as shown at the bottom of [Figure 16.3](#16_001.html#f16.3).

To configure an authorization trace, first locate the Authorization option under INDEXSERVER within the Component column. In the field just above the table, enter the search phrase “auth” to narrow the results. In the results, locate the row in which Authorization component is visible. Using the System Trace Level column for the same row, click the cell to reveal a dropdown list. In the dropdown list, choose Debug. Click OK at the bottom of the window to activate the authorization trace. The User-Specific Tracing section should now display User traces and will list the specific trace you just configured, with a pencil and X icon to its left, as shown in [Figure 16.4](#16_001.html#f16.4).

[![User-Specific Trace Configuration Section with Active Trace Enabled](bilderklein/klein16_004.png)](img-f16.4.html) 

**Figure 16.4**    User-Specific Trace Configuration Section with Active Trace Enabled

Remember to delete a trace when you’ve completed collecting trace data. To delete the trace, click the X icon next to the trace profile name (SYSTEMTRACE, as shown in [Figure 16.4](#16_001.html#f16.4)).

### 16.1.2    Enabling Tracing with SQL

User traces also can be configured using specific SQL statements. The trace configuration is stored in the global.ini configuration file. Using the ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION SQL syntax, you can make configuration changes to this file and enable a user-specific trace.

The first configuration option that must be specified is the trace user name. To configure the specific user, you must create a trace profile with the sql\_user option. The trace profile name is a concatenation of the static term traceprofile\_ followed by the user-specific profile name. The profile name will be used with other settings and will be appended to the trace file name. The following SQL syntax can be used to construct the required SQL code for your environment:

```
alter system alter configuration ('global.ini','SYSTEM') 
SET ('traceprofile_<Profile Name>', 'sql_user') = '<User Name>' 
with reconfigure;
```

The <Profile Name> variable must be replaced with the name of the trace profile, and the <User Name> variable must be replaced with the name of a user within the SAP HANA system. The following example demonstrates the SQL for the trace profile named USERAUTHTRACE for the user TEST\_SVC:

```
alter system alter configuration ('global.ini','SYSTEM') 
SET ('traceprofile_USERAUTHTRACE', 'sql_user') = 'TEST_SVC' 
with reconfigure;
```

Next, you must specify the trace level. The following SQL syntax can be used to construct the required SQL for your environment:

```
alter system alter configuration ('global.ini','SYSTEM') 
SET ('traceprofile_<Profile Name>', 'authorization') = 'debug' 
with reconfigure;
```

The <Profile Name> variable must be replaced with the name of the trace profile, which is the same profile name used in the previous example. The profile name must match the name used in other settings. The following example demonstrates the SQL code for the trace profile named USERAUTHTRACE:

```
alter system alter configuration ('global.ini','SYSTEM') 
SET ('traceprofile_USERAUTHTRACE', 'authorization') = 'debug' 
with reconfigure;
```

Remember to disable the trace when you’ve finished collecting trace details. To disable the trace profile with the name USERAUTHTRACE, use the following two SQL statements. The first statement removes the setting for a specific user:

```
alter system alter configuration ('global.ini', 'SYSTEM') 
unset ('traceprofile_USERAUTHTRACE', 'sql_user') with reconfigure;
```

The second statement removes the trace-level setting:

```
alter system alter configuration ('global.ini', 'SYSTEM') 
unset ('traceprofile_USERAUTHTRACE', 'authorization') with reconfigure;
```

Using SQL is a quick and easy way to enable an authorization trace within the SAP HANA system. In the following section, we’ll explore the process used to locate and review the trace files generated when the trace is active.

### 16.1.3    Viewing the Trace File in the SAP HANA Cockpit

Once the trace is enabled, you’ll need to perform a test using the user specified within the trace configuration. For example, you can log on as the user and attempt to recreate the action being denied. Conducting the troubleshooting exercise again is important for guaranteeing that the denied actions will be recovered in the trace file. Once you’ve concluded the troubleshooting, you can view the contents of the generated trace files.

Within SAP HANA database explorer of the SAP HANA cockpit, you’ll see trace files within the folder structure under a connected database in the Database Diagnostic Files folder. Under this folder, a subfolder will contain the host name of the SAP HANA server or servers. Expand the server host name node to reveal additional subfolders. The subfolders at this level will contain the name of the services active on the SAP HANA host, as shown in [Figure 16.5](#16_001.html#f16.5). Click on each folder to reveal the trace files in the section below the search bar. Use the search bar to filter the list of trace files presented.

[![Viewing Trace Files within the Database Diagnostic Files Folder Node in the SAP HANA Database Explorer of the SAP HANA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein16_005.png)](img-f16.5.html) 

**Figure 16.5**    Viewing Trace Files within the Database Diagnostic Files Folder Node in the SAP HANA Database Explorer of the SAP HANA Cockpit

Using the Search field, you can narrow the list of trace files to those generated by the authorization trace. Fortunately, the trace profile name you used during the trace configuration also can be used to locate the files. For example, you can enter “SYSTEMTRACE” to narrow the list of files to those containing our authorization trace details.

Trace files use a file extension of .trc, which stands for trace. Once you’ve located the trace file in the results, click the file, which will open a text viewer tab to the right of the database connection pane. A new tab will appear, titled with the name of the trace file. The file will default to the last lines generated. [Figure 16.6](#16_001.html#f16.6) shows an example of the data found in a trace file.

[![Detailed Data within Authorization Trace File](bilderklein/klein16_006.png)](img-f16.6.html) 

**Figure 16.6**    Detailed Data within Authorization Trace File

Once the file is open, The detailed data within the file isn’t always easy to decipher when the Debug trace level is specified, but typically you can press (Ctrl)+(F) to open a Find dialog window within the text viewer.

Using the Find dialog window, you locate the trace details related to your security model troubleshooting. In many cases, the phrases Return Not Authorized and Missing are located near the exact action and privilege being denied. You can also search for the specific SQL you executed, the name of the object you interacted with, or the privileges that you expect to be missing.

Using the Debug trace level can result in hundreds of thousands of lines during troubleshooting. If your trace file is too large for browser-based searching, right-click the trace file and choose the Download option to download the file. Once downloaded, you can open the file within a text-viewing application that offers more enhanced search capabilities.

When you’re done reviewing the trace file, don’t forget to disable the user-specific trace using the options described earlier in [Section 16.1](#16_001.html#h16.1).

Tracing alone doesn’t always provide all the information you need. In addition to tracing, SAP HANA offers several system-managed catalog views that provide the effective privileges for a grantee. These views can be queried using SQL statements and filter conditioning within the WHERE clause. In the next section, we’ll look at each of these views in more detail.

## 16.2    Querying the System to Review Effective Privileges

Determining the exact privileges that a user will inherit is often difficult given the layers produced within our security models. User accounts can be granted roles that themselves are granted an additional layer of nested roles. Also, determining the exact number of grantees with specific privileges granted for a given object is often difficult. To help security administrators understand the effective or net result of privileges, several system views have been provided.

Eight different views are available to help security administrators review effective privileges. These views provide access in the areas of granted privileges, granted roles, accessible views, effective privilege grantees, effective structured privileges, effective privileges, effective role grantees, and effective roles. In the following sections, we’ll explore how each of these view types help security administrators manage SAP HANA security models.

### 16.2.1    Granted Privileges

When an administrator needs to view the privileges explicitly granted to an individual user or runtime role, the GRANTED\_PRIVILEGES system view can be queried to list the privileges. This view doesn’t recursively check the privileges of roles granted to the grantee. To see the effective privileges assigned to a grantee, use the EFFECTIVE\_PRIVILEGES system view, which we’ll discuss in [Section 16.2.6](#16_002.html#h16.2.6).

Use the following SQL syntax to query the GRANTED\_PRIVILEGES system view:

```
SELECT * FROM "SYS"."GRANTED_PRIVILEGES" 
WHERE GRANTEE = '<USER OR ROLE NAME>'; 
```

Note that the GRANTED\_PRIVILEGES view doesn’t require a filter condition or statement within the WHERE clause. If executed without a filter, all grantees and their privileges will be returned. All columns within the view can be used to filter, sort, and group the data. [Table 16.1](#16_002.html#t16.1) lists each available column and provides descriptions of the values that each column can return.

 
| Column Name || Column Value Description |
| --- | --- |
| GRANTEE\_SCHEMA\_NAME || The grantee’s schema |
| --- | --- |
| GRANTEE || A runtime role or user account |
| GRANTEE\_TYPE || Static value of either USER or ROLE |
| GRANTOR || User that granted the privilege |
| OBJECT\_TYPE || Type of object granted |
| SCHEMA\_NAME || The owning schema of the object |
| OBJECT\_NAME || Object’s name |
| COLUMN\_NAME || Column name |
| PRIVILEGE || Name of the granted privileges |
| IS\_GRANTABLE || TRUE or FALSE: Was the privilege granted using WITH GRANT OPTION or WITH ADMIN OPTION? |
| IS\_VALID || TRUE or FALSE: Is the privilege valid? |

**Table 16.1**    Columns in GRANTED\_PRIVILEGES View

### 16.2.2    Granted Roles

If an administrator needs to view the roles explicitly granted to an individual user or runtime role, the GRANTED\_ROLES system view can be queried. This view doesn’t recursively check nested or effective roles granted to the grantee. To see the effective roles assigned to a grantee, use the EFFECTIVE\_ROLES system view, which is discussed in [Section 16.2.8](#16_002.html#h16.2.8).

Use the following SQL syntax to query the GRANTED\_ROLES system view:

```
SELECT * FROM "SYS"."GRANTED_ROLES" 
WHERE GRANTEE = '<USER OR ROLE NAME>'; 
```

Note that the GRANTED\_ROLES view doesn’t require a filter condition or statement within the WHERE clause. If executed without a filter, all grantees and their roles will be returned. All columns within the view can be used to filter, sort, and group the data. [Table 16.2](#16_002.html#t16.2) lists each available column and provides descriptions of the values that each column can return.

 
| Column Name || Column Value Description |
| --- | --- |
| GRANTEE\_SCHEMA\_NAME || The grantee’s schema |
| --- | --- |
| GRANTEE || A runtime role or user account |
| GRANTEE\_TYPE || Static value of either USER or ROLE |
| ROLE\_SCHEMA\_NAME || The role’s schema |
| ROLE\_NAME || The name of the granted role |
| GRANTOR || Name of the user account that granted the role |
| IS\_GRANTABLE || TRUE or FALSE: Was the privilege granted using WITH GRANT OPTION or WITH ADMIN OPTION? |
| IS\_GRANTED\_BY\_LDAP || TRUE or FALSE: Was the role granted by an LDAP group? |

**Table 16.2**    Columns in GRANTED\_ROLES View

### 16.2.3    Accessible Views

To list all catalog and column views that can be accessed by a given user, the ACCESSIBLE\_VIEWS system view can be queried. The view must be filtered with the condition USER\_NAME = 'Some User'. To return the accessible views for multiple users, use multiple USER\_NAME = 'Some User' conditions, with an OR operator separating each condition clause. For example, the following SQL code will return the views that can be accessed by User Name 1 and User Name 2.

```
SELECT * from "SYS"."ACCESSIBLE_VIEWS" 
WHERE (USER_NAME = '<User Name 1>' 
OR USER_NAME = '<User Name 2>');
```

All columns within the view can be used to filter, sort, and group the data. [Table 16.3](#16_002.html#t16.3) shows a list of each available column and provides description of the values that each column can return.

 
| Column Name || Column Value Description |
| --- | --- |
| USER\_NAME || Name of the user with access to the catalog or column view |
| --- | --- |
| SCHEMA\_NAME || The view’s schema |
| VIEW\_NAME || Name of the catalog or column view |
| ANALYTICAL\_PRIVILEGE\_NEEDED || TRUE or FALSE: Is an analytic privilege needed to query this view? |

**Table 16.3**    Columns in ACCESSIBLE\_VIEWS System View

### 16.2.4    Effective Privilege Grantees

When an administrator needs to view a list of grantees with assigned privileges, the EFFECTIVE\_PRIVILEGE\_GRANTEES system view can be queried. This view is designed to list grantees that have the specified access to a particular catalog object, system privilege, or analytic privilege. This view can be queried using a variety of different filter values. At a minimum, the OBJECT\_TYPE and PRIVILEGES columns must be included within the filter condition WHERE clause. Depending on the value specified in the OBJECT\_TYPE column, additional columns must also be included in the WHERE clause.

When you need to list grantees with a specific level of access to a schema, use the SQL syntax shown in [Listing 16.1](#16_002.html#l16.1).

```
SELECT * FROM EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGE_GRANTEES 
WHERE OBJECT_TYPE = 'SCHEMA' 
AND SCHEMA_NAME = '<schema_name>' 
AND PRIVILEGE = '<privilege>';
```

**Listing 16.1**    Example SQL Syntax for Identifying Users with Specific Privileges Granted to a Specific Schema

The filter conditions in the SQL code must include OBJECT\_TYPE = 'SCHEMA', with additional filter conditions on the SCHEMA\_NAME and PRIVILEGES columns.

When you need to list grantees with a specific level of access to a given catalog object, use the SQL syntax shown in [Listing 16.2](#16_002.html#l16.2).

```
SELECT * FROM EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGE_GRANTEES 
WHERE OBJECT_TYPE = '<object_type>' 
AND SCHEMA_NAME = '<schema_name>' 
AND OBJECT_NAME = '<object_name>' 
AND PRIVILEGE = '<privilege>';
```

**Listing 16.2**    Example SQL Syntax for Identifying Users with Specific Privileges Granted to a Specific Catalog Object

As shown in [Listing 16.2](#16_002.html#l16.2), four filter conditions must be satisfied to identify users with the specified privileges on the specified catalog object. The filter must include the OBJECT\_TYPE filter condition. For example, condition values TABLE, VIEW, PROCEDURE, INDEX, or other catalog objects are possible. The condition for the SCHEMA\_NAME column must contain the object’s schema name. The condition for the OBJECT\_NAME column must include the name of the object in question. The PRIVILEGE condition must include the object privileges. For example, SELECT, EXECUTE, DELETE, ALTER, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE can be included with this condition. A grantee will only be listed if the privileges are explicitly granted to the object. As a result, you should always check the object’s schema for the given permission in addition to the object itself. Recall that objects inherit privileges from their schemas; however, inherited privileges will not be calculated with the SQL statement in this section.

When you need to list grantees with a specific system privilege, use the following SQL syntax:

```
SELECT * FROM EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGE_GRANTEES 
WHERE OBJECT_TYPE = 'SYSTEMPRIVILEGE' 
AND PRIVILEGE = '<privilege>';
```

The OBJECT\_TYPE = 'SYSTEMPRIVILEGE' filter condition must be included, and the PRIVILEGES column must be included within the WHERE clause.

### 16.2.5    Effective Structured Privileges

To view the effective filter conditions applied for a given user and view, the EFFECTIVE\_STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGES view can be queried. When queried, three columns must be included in the WHERE clause: ROOT\_OBJECT\_NAME, ROOT\_SCHEMA\_NAME, and USER\_NAME. The ROOT\_OBJECT\_NAME column filter must reference the name of the catalog or column view, the ROOT\_SCHEMA\_NAME column filter must reference the root object’s schema, and the USER\_NAME column filter must reference the user that will query the view specified in the root object filter condition.

The SQL code shown in [Listing 16.3](#16_002.html#l16.3) can be customized to match objects within your environment.

```
SELECT * 
FROM "SYS"."EFFECTIVE_STRUCTURED_PRIVILEGES"
WHERE ROOT_SCHEMA_NAME = '_SYS_BIC' AND
ROOT_OBJECT_NAME = '<Column View Name>'
AND USER_NAME = '<User Name>';
```

**Listing 16.3**    Example SQL Statement Template for Querying the EFFECTIVE\_STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGES View

The SQL code shown in [Listing 16.4](#16_002.html#l16.4) is an example for identifying restrictions applied to the TEST\_SVC user when querying the enowa.infoview/CV\_INTERNET\_SALES column view.

```
SELECT * 
FROM "SYS"."EFFECTIVE_STRUCTURED_PRIVILEGES"
WHERE ROOT_SCHEMA_NAME = '_SYS_BIC' AND
ROOT_OBJECT_NAME = 'enowa.infoview/CV_INTERNET_SALES'
AND USER_NAME = 'TEST_SVC3';
```

**Listing 16.4**    SQL Code to Query EFFECTIVE\_PRIVILEGE\_GRANTEES View

All columns within the view can be used to filter, sort, and group the data. [Table 16.4](#16_002.html#t16.4) shows a list of each available column and provides descriptions of the values that each column can return.

 
| Column Name || Column Value Description |
| --- | --- |
| ROOT\_SCHEMA\_NAME || The column or catalog view’s schema. This column must be included in the filter. |
| --- | --- |
| ROOT\_OBJECT\_NAME || The column or catalog view’s name. This column must be included in the filter. |
| USER\_NAME || The name of the user account you’re testing. The view will return the effective restrictions applicable for the user. |
| USER\_ID || The numeric user ID of the user account you’re testing. The view will return the effective restrictions applicable for the user. |
| EFFECTIVE\_FILTER || All effective filter conditions combined into a single statement. |
| STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGE\_NAME || Name of the structured privileges. |
| STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGE\_ID || Numeric ID of the structured privileges. |
| STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGE\_FILTER || Single filter condition applied by the given structured privilege’s name. |
| STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGE\_STATUS || Indicates the status of the structured privileges. Possible values are APPLIED, NOT GRANTED, NO MATCHING ATTRIBUTE, or NO FILTER VALUES FOUND. |

**Table 16.4**    Columns in EFFECTIVE\_STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGES View

### 16.2.6    Effective Privileges

To see a complete listing of privileges that have been granted directly and indirectly, the EFFECTIVE\_PRIVILEGES view can be queried. This view returns the net effective privileges, even if they’re granted from roles. The view provides the source of the privileges and a list of objects related to the granted privileges.

The following example SQL statement can be used to list all the privileges granted to a particular user account:

```
SELECT * FROM "SYS"."EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGES" 
WHERE USER_NAME = '<USER_NAME>'; 
```

Replace the <USER\_NAME> variable with the user account in question. This view provides access to several columns that can be used to sort, group, and filter the view. [Table 16.5](#16_002.html#t16.5) provides a listing of the key columns available in this view.

 
| Column Name || Column Value Description |
| --- | --- |
| USER\_NAME || The name of the user related to the privileges. |
| --- | --- |
| GRANTEE\_SCHEMA\_NAME || The grantee schema name. |
| GRANTEE || The name of the user or role that provided the privilege. |
| GRANTEE\_TYPE || The type of grantee; outputs either USER or ROLE. |
| GRANTOR || The name of the user or role that granted the privilege. |
| GRANTOR\_TYPE || The type of grantor; outputs either USER or ROLE. |
| OBJECT\_TYPE || The catalog object type or the type of privilege. |
| SCHEMA\_NAME || If object type is schema, the name of the schema is returned. |
| OBJECT\_NAME || When applicable, the name of the object, for which the privilege is applied, is returned. |
| COLUMN\_NAME || The column name. |
| PRIVILEGE || The name of the privileges that has been granted. |
| IS\_GRANTABLE || When TRUE, the column indicates that the WITH GRANT OPTION, WITH ADMIN OPTION has been granted. |
| IS\_VALID || Returns TRUE or FALSE; when TRUE, the privilege is currently active and valid. |

**Table 16.5**    Columns in EFFECTIVE\_PRIVILEGES View

### 16.2.7    Effective Role Grantees

To generate a list of users and roles that have been granted a role, the EFFECTIVE\_ROLE\_GRANTEES view can be used. This view requires that the ROLE\_NAME column be included in the WHERE clause as a filter condition. To query this view, use the following SQL syntax:

```
SELECT * FROM "SYS"."EFFECTIVE_ROLE_GRANTEES" 
WHERE ROLE_NAME = '<role_name>'; 
```

The view must be queried with a WHERE clause containing a filter condition on the ROLE\_NAME column. Other columns within the view can also be used for sorting, filtering, and grouping. [Table 16.6](#16_002.html#t16.6) lists the available columns.

 
| Column Name || Column Value Description |
| --- | --- |
| ROLE\_SCHEMA\_NAME || The role’s schema name. |
| --- | --- |
| ROLE\_NAME || The name of the role in question. |
| GRANTEE || The name of the user or role that has been granted the role in question. |
| GRANTEE\_TYPE || The type of grantee in question. Choose USER or ROLE. |
| GRANTOR || The name of the user that granted the role. |
| GRANTED\_ROLE\_NAME || The name of the role that provided the granted role. When the granted role name and role are the same value, the role is directly granted. When the granted role name is different, the role was inherited from another role. |
| IS\_GRANTABLE || When TRUE, this column indicates that the WITH GRANT OPTION or WITH ADMIN OPTION has been granted, and the user can grant this role to other users or roles. |

**Table 16.6**    Columns in EFFECTIVE\_ROLE\_GRANTEES View

### 16.2.8    Effective Roles

To view a complete list of roles that have been directly and indirectly granted to a given user, the EFFECTIVE\_ROLES view can be used. This view is useful for listing the roles that a user has been granted, both directly and through role inheritance. To query this view, use the following SQL syntax:

```
SELECT * FROM "SYS"."EFFECTIVE_ROLES" 
WHERE USER_NAME = '<USER_NAME>';
```

The USER\_NAME column must be used in the WHERE clause as a filter condition. [Table 16.7](#16_002.html#t16.7) provides a list of the available columns.

 
| Column Name || Column Value Description |
| --- | --- |
| USER\_NAME || Name of the given user related to the roles that are listed. |
| --- | --- |
| GRANTEE || Lists the user name when the role is directly granted to the user. A role name is listed when the role is granted from the listed role name. |
| GRANTEE\_TYPE || Indicates the type of grantee. The USER or ROLE option will be listed. |
| GRANTOR || The user that granted the role. |
| ROLE\_SCHEMA\_NAME || The role’s schema name. |
| ROLE\_NAME || The name of the role. |
| IS\_GRANTABLE || When TRUE, this column indicates that the WITH ADMIN OPTION has been granted, and the user can grant this role to other users or roles. |

**Table 16.7**    Columns in EFFECTIVE\_ROLES View

## 16.3    Case Study: Identifying Deficiencies in Information View Access

E-Corporation has developed numerous information views within its SAP HANA environment. E-Corporation also has several users complaining that they can’t query the views. The E-Corporation security team members believe that they’ve set up the privileges properly but cannot determine why users can’t access information views. To help E-Corporation identify the missing privileges, the company has contracted a security consultant.

E-Corporation has provided the following information to the security consultant to help him properly identify the problem with the missing privileges:

*   HAUNJON is the name of one of the user accounts experiencing the access issue.
    
*   The name of the information view is ecorp.sales.view/CV\_SALES.
    

In the following sections, we’ll walk through the steps the security consultant will take to identify the issue.

### 16.3.1    Troubleshooting the Problem

To start the troubleshooting process, the security consultant has requested that E-Corporation execute the SQL statements shown in [Listing 16.5](#16_003.html#l16.5) and [Listing 16.6](#16_003.html#l16.6) to help identify why the user can’t query the information view.

```
SELECT * 
FROM "SYS"."EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGES" 
WHERE 
USER_NAME = 'HAUNJON' 
AND SCHEMA_NAME = '_SYS_BIC'
AND PRIVILEGE = 'SELECT'
AND IS_VALID = 'TRUE'
AND (OBJECT_NAME IS NULL OR OBJECT_NAME = 'ecorp.sales.view/CV_SALES');
```

**Listing 16.5**    SQL Code for Querying EFFECTIVE\_PRIVILEGES System View

The code shown in [Listing 16.5](#16_003.html#l16.5) will validate that the user has SELECT privileges on the \_SYS\_BIC schema. Information views are published as column views into the \_SYS\_BIC schema, so users must have the SELECT privilege on the schema or on the column views containing the ecorp.sales.view/CV\_SALES prefix. If the user has access to the schema or to the individual column view, records will appear when the view is queried.

```
SELECT * 
FROM "SYS"."EFFECTIVE_STRUCTURED_PRIVILEGES"
WHERE ROOT_SCHEMA_NAME = '_SYS_BIC' 
AND ROOT_OBJECT_NAME = 'ecorp.sales.view/CV_SALES'
AND USER_NAME = 'HAUNJON';
```

**Listing 16.6**    Example SQL for Querying the EFFECTIVE-STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGES System View

The code shown in [Listing 16.6](#16_003.html#l16.6) will validate that the user has the appropriate analytic privileges for the information view. In addition to requiring the SELECT object privilege on the \_SYS\_BIC schema, the user must also have an analytic privilege. In the SQL output, the STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGES\_STATUS column will indicate the status as either NOT AUTHORIZED or APPLIED. When the status is APPLIED, you can assume that the user has an analytic privilege.

### 16.3.2    Reviewing the Results

E-Corporation’s SAP HANA security administrators executed the two SQL statements. When executing the first statement, written against the EFFECTIVE\_PRIVILEGES view, several records were returned. Based on the results, the user does have SELECT privileges on the \_SYS\_BIC schema and should be able to query the information view. However, the results of the second SQL statement, written against the EFFECTIVE\_STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGES view, indicated that the user wasn’t authorized to access the view.

### 16.3.3    Reviewing the Solution

After the security consultant reviewed the results, he provided a solution. Because the EFFECTIVE\_STRUCTURED\_PRIVILEGES view indicated that the user account wasn’t authorized, the user doesn’t have the required analytic privileges. The consultant recommended that E-Corporation grant the required analytic privileges to a role that’s also granted to the user.

When the E-Corporation security team members received the recommendation from the security consultant, they didn’t initially agree with the recommendations. The security team was under the impression that users only need analytic privileges when the data requires row-level restrictions. The security consultant explained that all users must have an analytic privilege that references the information view they need, even if they don’t require restrictions. SAP HANA requires that each user have both an object privilege and analytic privilege when querying an information view.

The E-Corporation security team now understands the issue. To resolve the issue, the team members created a new analytic privilege that references the information view. After granting this analytic privilege to one of the user’s roles, the user successfully queried the information view.

## 16.4    Summary

Using a user-specific trace to record authorization debug information is an excellent way to determine the permissions that a user is lacking when attempting to perform an action that isn’t authorized. In addition to security tracing, security administrators can also use several security-related views within the SYS schema to list the explicit and effective security for a given user, role, or grantee.

# 17    Security Recommendations

Knowing how to configure and implement security within SAP HANA is vital, but you’ll often need guidelines based on established best practices. In this chapter, we’ll provide several recommendations for securing an SAP HANA system based on the principles covered in this book.

Throughout this chapter, we’ll identify several important security configuration options within SAP HANA, while by no means a complete list. Your organization should consult its security teams when adopting any recommendations from this chapter. We’ll include recommendations related to password authentication, encryption, high-level privileges, the SYSTEM account, escalation vulnerabilities, appliance handover, and audit policies.

## 17.1    Password Authentication Settings

SAP HANA provides an internal user and password authentication mechanism. Any user with an enabled password should comply with industry and organizational password standards, so now, let’s review recommendations related to standard user password policies and service accounts.

### 17.1.1    Standard User Password Policies

Standard users are users related to actual people that log on to the SAP HANA system using an SAP HANA-managed user name and password. Out of the box, SAP password authentication requires only a single token for authentication: That token comes in the form of a password. Therefore, security administrators must implement measures to strengthen the passwords used by users.

Six key password policy items need to be addressed with any SAP HANA system: password lifetime, complexity, number of reused passwords, lockout policy, initial password policy, and password disabled option.

#### Password Lifetime

Passwords should be configured so that they expire after a specified number of days; in SAP HANA, the default is 182 days. Depending on the required password complexity and length, this number might need to be lowered. For example, many organizations require passwords to expire every 90 days because they require only 8 characters and require only limited complexity. Consult with your organization’s security team for a policy appropriate for your situation.

In addition to the maximum password lifetime, a minimum password lifetime should be implemented to prevent users from making frequent, consecutive password changes. For example, a user might try to change his password several times to circumvent the password reuse policy. The default value of one day will generally discourage users from circumventing the reuse policy, but the value should be increased if users frequently abuse the policy.

#### Password Complexity

Passwords should require a minimum number of character types to decrease the likelihood that both software programs and other users might guess them. By default, passwords require an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, and a number in SAP HANA. The default minimum length is 8 characters. Organizations can increase the complexity requirement for passwords by requiring a special character in addition to the other character types. Complexity can also be increased by increasing the minimum number of required characters and preventing the use of common dictionary words in passwords.

#### Number of Reused Passwords

When changing passwords, based on the maximum lifetime, organizations should prevent users from reusing passwords for a time. The default value for SAP HANA is the five previous passwords. Multiply 5 times 182 days, and you’ll see that passwords can’t be reused for about 2.5 years by default in SAP HANA. This calculation assumes that users don’t change their passwords before the expiration date.

Your organization should review this setting and increase this number as needed based on the configured minimum and maximum password lifetime. For example, many organizations increase this value to 12 previous passwords to reduce the likelihood that a password is compromised.

#### Lockout Policy

When a password is entered incorrectly a specified number of times, the account should be locked out or restricted from use until the owner and administrator can review the cause. SAP HANA defaults to a value of six invalid passwords before an account is locked out. In addition, SAP HANA defaults to 1,440 minutes or one day until the system automatically removes the lockout.

Your organization should review these default settings and implement a policy based on its security team’s requirements. For example, many organizations will increase the number of failed attempts from 6 to 10 but also force an account to remain locked out indefinitely. When locked out indefinitely, only an administrator can remove the account lockout condition, which forces the user and administrator to communicate about the cause of the lockout, thus helping identify instances in which someone else might be trying to guess the account password.

#### Initial Password

When an administrator creates an account for a user, she establishes an initial password. SAP HANA defaults to forcing a user to change this initial password the first time they log on. An administrator should never know a user’s password in the long term. Therefore, users must change this password as soon as possible. SAP HANA also disables an account if this initial password isn’t changed within 7 days of its creation.

These settings are crucial, and the default values within SAP HANA are typically acceptable. However, your organization should consult its security policy team about its own required settings. For example, some organizations might increase the initial password lifetime if new users typically don’t access the system within the first 30 days of the account creation. However, when increasing this policy setting, security administrators should choose an initial password that is unique for each user, which will reduce the likelihood of a new user account being compromised.

#### Disable Password Authentication

Organizations that use third-party authentication and single sign-on (SSO) with SAP HANA accounts don’t necessarily need password authentication enabled for a given user. The following SQL code will disable password authentication for a given user:

```
ALTER USER <USER_NAME> DISABLE PASSWORD;
```

Users configured with a Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) or Kerberos identity can still authenticate using a third-party authentication mechanism without the need to authenticate with SAP HANA via a password managed by SAP HANA. This methodology eliminates the need to manage passwords for a user.

### 17.1.2    Service Accounts

Service accounts or technical user accounts will probably need to be created within your SAP HANA system. These accounts are used by software applications to authenticate with the SAP HANA system. For example, a service account is set up to allow SAP NetWeaver to manage the SAP HANA relational database management system (RDBMS). Also, the password lifetime limit for such accounts is often disabled, which ensures that the password doesn’t expire and thus stop the external application from functioning. In fact, the SAP HANA Security Checklist tool, found in the SAP HANA cockpit, will specifically warn you if a service account has a nonexpiring password. While this warning is warranted, you simply can’t just remove the setting without putting your production systems at risk when the password expires. To that end, when establishing service accounts, we recommend the following guidelines:

*   Generate a 64-character or longer password using a secure random password generator. This approach helps prevent the password from being compromised by software applications designed to decrypt a password store or brute force a password.
    
*   Limit the overall privileges assigned to service accounts. Only grant what’s necessary for the account to service the application’s use within SAP HANA.
    
*   Plan to generate a new password every year—and remember that applications using the service account must also support changes to the password. Changing this password is important because this password can easily be compromised due to human error. For example, media containing the password might be unencrypted and easy to compromise.
    
*   Use a secure password manager application to store the password. These applications typically have their own internal security mechanisms and auditing capabilities to help organizations manage service account passwords that are accessible by multiple users. For example, the password can be checked out for testing. When checked out, SAP HANA security administrators can correlate the use of the account with SAP HANA audit logs.
    
*   SAP HANA audit policies should be created to monitor service account activity, especially for critical actions. Not all actions need to be monitored, but we highly recommend that important actions be audited.
    
*   An acceptable use policy for service accounts should be drafted. These policies should limit how these accounts are used within your organization and should establish guidelines for password policies, limitations for use, and limitations of individuals with access to the accounts’ passwords.
    

## 17.2    Encryption Settings

SAP HANA 2.0 supports communication encryption, backup encryption, data volume encryption, and log volume encryption. SAP HANA 1.0 only supports communication encryption and data volume encryption. Encrypting communication protocols protect information as data is transmitted between a client application and the SAP HANA server. Backup, data, and log volume encryption protects the data from individuals with physical access to the SAP HANA file systems. When data and log volume encryption is enabled, data can only be accessed through SAP HANA’s supported authentication and internal authorization mechanism.

Communication encryption should be used anytime information travels over untrusted and insecure networks, which might include your organization’s internal network but definitely includes access over a public network. For example, if your SAP HANA system is hosted by a cloud provider, the communications protocols should be encrypted using Transport Layer Security (TLS), and clients should be required to connect using TLS.

Backup, data, and log volume encryption should be used if absolute control over the physical access to the SAP HANA server or storage is in question. For example, if the server’s data center is shared by multiple organizations or hosted with a cloud provider, then data and log volume encryption is highly recommended.

## 17.3    Identifying Users with Elevated Privileges

When implementing a security model, your organization should maintain a list of users that have been granted a high level of access to the SAP HANA system. The term high-level access loosely describes having privileges that are inherently risky for a user to possess. Many system privileges within SAP HANA are inherently risky to grant to other users, but other types of privileges can also be risky.

Organizations using SAP HANA can’t entirely avoid granting these privileges to some of their users. However, the system should be scrutinized and frequently audited to ensure that users have the appropriate privileges based on their established job functions and based on the organization’s defined division of duties.

In this section, we’ll identify system, package, and analytic privileges that are inherently risky and list default roles that are inherently risky. In addition, we’ll help you identify user accounts with these privileges using SQL statements.

### 17.3.1    System Privileges

With a few exceptions, most system privileges are inherently risky because they allow a user to make changes to the system. However, the DATA ADMIN, USER ADMIN, ROLE ADMIN, AUDIT OPERATOR, and INIFILE ADMIN system privileges, in our opinion, are some of the riskiest privileges that can be granted. Users with these system privileges should be limited, and their actions should be routinely audited. Let’s look at each of these system privileges in more detail.

#### Data Admin

Grantees with the DATA ADMIN system privilege can query all system views. These users can also execute Data Definition Language (DDL) SQL commands against any table in any schema. The DDL commands include items such as ALTER, DROP, and CREATE. This privilege should only be granted when necessary. To identify grantees with this privilege, execute the SQL code shown in [Listing 17.1](#17_003.html#l17.1).

```
SELECT * 
FROM SYS.EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGE_GRANTEES 
WHERE OBJECT_TYPE = 'SYSTEMPRIVILEGE' 
AND PRIVILEGE = 'DATA ADMIN' 
AND GRANTEE NOT IN ('SYSTEM','_SYS_REPO');
```

**Listing 17.1**    SQL Code to Identify Grantees with DATA ADMIN System Privilege

Note that the code shown in [Listing 17.1](#17_003.html#l17.1) excludes the SYSTEM and \_SYS\_REPO default accounts from the results.

#### User Admin

The USER ADMIN system privilege allows a grantee to CREATE, ALTER, or DROP any user within the system and includes actions such as password resets, third-party identity management, and deleting users. In most cases, this privilege should only be granted to users tasked with the administration of user accounts.

To identify grantees with this privilege, execute the SQL code shown in [Listing 17.2](#17_003.html#l17.2).

```
SELECT * 
FROM SYS.EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGE_GRANTEES 
WHERE OBJECT_TYPE = 'SYSTEMPRIVILEGE' 
AND PRIVILEGE = 'USER ADMIN' 
AND GRANTEE NOT IN ('SYSTEM','_SYS_REPO');
```

**Listing 17.2**    SQL Code to Identify Grantees with USER ADMIN System Privilege

Note that the code shown in [Listing 17.2](#17_003.html#l17.2) excludes the SYSTEM and \_SYS\_REPO default accounts from the results.

#### Role Admin

The ROLE ADMIN system privilege allows a grantee to CREATE and DROP standard roles. This privilege also allows the grantee to grant an existing standard role to another grantee, even if the ROLE ADMIN privilege holder is not explicitly assigned the WITH ADMIN option. Therefore, organizations can’t limit which roles can be granted if a user possess the ROLE ADMIN system privileges. In addition, your organization should limit their use of standard roles in favor of repository-based roles. With these risks in mind, this privilege should be granted only when necessary.

To identify grantees with this privilege, execute the SQL code shown in [Listing 17.3](#17_003.html#l17.3).

```
SELECT * 
FROM SYS.EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGE_GRANTEES 
WHERE OBJECT_TYPE = 'SYSTEMPRIVILEGE' 
AND PRIVILEGE = 'ROLE ADMIN' 
AND GRANTEE NOT IN ('SYSTEM','_SYS_REPO');
```

**Listing 17.3**    SQL Code to Identify Grantees with ROLE ADMIN System Privilege

Note that the code shown in [Listing 17.3](#17_003.html#l17.3) excludes the SYSTEM and \_SYS\_REPO default accounts from the results.

#### Audit Operator

The AUDIT OPERATOR system privilege allows a grantee to clear the audit logs, which should only be granted when necessary. Typically, audit log-related system privileges are never assigned to security administrators, which ensures that the security administrator can’t change an audit policy or clear the audit logs to cover his tracks.

To identify grantees with this privilege, execute the SQL code shown in [Listing 17.4](#17_003.html#l17.4).

```
SELECT * 
FROM SYS.EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGE_GRANTEES 
WHERE OBJECT_TYPE = 'SYSTEMPRIVILEGE' 
AND PRIVILEGE = 'AUDIT OPERATOR' 
AND GRANTEE NOT IN ('SYSTEM','_SYS_REPO');
```
