**Listing 17.4**    SQL Code to Identify Grantees with AUDIT OPERATOR System Privilege

Note that the code shown in [Listing 17.4](#17_003.html#l17.4) excludes the SYSTEM and \_SYS\_REPO default accounts from the results.

#### INIFILE Admin

The INIFILE ADMIN system privilege allows a grantee to change any SAP HANA configuration setting. Changes to the system configurations are extremely risky within a production landscape and can also affect operations in nonproduction landscapes. Therefore, this system privilege should only be granted to administrators responsible for implementing system configuration changes.

To identify grantees with this privilege, execute the SQL code shown in [Listing 17.5](#17_003.html#l17.5).

```
SELECT * 
FROM SYS.EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGE_GRANTEES 
WHERE OBJECT_TYPE = 'SYSTEMPRIVILEGE' 
AND PRIVILEGE = 'INIFILE ADMIN' 
AND GRANTEE NOT IN ('SYSTEM','_SYS_REPO');
```

**Listing 17.5**    SQL Code to Identify Grantees with INIFILE ADMIN System Privilege

Note that the code shown in [Listing 17.5](#17_003.html#l17.5) excludes the SYSTEM and \_SYS\_REPO default accounts from the results.

### 17.3.2    Root Package Privileges

When a grantee has root package privileges, that user is assumed to have the granted privileges on all packages within the repository. Identifying users with root package privileges that allow changes to the repository is important. The following package privileges allow for changes to the repository:

*   REPO.EDIT\_NATIVE\_OBJECTS
    
*   REPO.ACTIVATE\_NATIVE\_OBJECTS
    
*   REPO.MAINTAIN\_NATIVE\_PACKAGES
    

The REPO.READ privilege allows a user to view all repository objects without making changes. At the root level, this privilege should be limited to only grantees that need to view all repository objects. Limiting who can see everything is best because this information can be used to construct more sophisticated hacks.

When a grantee has been granted root package privileges, those privileges will be assigned to a special package object named .REPO\_PACKAGE\_ROOT. Privileges assigned to this object will be inherited by all packages and development artifacts within the repository. We recommend that you limit root package access because the repository often contains repository roles, and users can potentially elevate their own privileges if they can modify a repository role that they’re granted.

To identify grantees with risky root package privileges, execute the SQL code shown in [Listing 17.6](#17_003.html#l17.6).

```
SELECT * 
FROM SYS.EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGE_GRANTEES 
WHERE OBJECT_TYPE = 'REPO' 
AND (PRIVILEGE = 'REPO.EDIT_NATIVE_OBJECTS'
 OR PRIVILEGE = 'REPO.ACTIVATE_NATIVE_OBJECTS' 
 OR PRIVILEGE = 'REPO.MAINTAIN_NATIVE_PACKAGES')
AND OBJECT_NAME = '.REPO_PACKAGE_ROOT'
AND GRANTEE NOT IN ('SYSTEM','_SYS_REPO')
ORDER BY GRANTEE;
```

**Listing 17.6**    SQL Code to Identify Grantees with Risky Root Package Privileges

To identify grantees with the root package REPO.READ privilege, execute the SQL code shown in [Listing 17.7](#17_003.html#l17.7).

```
SELECT * 
FROM SYS.EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGE_GRANTEES 
WHERE OBJECT_TYPE = 'REPO' 
AND (PRIVILEGE = 'REPO.READ')
AND OBJECT_NAME = '.REPO_PACKAGE_ROOT'
AND GRANTEE NOT IN ('SYSTEM','_SYS_REPO')
ORDER BY GRANTEE;
```

**Listing 17.7**    SQL Code to Identify Grantees with Read-Only Root Package Privilege

### 17.3.3    Bypass Analytic Privileges

In SAP HANA, an analytic privilege check can be bypassed in two ways. Analytic privileges protect data within the SAP HANA system. To ensure that these privileges haven’t been bypassed, you’ll need to review grantees with the \_SYS\_BI\_CP\_ALL analytic privilege and identify information views that have disabled analytic privilege checks.

#### SYS\_BI\_CP\_ALL

Information views require that all grantees have analytic privileges before the view can be queried. Information views, configured using the classic XML-based analytic privilege model, are automatically assigned to a special system of managed analytic privileges named \_SYS\_BI\_CP\_ALL. This analytic privilege provides unrestricted access to all information views using the classic XML-based analytic privilege check.

Grantees with this privilege won’t be subject to any data-level restrictions, even if these users are assigned custom analytic privileges that have restrictions. When a grantee has multiple analytic privileges, they’re effectively combined using an OR condition. For example, if a grantee has an analytic privilege where REGION = 'North' and the \_SYS\_BI\_CP\_ALL analytic privilege, the system will generate the effective filter restriction of (1=1) OR (REGION = 'North'). Because the first condition (1=1) is always TRUE, the system ignores the remaining restrictions. Therefore, the \_SYS\_BI\_CP\_ALL analytic privileges will always grant access to all data and all information views with a classic XML-based check.

Note that this arrangement doesn’t apply to information views that use SQL-based analytic privileges; in other words, the \_SYS\_BI\_CP\_ALL analytic privilege doesn’t apply to information views with the SQL-based check.

To identify grantees with the \_SYS\_BI\_CP\_ALL analytic privilege, execute the SQL code shown in [Listing 17.8](#17_003.html#l17.8).

```
SELECT * 
FROM EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGE_GRANTEES 
WHERE OBJECT_TYPE = 'ANALYTICALPRIVILEGE' 
AND OBJECT_NAME = '_SYS_BI_CP_ALL' 
AND PRIVILEGE = 'EXECUTE' 
AND GRANTEE NOT IN ('SYSTEM','MODELING', 'CONTENT_ADMIN');
```

**Listing 17.8**    SQL Code to Identify Grantees with Risky Analytic Privileges

Two default roles grant the SYS\_BI\_CP\_ALL analytic privilege: MODELING and CONTENT\_ADMIN. These roles should never be used within a security model because of their inherent risk. To identify grantees with these roles, execute the SQL code shown in [Listing 17.9](#17_003.html#l17.9).

```
SELECT * 
FROM EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGE_GRANTEES 
WHERE OBJECT_TYPE = 'ANALYTICALPRIVILEGE' 
AND OBJECT_NAME = '_SYS_BI_CP_ALL' 
AND PRIVILEGE = 'EXECUTE'
AND GRANTEE NOT IN ('SYSTEM')
AND GRANTOR IN ('MODELING', 'CONTENT_ADMIN')
AND GRANTOR_TYPE = 'ROLE';
```

**Listing 17.9**    SQL Code to Identify Grantees with Risky Default Roles

#### Information Views with No Analytic Privilege Checks

To identify information views with no analytic privilege checks enabled, you must query table ACTIVE\_OBJECT in the \_SYS\_REPO schema. For example, to identify information views with disabled analytic privilege checks, you can execute the SQL code shown in [Listing 17.10](#17_003.html#l17.10).

```
SELECT *
FROM "_SYS_REPO"."ACTIVE_OBJECT" 
WHERE 
( UPPER("CDATA") LIKE  UPPER('%checkAnalyticPrivileges="false"%') 
AND 
"OBJECT_SUFFIX" 
IN ('analyticview', 'calculationview', 'attributeview'));
```

**Listing 17.10**    SQL Code to Identify Information Views with Risky Analytic Privilege Check Settings

Any information view with its analytic privilege check disabled can be queried by any grantee with the SELECT privilege on the \_SYS\_BIC schema or the SELECT privilege on the associated column view. In addition, no filter restrictions can be applied to the information view. Therefore, your organization should maintain a listing of insecure information views and document the reasons for their configured states.

In addition to listing information views without an analytic privilege checks, you can also list those with different analytic privilege check types. To list all information views with either classic XML-based analytic privilege checks or with SQL-based analytic privilege checks, execute the SQL code shown in [Listing 17.11](#17_003.html#l17.11).

```
SELECT 'XML BASED AP CHECK' AS AP_TYPE, *
FROM "_SYS_REPO"."ACTIVE_OBJECT" 
WHERE 
( UPPER("CDATA") LIKE UPPER('%applyPrivilegeType="ANALYTIC_PRIVILEGE"%'))
AND "OBJECT_SUFFIX" 
IN ('analyticview', 'calculationview', 'attributeview')

UNION ALL

SELECT 'SQL BASED AP CHECK' AS AP_TYPE, *
FROM "_SYS_REPO"."ACTIVE_OBJECT" 
WHERE 
( UPPER("CDATA") LIKE UPPER('%applyPrivilegeType="SQL_ANALYTIC_PRIVILEGE"%'))
AND "OBJECT_SUFFIX" 
IN ('analyticview', 'calculationview', 'attributeview'); 
```

**Listing 17.11**    SQL Code to List All Information Views by Analytic Privilege Type

### 17.3.4    Default Standard Roles

In general, standard users shouldn’t be granted the default roles included with the SAP HANA installation, some of which grant high privilege levels. In this section, we’ll discuss two of these roles: CONTENT\_ADMIN and MODELING.

#### Content Admin

The CONTENT\_ADMIN role is intended for grantees that manage the development repository and related areas of the system. We don’t recommend using this role because of the following risks associated with granting this role:

*   Many of this role’s system, object, and package privileges are granted with the Grantable to Others option enabled, which allows a grantee with the CONTENT\_ADMIN privilege to grant many privileges to other grantees. These actions are typically reserved for security administrators, not lead developers.
    
*   This role grants the \_SYS\_BI\_CP\_ALL analytic privilege, which bypasses all data security settings implemented on applicable information views. You should use caution when granting this privilege to any user.
    
*   This role grants full root package privileges and the ability to grant those privileges to other grantees, which is risky in most scenarios, but especially when repository-based roles have been implemented. Users with the CONTENT\_ADMIN role could elevate their privileges by modifying existing repository-based roles.
    

To identify grantees with this role, execute the SQL code shown in [Listing 17.12](#17_003.html#l17.12).

```
SELECT * FROM 
SYS.GRANTED_ROLES 
WHERE 
ROLE_NAME = 'CONTENT_ADMIN' 
AND GRANTEE NOT IN ('SYSTEM');
```

**Listing 17.12**    SQL Code to Identify Grantees with CONTENT\_ADMIN Role

#### Modeling

The MODELING role is intended for grantees that work within the development repository and related areas of the system. We don’t recommend using this role because of the following risks associated with granting this role:

*   This role grants the \_SYS\_BI\_CP\_ALL analytic privilege, which bypasses all data security settings implemented on applicable information views. Organizations should use caution when granting this privilege to any user.
    
*   This role grants root package privileges for native objects, which is risky in most scenarios, but especially when repository-based roles have been implemented. Users with the MODELING role could elevate their privileges by modifying existing repository-based roles.
    

To identify grantees with this role, execute the SQL code shown in [Listing 17.13](#17_003.html#l17.13).

```
SELECT * FROM 
SYS.GRANTED_ROLES 
WHERE 
ROLE_NAME = 'MODELING' 
AND GRANTEE NOT IN ('SYSTEM');
```

**Listing 17.13**    SQL Code to Identify Grantees with MODELING Role

### 17.3.5    WITH GRANT or WITH ADMIN

When a grantee is granted a privilege, an additional option allows the grantee to also grant the same privilege to another user or role. The option is named WITH GRANT or WITH ADMIN when using SQL to grant privileges. When using a graphical user interface (GUI), the option is named Grantable to Others. Only grantees that manage security should have this additional privilege option.

To identify grantees with this additional capability, execute the SQL code shown in [Listing 17.14](#17_003.html#l17.14).

```
SELECT DISTINCT "GRANTEE", "GRANTEE_TYPE", "PRIVILEGE", "IS_GRANTABLE"
FROM "SYS"."GRANTED_PRIVILEGES" 
WHERE "IS_GRANTABLE" = 'TRUE'
AND GRANTEE 
NOT IN ('PUBLIC','SYSTEM','_SYS_REPO','SYS','_SYS_AFL','_SYS_DI_SU')
AND GRANTEE NOT LIKE '_SYS%'
AND GRANTEE NOT LIKE 'SYS_%'
AND GRANTEE NOT LIKE 'USR_%'
AND GRANTEE NOT LIKE 'AFL__%'
AND GRANTEE NOT LIKE 'SBSS_%'
AND GRANTEE NOT LIKE 'XSSQLCC_%'
ORDER BY 1 DESC;
```

**Listing 17.14**    SQL Code to Identify Grantees Who Can Grant Privileges

Note that the code shown in [Listing 17.14](#17_003.html#l17.14) attempts to remove many of the internal system-generated accounts because SAP controls the privileges for these accounts. However, if your organization creates users following a naming convention similar to the one SAP uses, then the code shown in [Listing 17.14](#17_003.html#l17.14) will need to be modified.

In newer versions of SAP HANA, multiple grantees are generated with a name that appears to be a random combination of letters and numbers. These accounts should be ignored; they’re managed by the system or are disabled.

### 17.3.6    Trace, Dump File, and Debug Access

While it a database administrator may need to review trace files and to debug SQL often, security information can be revealed when a high level of trace is enabled. SAP states that the default trace levels do not expose such information. However, if the trace settings are modified and configured to record a deeper level of activity, traces can contain compromising information. Therefore, we recommend you follow these rules:

*   Only enable high level tracing when required and disable tracing quickly after the debugging information is captured.
    
*   Have a security team review the trace files for confidential security information. This data should be masked or removed from the file.
    
*   Delete trace files from the OS and other file systems once the analysis is completed.
    

You must know which users have the system privileges necessary to change trace settings and to audit for any configuration settings that increase tracing levels. The following SQL will help you identify the grantees that have these system privileges:

```
SELECT * FROM GRANTED_PRIVILEGES WHERE PRIVILEGE='DEBUG' OR PRIVILEGE='ATTACH DEBUGGER' or PRIVILEGE='TRACE ADMIN';
```

## 17.4    Disabling the SYSTEM Account

After the system has been set up and a security model is established, we recommend that organizations disable the SYSTEM account. This account should only be enabled under extreme circumstances. When enabled, its actions should be fully audited by a member of the security team. Disabling the SYSTEM account is important for the following reasons:

*   The account has almost complete access to all aspects of the system, which is risky because of its default capabilities.
    
*   The SYSTEM account is a well-known administrative account often exploited by hackers inside and outside the organization. If disabled, then the account can’t be exploited.
    
*   The SAP HANA auditing mechanism can’t always identify the actual user executing actions as the SYSTEM account. Therefore, little or no accountability is expected when this account is used.
    
*   The account offers no division of duties.
    

To disable the SYSTEM account, execute the following SQL code while logged in as a different user:

```
ALTER USER SYSTEM DEACTIVATE;
```

To validate that the SYSTEM account has been disabled, execute the following SQL code:

```
SELECT * FROM USERS
WHERE USER_NAME = 'SYSTEM'
AND USER_DEACTIVATED = 'TRUE';
```

If a record is returned containing the SYSTEM account details, the account has been disabled. If you need to reactivate the SYSTEM account, execute the following SQL code:

```
ALTER USER SYSTEM ACTIVATE;
```

## 17.5    Identifying Privilege Escalation Vulnerabilities

When an organization uses repository-based roles, restricting access to the areas of the package hierarchy that contain the repository-based roles is important. Only grantees authorized to manage the repository roles should have edit access to the package containing those roles.

To identify grantees with access to repository roles, you must create a SQL query that checks each level of the package hierarchy. For example, let’s assume that our repository roles are stored in the package Security.roles. To list users with potential access to the repository roles, you must check the root package, the Security package and the Security.roles package for package privileges, as shown in [Listing 17.15](#17_005.html#l17.15).

```
SELECT * 
FROM SYS.EFFECTIVE_PRIVILEGE_GRANTEES 
WHERE OBJECT_TYPE = 'REPO' 
AND (PRIVILEGE = 'REPO.EDIT_NATIVE_OBJECTS'
 OR PRIVILEGE = 'REPO.ACTIVATE_NATIVE_OBJECTS' 
 OR PRIVILEGE = 'REPO.MAINTAIN_NATIVE_PACKAGES')
AND (OBJECT_NAME = 'Security'
OR OBJECT_NAME = 'Security.roles'
OR OBJECT_NAME = '.REPO_PACKAGE_ROOT')
AND GRANTEE NOT IN ('SYSTEM','_SYS_REPO')
ORDER BY GRANTEE;
```

**Listing 17.15**    SQL Code to Identify Grantees with Access to Change Repository Roles

The code shown in [Listing 17.15](#17_005.html#l17.15) excludes the SYSTEM and \_SYS\_REPO accounts from the validation check because it’s assumed that they’ll always have access to all packages. Any grantee listed in the results can potentially access the repository and escalate their own privileges. Therefore, only authorized users or roles should be listed.

## 17.6    Handover from Hardware Vendors

Under the SAP HANA appliance or Tailored Datacenter Integration (TDI) delivery models, SAP HANA is often deployed by a hardware vendor or certified individual. Because individuals outside your organization often deploy the SAP HANA system, several key user account passwords and encryption keys must be changed after the appliance has been handed over to your organization, such as the following:

*   Operating system users  
    During the installation of SAP HANA, the operating system user root (sapadm) and <sid>adm are created. The <sid> portion of the <sid>adm account will be the three-character SAP System Identification (SID) chosen during the installation. For example, if the instance SID is HDB, then the operating system user will be named hdbadm. More than one SID can exist on an SAP HANA operating system, and each SID will have a dedicated user account.
    
    Once the system has been handed over from the vendor, the password for each of these accounts should be changed. In addition, any additional vendor accounts created should be disabled or deleted from the system.
    
*   Database accounts  
    During installation, the vendor must establish a password for the SYSTEM user account. Once handover is complete, the SYSTEM account password should be changed. As noted in [Section 17.4](#17_004.html#h17.4), this account also should be disabled once the system is in full operation. If the vendor created any additional accounts, those accounts should also be disabled or dropped from the system.
    
*   Encryption root keys  
    Hardware vendors often use a disk image when deploying SAP HANA. Because this image might be used at multiple client sites, all encryption root keys must be changed. Even if the vendor doesn’t use a disk image, they have access to copy the encryption root keys, and therefore, all encryption root should be changed.
    

## 17.7    Creating Audit Policies

Auditing is disabled by default, and no audit policies are included with the system. The auditing mechanism should be enabled, and audit policies should be created.

To validate that auditing is enabled, execute the following SQL code:

```
SELECT * FROM "SYS"."M_INIFILE_CONTENTS" 
WHERE SECTION = 'auditing configuration' 
AND KEY = 'global_auditing_state';
```

If the column value returns TRUE, then the audit mechanism is enabled.

In addition to enabling auditing, you must also ensure that specific policies have been defined. Without any active policies, most events aren’t recorded. To validate that active audit polies exists, execute the following SQL code:

```
SELECT *
FROM "SYS"."AUDIT_POLICIES" 
WHERE "IS_AUDIT_POLICY_ACTIVE" = 'TRUE';
```

If any policies are listed, you can assume that the listed audit actions are being captured.

## 17.8    Summary

To properly secure an SAP HANA system, you must first understand the mechanics of the SAP HANA security model. The relationships among users, roles, and privileges are key to this understanding. However, you must also take advice from others when defining a model based on best practices. In this chapter, we introduced you to many of those best practices and provided SQL statements to help you check your organization’s adherence to those standards.

# 18    SAP HANA XSA Security

SAP HANA extended application services, advanced model (SAP HANA XSA) is the next evolution of SAP HANA extended application services, classic model (SAP HANA XS). The new SAP HANA XSA provides a more robust application server environment that supports multiple runtimes and programming languages.

In this chapter we’ll take a closer look at the security structure of the SAP HANA XSA platform. We’ll first start with an overview of the SAP HANA XSA platform. We’ll then discuss SAP HANA XSA users, role collections, organizations, and spaces and describe how they are administered and secured. We’ll briefly discuss SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, why it is needed, and how you’ll secure access to the application. Finally, we’ll review the architecture of the SAP HANA Deployment Infrastructure (HDI) container, discuss how runtime security works within the HDI container, explore how HDI container roles work, and show you how security administrators will manage runtime access to objects outside of an HDI container.

## 18.1    Overview of SAP HANA XSA

The SAP HANA extended application services, advanced model (SAP HANA XSA) platform provides a versatile and robust application server and development environment. The SAP HANA XSA platform was introduced with SAP HANA 1.0 SPS 11 as the demand for application development within a multi-target application (MTA) framework, with the Cloud Foundry platform, and with SAP’s software-as-a-service (SaaS) platform offerings was increasing. Part of the overall SAP HANA platform, SAP HANA XSA can be installed alongside the core SAP HANA database services.

With SAP HANA 2.0, the SAP HANA XSA framework has become the default and recommended framework for application development with SAP HANA. Still, rarely will you find an organization utilizing the SAP HANA XSA framework within an on-premise SAP HANA 2.0 deployment for a variety of reasons. Although SAP HANA XSA offers a significantly enhanced application development framework, it also greatly increases the complexity of development, administration, and security, based on our personal experience.

When SAP HANA was initially released, SAP HANA extended application services, classic model (SAP HANA XS ) was notable because SAP HANA XS was closely coupled with the database services within SAP HANA. This feature of SAP HANA, where the database was designed to do all the application’s data management and the web application server was simply designed to visualize results, is unique. Purely from an application development standpoint, this architecture had limitations. First, SAP HANA XS only provided a single repository and framework where applications could be deployed, which created challenges for organizations that had multiple versions of applications and for organizations that were hosting multiple development groups in a single SAP HANA instance.

However, outside of the application design paradigm, the SAP HANA XS repository provides a simple and elegant solution for managing database security and business intelligence-related content. In these two areas alone, the expanded functionalities of SAP HANA XSA are not necessary, and in most instances, SAP HANA XSA’s increased complexity and administration cost are not warranted.

The SAP HANA XSA framework is decoupled from the SAP HANA database. [Figure 18.1](#18_001.html#f18.1) shows a basic overview of the architecture. Notice that the SAP HANA database is separate from the SAP HANA XSA platform. The SAP HANA XSA platform communicates with the SAP HANA database via SQL. Clients will access the SAP HANA XSA via HTTP/HTTPS. Most organizations will install SAP HANA XSA services on the same physical host as the SAP HANA index server, otherwise known as the core database service.

SAP HANA XSA is comprised of three distinct SAP HANA platform services: xscontroller, xsexecagent, and xsuaaserver. Each service performs different tasks within the SAP HANA XSA platform, and each service interacts with components of the SAP HANA database. In general, SAP HANA XSA services use SQL protocols to interact with the SAP HANA database. SAP HANA XSA will create and interact with objects in the database including users, schemas, tables, containers, roles, and other items.

As of SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, the SAP HANA XS framework, the \_SYS\_REPO user concept, the package hierarchy, and repository roles still technically all work. Tools such as the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor are still functional under the SAP HANA XS services and can still be utilized to create repository-based roles and business intelligence content. Other tools like SAP HANA application lifecycle management are also available to help you transport content between SAP HANA systems.

[![Basic SAP HANA XSA Architecture](bilderklein/klein18_001.png)](img-f18.1.html) 

**Figure 18.1**    Basic SAP HANA XSA Architecture

Finally, all the functionalities found in SAP HANA Studio work even with SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04-based systems. In this book, much of our discussion is focused on solutions based on the SAP HANA XS model. This focus is because its replacement by the SAP HANA XSA framework does not currently provide enough control over security nor does it offer scalable security mechanisms to properly manage an SAP HANA database security model. Our hope is that SAP will address these gaps before the SAP HANA XS environment is removed from the platform.

With the SAP HANA XSA framework, SAP HANA development occurs within a service layer called the SAP HANA Deployment Infrastructure (HDI). While the infrastructure of an HDI container is quite different from the SAP HANA XS-based model, think of HDI containers in SAP HANA XSA as a replacement for the XS \_SYS\_REPO repository. An SAP HANA instance can only have a single XS \_SYS\_REPO repository. However, that same instance can support multiple HDI containers. This versatility allows you to both segregate one HDI container from another as well as deploy multiple versions of the same object into the same database instance. We’ll discuss HDI containers in more detail in [Section 18.4](#18_004.html#h18.4).

In the subsequent sections of this chapter, we’ll review HDI containers and show you the mechanisms for securing the database artifacts that HDI containers produce. In the next section ([Section 18.2](#18_002.html#h18.2)), we’ll provide you an overview of the security mechanism of the SAP HANA XSA platform. Because SAP HANA XSA is largely decoupled from the database, it has its own independent authorization mechanism and organizational structure. Note that SAP HANA XSA shares users and authentication mechanisms with its associated tenant or SYSTEM database. Let’s look at the process you’ll use to govern the SAP HANA XSA platform.

## 18.2    Managing Space Access, Users, and Roles Collections in SAP HANA XSA

Within SAP HANA, the development environment of SAP HANA XSA is structured into units called organizations and spaces. This structure is required to support a multi-target application (MTA) architecture. An MTA is designed to help consolidate application development by compartmentalizing the components of a typical web application solution while hosting these components in a single platform. Most web application components are developed in a variety of different coding languages, perhaps each with their own environments, lifecycle management, and disconnected operating system services. With the MTA architecture, you can combine and manage these diverse elements into a single solution. This consolidation enables you to manage dependencies, services, code, lifecycle, and security within a single platform. For example, a typical web application consists of a Java application server backend, a Node.js and HTML frontend, and a database backend for data storage. With SAP HANA and the SAP HANA XSA platform, you can manage the code, services, and lifecycle all within one or more HDI container spaces. SAP HANA XSA provides the runtime for each code base and provides the database backend.

Within the SAP HANA XSA MTA architecture, application development content is organized into organizations and spaces. Let’s start with an explanation of spaces. A space defines a container where all applications within that container share common code and resources and trust each other. Spaces can be shared by multiple developers, but developers can also have their own “sandboxes” for testing. Remember that a space has both runtime and design-time aspects. Design-time code is not directly accessible within a space between developers. Developers must share their code outside of the SAP HANA XSA tools. SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, hosted as an application within the SAP HANA XSA, is tightly integrated with GitHub, a web-based platform, designed to host code. GitHub is well suited for version control and developer collaboration. Its cloud-based or on-premises services help developers work together on projects.

Organizations are units that can be associated with one or more spaces. Spaces can only be associated with one organization. This grouping helps from a security standpoint and has limited impact on the runtime aspects of a space. The only impact would be organization-specific domains used in the crafting of the application’s external URLs. In SAP HANA XSA, you’ll use organizations to host one or more spaces. In turn, you can establish security at the organization level, allowing each space to inherit that same security.

Within SAP HANA XSA, you can create users, role collections, organizations, and spaces. These components are the basis for security within SAP HANA XSA. When SAP HANA XSA was first introduced, you could use a combination of the SAP HANA XS command line and the SAP HANA XSA administration graphical user interface (GUI) to administer SAP HANA XSA. However, starting with SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 03, the SAP HANA XSA cockpit was introduced, and the SAP HANA XSA administration tools were deprecated. With all versions of SAP HANA XSA, the SAP HANA XS command line utility for SAP HANA XSA can also be utilized for administration. However, for simplicity, we’ll focus on the SAP HANA XSA cockpit in this chapter.

In this section, we’ll first walk you through accessing applications in SAP HANA XSA and then move on to the process for creating SAP HANA XSA users and for establishing SAP HANA XSA security using the SAP HANA XSA cockpit.

### 18.2.1    Accessing Applications

When SAP HANA XSA is installed and applications are imported into its platform, one option is to give each application its own dedicated TCP/IP port. You’ll use the port and the host name of the SAP HANA XSA application server to craft the URL for accessing applications hosted within SAP HANA XSA. The most definitive way to find the port of an SAP HANA XSA application is to use the command line utility to list each application and the URL with the port that is listening to service browser access. The SAP HANA XS command line can be accessed through the operating system of the SAP HANA database, but you can also download and install it. See SAP Note 2242468 for instructions on installing the SAP HANA XSA command line. However, in this chapter, we’ll focus on using the command line installed on the SAP HANA server.

To access the SAP HANA XSA command line on the SAP HANA server, log on using Secure Shell (SSH) and your provided credentials. If you have the password for the <sid>adm Linux user account, log on with those credentials. If not, start by switching to that user’s session using the following commands:

```
sudo -i -u <sid>adm
```

To access the SAP HANA XSA command line, start by logging into SAP HANA XSA using the following command:

```
xs login
```

If the SAP HANA XSA command line interface requests the URL for the application programming interface (API) endpoint, enter the following:

```
https://<hana-xsa-hostname>:30030/
```

When requested, log on with the default SAP HANA XSA credentials or credentials provided to you from the SAP HANA XSA admin. Note that the default SAP HANA XSA account user is typically XSA\_ADMIN, but during installation, a custom name can be provided.

Run the following command to list the SAP HANA XSA applications currently deployed:

```
xs a
```

A list of installed applications will appear, as shown in [Figure 18.2](#18_002.html#f18.2). The name of the application will appear in the first column, and the URL used to access the application will appear on the far-right column.

To access the xsa-cockpit application, locate it in the list of applications. Note the URL and port needed to access the application. As shown in [Figure 18.2](#18_002.html#f18.2), we’ll use the following partially masked URL:

```
https://##hana-01:51030
```

[![Listing SAP HANA XSA Applications and URL with Port Information](bilderklein/klein18_002.png)](img-f18.2.html) 

**Figure 18.2**    Listing SAP HANA XSA Applications and URL with Port Information

Enter this URL into a supported browser. For this book, we’re using the Chrome browser to access the application. The web application will redirect you to the SAP HANA XSA login. Enter credentials with access to the SAP HANA XSA cockpit. Once loaded, you’ll land on the SAP HANA XSA cockpit Home screen, as shown in [Figure 18.3](#18_002.html#f18.3).

[![Homepage of the SAP HANA XSA CockpitSAP HANA XSA cockpit](bilderklein/klein18_003.png)](img-f18.3.html) 

**Figure 18.3**    Homepage of the SAP HANA XSA Cockpit

The interface is divided into two panes. On the left is an accordion menu with options for managing Organizations, Security, Tenant Databases, Host Management, User Management, and More. On the right side are additional options specific to each item selected within the accordion menu.

### 18.2.2    Managing SAP HANA XSA Users

To create and manage SAP HANA XSA users, click the User Management menu option, as shown in [Figure 18.4](#18_002.html#f18.4). On the right, you’ll see a list of users that have already been configured in the SAP HANA XSA system. These users correspond to users in the tenant database or SYSTEMDB that operates SAP HANA XSA. However, only the user account and password apply within SAP HANA XSA security. SAP HANA database roles, granted to these same users, have no bearing on their access within the SAP HANA XSA platform. SAP HANA XSA uses a separate application role security mechanism to determine application-level authorizations. We call these SAP HANA XSA role collections.

To create a new user, click the New User button located just above the list of users, as shown in [Figure 18.4](#18_002.html#f18.4). A new window will appear requesting the User Name, First Name, Last Name, E‐Mail, and Password. Enter the requested information for the new user and then click the Create button. Click the Migrate SAP HANA User button to import an existing user within the associated SAP HANA tenant or SYSTEMDB. The new or existing user will now be listed in the interface.

[![SAP HANA XSA Cockpit User Management Interface](bilderklein/klein18_004.png)](img-f18.4.html) 

**Figure 18.4**    SAP HANA XSA Cockpit User Management Interface

Next to each user is a series of icons. Click the pencil icon to edit the existing user’s name and email address. Click the key icon to manage the user’s password. Click the trashcan icon to delete the user from SAP HANA XSA and the database.

### 18.2.3    Managing SAP HANA XSA Role Collections

To manage role collections, click the Security option within the accordion menu to reveal the Role Collections option. On the right side of the interface, you’ll see a listing of existing role collections, as shown in [Figure 18.5](#18_002.html#f18.5).

[![SAP HANA XSA Role Collection Management Interface](bilderklein/klein18_005.png)](img-f18.5.html) 

**Figure 18.5**    SAP HANA XSA Role Collection Management Interface

Role collections are comprised of elements defined within the SAP HANA XSA application at design time using the xs-security.json file. This file is added to the application’s project via SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA. Within this file, each application will have an application identifier or xsappname again defined in the xs-security.json file. Application roles are also defined in the xs-security.json file within the scopes section. The description of each scope item will be presented as a role when defining a role collection within the SAP HANA XSA cockpit.

Finally, scope items will be organized into role templates (role-template section) within the xs-security.json file. Again, these items will be presented to you when defining the role collection in the SAP HANA XSA cockpit. However, note that the actual SAP HANA XSA application roles and role templates are defined by the developer and configured within the xs-security.json file that is part of the overall design-time SAP HANA XSA code and project.

###### More Information on Defining Roles within an SAP HANA XSA Application

For more information on defining roles and roles templates within your SAP HANA XSA application, refer to the SAP HANA Developer Guide for XS Advanced Model, available at [http://s-prs.co/v498220](http://s-prs.co/v498220).

The “Assign Functional Authorization Scopes for an XS Advanced Application” section provides more details on the structure of the xs-security.json file.

To define a role collection, click the New Role Collection button. The New Role Collection window will appear. Enter the name and a description for the role collection. Click Save and the role collection will now be present in the list.

To add SAP HANA XSA application roles to the role collection, locate the collection in the list and click its name. A new interface will appear where you can add SAP HANA XSA application roles. Click the Add Role button. The Add Role popup window will appear. Using the cascading Application Identifier, Role Template, and Role dropdown lists and locate an application role for the collection, as shown in [Figure 18.6](#18_002.html#f18.6). Click the Save button once you’ve located the role.

[![Defining a Role Collection within the SAP HANA XSA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein18_006.png)](img-f18.6.html) 

**Figure 18.6**    Defining a Role Collection within the SAP HANA XSA Cockpit

You can delete the assigned application role from the list by clicking the trashcan icon located on the right of each assigned role. No general save button for the role collection is available when viewing the role list. Once you click save in Add Role popup window, as shown in [Figure 18.6](#18_002.html#f18.6), the role is considered assigned to the role collection. To navigate back to the list of role collections, click the Home button at the top part of the interface on the right side. To delete a role collection, click the trashcan icon to its right. To edit a role collection, click the pencil icon to its right within the list, as shown in [Figure 18.5](#18_002.html#f18.5).

To grant or revoke a role collection associated with a user, return to the User Management interface found within the accordion menu of the SAP HANA XSA cockpit Home screen. Locate a user within the list. To the right of the user, within the list, click the user and padlock icon. The Assign Role Collections : <USER> window will appear, as shown in [Figure 18.7](#18_002.html#f18.7). Click the Add button within the popup window and then use the search bar to filter the list. Select the checkbox to the left of each desired role collection. Click the OK button to assign the role collection to the user. You’ll return to the Assign Role Collections : <USER> popup window.

[![Granting or Revoking a Role Collection Associated with a User in the SAP HANA XSA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein18_007.png)](img-f18.7.html) 

**Figure 18.7**    Granting or Revoking a Role Collection Associated with a User in the SAP HANA XSA Cockpit

To delete an assigned role collection, locate it in the Assign Role Collections : <USER> popup window and click the trashcan icon to its right. Click the Save button to activate the assigned role collections for the given user.

### 18.2.4    Managing Organization and Space Access

Developers will need to be assigned access to an organization or a space within an organization allowing them to create a container and deploy design-time content within an HDI container. To create and manage organizations and spaces, click the Organizations menu option from the SAP HANA XSA cockpit Home screen, as shown in [Figure 18.8](#18_002.html#f18.8). Locate an existing organization on the page. A separate tile will be created for each organization, with the title of each tile being the organization. Click the organization tile to drill into the configuration options and spaces associated with it.

[![Managing Organizations and Spaces in SAP HANA XSA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein18_008.png)](img-f18.8.html) 

**Figure 18.8**    Managing Organizations and Spaces in SAP HANA XSA Cockpit

When you click into the organization, the accordion menu changes on the right and includes new menu options for the organization. Click the Members menu option. A list of organization members will appear. To add a new member, click the Add Members button. When adding a member, you can grant one of two privileges. The first privilege is the organization manager, which grants full access to the organization and all spaces within the organization. Select the checkbox beside the Organization Manager role to grant it to the member. Grant the organization auditor role for members that only need read access to the organization and all spaces within the organization. Modify the assignments by using the pencil icon to the right of each listed member. You can also delete a member by clicking the trashcan icon to the right of each member.

To access the spaces within the selected organization, click the spaces button in the accordion menu to the right. Spaces within a selected organization will be displayed as tiles on the right side of the interface. Click the name of a space to drill down into the space options. Again, the accordion menu will change to show options specific to the management of spaces. Once again, click the Members menu item in the space-specific accordion menu. A list of existing members will appear on the right, as shown in [Figure 18.9](#18_002.html#f18.9).

[![Managing Members within a Space Using the SAP HANA XSA Cockpit](bilderklein/klein18_009.png)](img-f18.9.html) 

**Figure 18.9**    Managing Members within a Space Using the SAP HANA XSA Cockpit

Use this interface, shown in [Figure 18.9](#18_002.html#f18.9), to add members and space-specific role assignments. Three space roles are available. A space manager will have the ability to change various options for a given space using the SAP HANA XSA cockpit or other available interfaces. The space developers role grants a member the ability to manage applications and services deployed to the space. For example, a developer needs this access to use this space within SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA to build a project or deploy it to its runtime HDI container. The space auditors role allows a member to view the configuration of the space without the ability to make changes. Developers cannot deploy runtime content with this role. Again, be sure you understand that SAP HANA XSA users will often need access to an organization or space within to deploy applications based on that space. Also, organization and space access is managed independently of application access granted with role collections.

You should now understand how users, organizations, spaces, and role collections are managed within the SAP HANA XSA platform using the SAP HANA XSA cockpit. Note that SAP HANA XSA role collections and SAP HANA XSA application roles are decoupled from the SAP HANA database. Thus, developers cannot deploy applications that are runtime without to proper access to a space. Next, we’ll review another important tool that developers use in the SAP HANA XSA platform from a security standpoint, SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA.

## 18.3    Working with SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA

SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, a web-based application hosted within the SAP HANA XSA platform, is used by developers to create applications for the SAP HANA XSA platform. SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA can also be used by developers to create SAP HANA database catalog objects, SAP HANA calculation views, SAP HANA core data services (CDS) artifacts, and SAP HANA XSA-based repository roles. From a security perspective, you can use SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA to manage roles deployed within a specific HDI container. As an SAP HANA and SAP HANA XSA security administrator, you must understand the role of this tool and the steps required to grant developers access to it. In the next section, we’ll provide an overview of the tool and the components that govern its security.

### 18.3.1    SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA Overview

SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA is deployed within the SAP HANA XSA platform. Before you can access SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, you’ll need to verify a few items. First, when SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA 2.0 is installed to the SAP HANA XSA platform, the deployment does not create role collections in the SAP HANA XSA cockpit. You must log on to the SAP HANA XSA cockpit and create two new role collections. You only need to do this once in most cases. For example, you can create the role collections shown in [Table 18.1](#18_003.html#t18.1).

 
| Role Collection Name || Application Identifier || Included Role/Role Template |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ZXS\_WEBIDE\_ADMIN || webide!i1 || WebIDE\_Administrator |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ZSX\_WEBIDE\_DEVELOPER || webide!i1 || WebIDE\_Developer |

**Table 18.1**    Example Roles Collections to Create before Accessing SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA

With the two role collections created, SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA user must be granted at a minimum the ZSX\_WEBIDE\_DEVELOPER role collection example shown in [Table 18.1](#18_003.html#t18.1). The application role WebIDE\_Developer allows a user to access SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA and the SAP HANA database explorer. The WebIDE\_Administrator role grants access to additional tools within SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA such as the space enablement tool.

In addition to these custom role collections, a user might also need the following SAP HANA XSA privileges depending on their function:

*   At a minimum, the user needs the role collection XS\_CONTROLLER\_USER granted to work with spaces and organizations when building projects or deploying them to the runtime.
    
*   For a given space, they’ll need the space role space developers to build or deploy projects to the runtime.
    

If you have an SAP HANA XSA user and have the correct access to the space, organization, and SAP HANA XSA platform, you should be able to log on to the SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA application. Before you can log on, you must identify the URL used to access the SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA application. If you’re unsure of the URL, you can access the SAP HANA XSA command line and run the following commands to list each deployed application and its URL:

```
xs login
xs a
```

Once you have the URL, access SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA and provide your credentials. You’ll then land on the application’s homepage, as shown in [Figure 18.10](#18_003.html#f18.10).

[![SAP Web IDE for SAP HANASAP Web IDE for SAP HANAhomepage Homepage](bilderklein/klein18_010.png)](img-f18.10.html) 

**Figure 18.10**    SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA Homepage

The interface is divided into menu icon options on the left, a file menu bar on the top a workspace area containing your code, and then a working area on the right. As you open objects in the workspace, they will open in the working area on the right.

In this section, we won’t go into detail about how to use SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA to develop content. That topic is beyond the scope of this book. The goal of this section is to make sure administrators understand how to set up security for SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA and how users access the application.

###### More Information on Development within SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA

You can find more information on SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA within the SAP HANA Developer Guide for SAP HANA XSA, available at [http://s-prs.co/v498221](http://s-prs.co/v498221).

Look for the section titled “SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA Reference.”

### 18.3.2    SAP HANA Database Explorer in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA

SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA also provides the SAP HANA database explorer where you can connect to an SAP HANA database or HDI container schema to look for and work with catalog objects at runtime. From SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA homepage, locate the file menu bar and select Tools • Database Explorer to access the SAP HANA database explorer.

Within this interface, you can add connections by clicking the large plus sign (+) in the pane just below the file menu bar. You can connect to the following Database Types: SAP HANA database, SAP HANA database (Multitenant), HDI Container, or a specific Application Managed Service Instance. Select the HDI Container option to connect to the HDI container schema. In the HDI Schema list, locate the service instance name for your HDI container. The service instance name starts with your current logon user name and ends with your container name flowed by \-hdi\_db. To connect to classic SAP HANA database objects, select either SAP HANA database or SAP HANA database (Multitenant) and fill in the connection information for the database.

Once you’ve established a connection to the database, you can access the SQL console where you can execute SQL statements. In addition to the standard SQL console, you can also choose the Open SQL Console (Admin) option, which launches the console as a system user with API access to the HDI container schemas and procedures. Note that you can only launch this console if you’re using an HDI container service-based connection. You can use this admin console to grant users access to runtime HDI container objects.

For each connection, you’ll be provided with a graphical list of various catalog object types. For example, if you’re searching for a table, click the table icon and then use the search bar in the pane below to locate a table by name. Once you locate an object in the list, double-click the object to reveal its metadata, or right-click the object to launch a popup window containing options for interacting with the selected object. You should now have a basic understanding of the SAP HANA database explorer within SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA.

###### More Information on the SAP HANA Database Explorer

For more information on the SAP HANA database explorer, refer to the SAP HANA Database Explorer Guide, available at [http://s-prs.co/v498222](http://s-prs.co/v498222).

In the next section, we’ll go into more detail about HDI containers from a security perspective, and we’ll also revisit the SAP HANA database explorer using an example use case. We’ll also further explore SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA as we’ll discuss how HDI container roles are created.

## 18.4    HDI Containers and Security

With the SAP HANA XSA framework, SAP HANA development occurs within a service layer called the SAP HANA Deployment Infrastructure (HDI). Like the SAP HANA XS or \_SYS\_REPO model, HDI containers have a design-time concept and a runtime concept, but as you’ll see, HDI has several differences. When creating an HDI container, SAP HANA will separate out a design-time container and a runtime container. The design-time container will host metadata and code representing database artifacts and applications. The design-time container is not part of the runtime SAP HANA database but is always attached to its corresponding runtime container. The runtime container represents deployed objects that have been activated in the SAP HANA database within a specified SAP HANA XSA space. A runtime container is part of the SAP HANA database, and when built, several corresponding database objects will be created.

From a security perspective, each HDI container is isolated from other containers and even from other SAP HANA database catalog objects out of the box. In general, a container only has access to runtime objects within that same container. HDI container-based roles, like repository roles in SAP HANA XS, can be created within the container and granted to developers and users. At design time, no known security exists: Design-time workspace security is decoupled from the SAP HANA database. A developer has access to all development artifacts within the design-time container assuming the code was shared with them from outside of SAP HANA. If they import that same content into their SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA workspace and have been granted access to the corresponding SAP HANA XSA managed organization or space, they can potentially modify security at runtime.

This arrangement alone poses the most pressing security concern when using HDI containers to manage HDI-based repository roles. In theory, a developer could escalate their own privileges or the privileges of other users by modifying the makeup of an HDI container-based role. In addition, a developer could modify analytic privileges that govern access to data. In our opinion, a developer should not have the ability to elevate their own privileges inside or outside a container. With the SAP HANA XS repository, you could use package organization and package privileges to prevent developers from elevating their own privileges at design time. With the SAP HANA XSA development environment, you would have to set up and manage a complex landscape of independent HDI containers to decouple security objects from development objects. This decoupling is complex because HDI containers are not aware of each other, nor do they have access to each other’s content without a significant amount of repetitive administration.

To this end, we recommend that administrators continue to manage their SAP HANA security model using the SAP HANA XS repository-based roles and continue developing SAP HANA calculation views, database objects, and other items in SAP HANA XS until SAP addresses these security concerns. This recommendation is limited to the use of SAP HANA as a business intelligence solution or where the security of data is crucial. If you’re simply managing applications like OData services or GUIs, the current security capabilities of SAP HANA XSA are probably sufficient.

Now, let’s take a closer look at the architecture of the HDI container.

### 18.4.1    Security Architecture of the HDI Container

At runtime, an HDI container is comprised of a series of database schemas. The name of the schemas is directly based on the name of the project you define in the SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA workspace. For example, if you create the project shown in [Figure 18.11](#18_004.html#f18.11), with the name MyProj, any corresponding runtime objects will be stored in a schema named MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1.

[![Example SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA Project Structure](bilderklein/klein18_011.png)](img-f18.11.html) 

**Figure 18.11**    Example SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA Project Structure

A corresponding database user named MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1 will also be created, and that user will be the owner of any runtime object deployed to the database. Note that all users created by this process are restricted users that have no critical privileges, nor can they be used to access the database. These users also have no known password. In some cases, the user accounts are also deactivated. SAP HANA XSA includes a Node.js application that will broker the creation of objects from their design-time scripts in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA to their runtime equivalents within the database. In addition to the creation of the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1 user, other user accounts and schemas are also created for the storage of metadata and to host other deployment APIs. Using the same example, you’ll find the following users and schemas in an SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04 system:

*   One user and schema named MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1#DI. This user and schema contain APIs as stored procedures and metadata tables. For example, you can use a stored procedure in this schema to grant standard users access to the HDI schema MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1.
    
*   The object owner user and schema named MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1#OO. This user is an important user from a security standpoint, which we’ll explain in more detail shortly.
    
*   Multiple users using the naming pattern MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1\_<GUID>\_DT. What roles these users play is unclear, but from a security standpoint, they can use EXECUTE on some critical API stored procedures in the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1#DI schema.
    
*   Multiple users using the naming pattern MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1\_<GUID>\_RT. What roles these users play is unclear, but from a security standpoint, they can use EXECUTE on some critical API stored procedures in the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1#DI schema.
    

From a complete list of granted privileges, users, schemas, and other database objects associated with our example HDI container named MYPROJ, you can run the example SQL statements shown in [Listing 18.1](#18_004.html#l18.1) to see details concerning the deployment.

```
SELECT * FROM SYS.SCHEMAS WHERE SCHEMA_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.TABLES WHERE SCHEMA_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.VIEWS WHERE SCHEMA_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.PROCEDURES WHERE SCHEMA_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.OWNERSHIP WHERE SCHEMA_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.USERS WHERE USER_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.ROLES WHERE ROLE_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.GRANTED_ROLES WHERE ROLE_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.SYNONYMS WHERE SCHEMA_NAME like '%MYPROJ%'; 
SELECT * FROM SYS.GRANTED_PRIVILEGES 
WHERE  SCHEMA_NAME like 'MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#%';
```

**Listing 18.1**    Example SQL to See What Is Created in the SAP HANA Database to Support an HDI Container

In addition to these users, two roles are also created. The first is the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1::access\_role, and the second is the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1::external\_privileges\_role. MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1::access\_role is granted limited object privileges on the schema MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1 and is also granted privileges defined in .hdbgrants scripts for the application user or within the application\_user value array. The role MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1::external\_privileges\_role has no defined privileges by default.

The user account that ends in “#OO” or MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1#OO using our working example is the first account we’ll examine. “OO” is short for “object owner,” and we’ll use the term #OO at times in this chapter when referring to this user. By default, this user has limited access to the database but has the CREATE ANY, CREATE VIRTUAL PACKAGE, and SELECT METADATA object privilege on the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1 schema. On its own schema, this user is only granted the CREATE TEMPORY TABLE object privilege. This user is also granted the roles \_SYS\_DI\_OO\_DEFAULTS and the PUBLIC role. The \_SYS\_DI\_OO\_DEFAULTS role provides “API”-like access to stored procedures and access to metadata views for manipulating the runtime objects in an HDI container. This role is also granted to all #OO users by default. Any privileges this role has been granted would apply to all #OO users in the database. However, we do not recommend leveraging this role in your security model design.

Out of the box, the #OO user will have access to objects in the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1 schema because it is the creator or “object owner” of all objects in that schema. In SAP HANA, if you create a catalog object, you have full privileges access to it. When an HDI container requires access at runtime to non-HDI container catalog objects (i.e., classic runtime objects in the database) or other runtime objects deployed by another HDI container, the #OO user must also have access to those catalog objects. For example, if you’ve deployed SAP S/4HANA on the SAP HANA database and SAP S/4HANA created the schema SAPABAP1, you would need to log on to SAP HANA as SAPABAP1 and run the following statement for the HDI container MyProj to access tables in that schema at runtime:

```
GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA SAPABAP1 TO MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#OO WITH GRANT OPTION;
```

A second process exists that SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA developers can use to grant the #OO user access to external objects using standard database role, .hdbgrants files, user-defined services, and .hdbsynonym files within your projects. We’ll explain this process in more detail in [Section 18.4.3](#18_004.html#h18.4.3).

The second user of interest is the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1#DI user, or #DI user for short. This user is the owner of a schema that contains tables, views, and stored procedures that are important to the mechanics of the HDI container at runtime. As mentioned earlier, you cannot log on as this user. Therefore, you would technically need another database user that has EXECUTE access to this schema, or the procedures within the schema, before you can grant external access outside of the HDI container. This process is quite complicated and requires executing a series of stored procedures in a variety of schemas and as different users to effectively give a non-HDI user the ability to grant access to the HDI user schema instead of creating SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA developer artifacts. Luckily, with SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, the SAP HANA database explorer provides an option for a user to open the SQL console as the “admin” or as \_SYS\_DI or as other technical system-generated users with EXECUTE access on the procedures.

###### Users with EXECUTE Access to the #DI Schema Procedures

Note that we could not determine the exact user that is impersonated when launching the SQL console as an admin within the SAP HANA database explorer. By querying the SAP HANA metadata views, we could see that the system account \_SYS\_DI is the owner of the procedures within the #DI schema. We can also see that other system-generated users also have the access. For example, the following SQL will list the user account with EXECUTE access on the procedure for the HDI container named MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1:

```
SELECT * FROM SYS.GRANTED_PRIVILEGES 
WHERE  SCHEMA_NAME like 'MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#%' 
and OBJECT_NAME like 'GRANT_CONTAINER_%'
```

You can also query the ownership view to see the owner of the procedures. The following SQL will list the owners of the procedures for the HDI container named MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1:

```
SELECT * FROM SYS.OWNERSHIP 
WHERE SCHEMA_NAME like '%MYPROJ%'
and OBJECT_NAME like 'GRANT_CONTAINER_%';
```

Opening the SQL console as the “admin” is a shortcut explained in Sections [Section 18.3.2](#18_003.html#h18.3.2) and [Section 18.4.3](#18_004.html#h18.4.3). Another option, which we’ll discuss later in [Section 18.4.2](#18_004.html#h18.4.2), is to create HDI container roles and then grant them to users. However, you’ll still need to use the SAP HANA database explorer’s SQL console run as an admin to grant the role to other users. Therefore, technically, you have two additional options to achieve the same result. However, these “easier” options give SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA developers security access and the ability to escalate their own privileges at runtime. This access is a major security concern because you cannot selectively prevent the editing of objects at design time like you could in the SAP HANA XS \_SYS\_REPO platform.

In the next section, we’ll review HDI container roles and how they you can use them to provide access to catalog objects, schemas, calculation views, and other items within an HDI container.

### 18.4.2    HDI Container Roles

Effectively, you’ll use HDI container roles as the basis for granting database users access to runtime objects within an HDI container’s schema. Once an HDI container role is created, you can then use a special SQL console, found in the SAP HANA database explorer, to execute special stored procedures that can grant HDI container roles to users. Within this section, we’ll provide an overview of HDI container roles, describe the steps for granting HDI container roles using the SAP HANA database explorer, and finally describe the steps required to authorize a standard database user EXECUTE access to the store procedures in the HDI container’s #DI schema.

#### Defining HDI Container Roles

HDI container roles are like legacy the SAP HANA XS repository roles we discussed in [Chapter 6](#06_001.html#h6); however HDI container roles can only provide security access to objects within the container by default. For the HDI role to reference external catalog objects, the #OO user must have the same access to the external catalog object including the WITH GRANT OPTION. In most cases, HDI container roles are created by developers within their project. As such, HDI container roles are not a feasible alternative to the SAP HANA XS repository-based roles that you could use to manage an entire database system’s security model. This limitation is the case for two major reasons:

*   First, no design-time security exists to prevent developers from manipulating HDI container roles when they have access to the design-time content and the ability to deploy it to container at runtime. Without this protection, developers could elevate their access to HDI content, external objects, and data within the SAP HANA database, thus bypassing standard security-based segregations. In this case, we’re specifically referring to tables, analytic privileges, and calculation views typically used in an SAP HANA-based business intelligence solution.
    
*   Second, the HDI container database #OO user, by default, has no access to objects outside of the container. This user would need access similar to what the \_SYS\_REPO user had if you were to create system-wide HDI container roles to manage the entire database’s security model. This approach would in turn give anyone with the corresponding HDI container design-time access the ability escalate their own privileges if even a single HDI container role was granted to the developer’s user account. In addition, granting HDI container roles to standard SAP HANA users is difficult, as is setting up cross-HDI container access exclusively for a security team. A complex SQL statement is required to grant HDI container roles, and complex scripts are required to grant cross-container access. This model would not be compliant with the segregation of duties and would not be secure, nor would this solution be scalable as a system-wide security model.
    

This process would also not be a one-time activity since, as each additional HDI container is created, access to runtime objects within that container would need to be granted to the legacy containers containing HDI roles used to govern the SAP HANA security model. The tedious nature of this arrangement also makes this solution unscalable.

Hopefully, SAP HANA will one day devise a solution where a system-managed HDI container is deployed within every SAP HANA database. A container that would have access to all new HDI containers and any classic runtime database objects in a way that is both secure from a design-time perspective and scalable from a management perspective. In the SAP HANA XS model, the \_SYS\_REPO service account was deployed with a high level of database access and had access to grant access to all design-time objects it owned. You could also easily grant \_SYS\_REPO access to runtime objects that were not created at design time. Furthermore, this grant activity only needs to be executed one time for each newly created runtime schema.

With that said, in this section, we’ll explain the makeup of HDI container roles and show you how they can be granted to users. An understanding of this process is necessary even if not recommended for supporting a system-wide security model. Some organizations have already began developing content within SAP HANA XSA, where establishing security for HDI containers is important.

HDI container roles are design-time scripts, using a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)-compliant syntax, that when built or activated, create runtime roles in the SAP HANA database. The privileges specified within the script must be possessed by the HDI #OO user, and the privileges must include the WITH GRANT OPTION. For catalog objects created in the HDI container, the #OO user will be the owner and therefore will have the necessary privileges.

For objects outside the container, #OO users will need to be granted permission, will need references to external schemas, and will need synonyms to reference external catalog objects. The synonym is required so that the .hdbrole can find the external object in the database. Based on testing, the .hdbrole only looks for catalog objects in the HDI container schema. Synonyms allow you to alias external objects in a way that the .hdbrole builder can find them. You can easily define a .hdbsynonym file to create the needed synonyms, and SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA has a GUI to help you create synonyms.

For external schemas, you’ll also need a schema reference, which can be configured in a .hdbconfig file. No GUI exists for this file, and we’ll share the JSON syntax for this file in [Listing 18.5](#18_004.html#l18.5). Let’s start by looking at the syntax for the .hdbrole file. [Listing 18.2](#18_004.html#l18.2) shows a basic .hdbrole file with no privileges being granted.

```
{ 
  "role":{ 
                "name":"MyProj.db.roles::EMPTYROLE" 
          }
 }
```

**Listing 18.2**    A Basic .hdbrole File with No Privileges Being Granted

The format starts with opening and closing curly brackets, as in {<some text>}. At the next value level, you’ll define a JSON value titled “role”: { <some text> }. Within that value pair level, you’ll define the “name”:”<namespace + role name>”,{<privilege text>} value. The namespace follows the project’s folder structure. For example, if you create this role in the MyProj project and store the role in the folder path MyProj • db • src • roles, the namespace would be MyProj.db.roles:: followed by the name of the role.

The remaining structure varies based on the privilege type. To further describe the syntax, let’s specify some requirements and then provide an example .hdbrole script. For example, let’s say you need to create a role granting SELECT access on the HDI table MyProj.db::CUSTOMERS, the external table in the SYSTEM schema CUSTOMERS, the entire SYSTEM schema, and the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1 schema. You would define the role using the code shown in [Listing 18.3](#18_004.html#l18.3).

```
{ 
  "role":{ 
    "name":"MyProj.db.roles::TABLE_READ_ONLY_ACCESS", 
      "object_privileges":[ 
      { 
       "name":"MyProj.db::CUSTOMERS", 
       "type":"TABLE", 
       "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
      } ,
      { 
       "name":"MyProj.db::CS_CUSTOMERS", 
       "type":"TABLE", 
       "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
      }
    ],
      
      "schema_privileges":[  
{  
    "reference":"REF_SYSTEM",
    "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
},
{  
    "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
}
  ]
    }
   }
```

**Listing 18.3**    Example .hdbrole

In addition to the .hdbrole file, you’ll also need to define .hdbsynonym and .hdbroleconfig files for the externally referenced catalog table objects and schemas. [Listing 18.4](#18_004.html#l18.4) shows the syntax of the required SYSTEM.hdbsynonym file. This file is required because “MyProj.db::CS\_CUSTOMERS” is actually a synonym pointing to the SYSTEM.CUSTOMERS table.

```
{
  "MyProj.db::CS_CUSTOMERS": {
    "target": {
      "object": "CUSTOMERS",
      "schema": "SYSTEM"
    }
  }
}
```

**Listing 18.4**    Required SYSTEM.hdbsynonym File for External Catalog Object References

The synonym is created in the HDI schema MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1 and is required when objects within an HDI container must reference objects outside the HDI container. Again, the #OO user must have access to this object, or the project will fail to build.

In addition, you’ll need to create a .hdbroleconfig file that describes a reference to the external schema SYSTEM. [Listing 18.5](#18_004.html#l18.5) shows an example of the file that is required. This JSON file requires that you map the HDI container role, by name, to an external schema reference or alias. You’ll then use the reference name "REF\_SYSTEM" within the definition of your .hdbrole file.

```
{ 
  "MyProj.db.roles::TABLE_READ_ONLY_ACCESS":{ 
    "REF_SYSTEM":{ 
      "schema":"SYSTEM" 
    }
  } 
}
```

**Listing 18.5**    Required ROLEREF.hdbroleconfig File for External Schema References

Now that we’ve reviewed the example file, let’s look at some other syntax values that you can use. An .hdbrole file can reference existing roles in the HDI container within the "global\_roles" value array. The following code is an example of the value string used to reference existing roles:

```
"global_roles":[ 
    "HDI_ROLE_1", 
    "HDI_ROLE_2" 
]
```

System privileges can be configured using the "system\_privileges" value array. In the following example, we are referencing two system privileges:

```
"system_privileges":[  
   "BACKUP ADMIN",
   "USER ADMIN"
 ]
```

Analytics privileges or structured privileges can be referenced using the "schema\_analytic\_privileges" value array. The syntax required depends on the referenced object. If you’re referencing an analytic privilege that is within your HDI container, you would use the following syntax:

```
"schema_analytic_privileges":[
{
"privileges": ["MyProj.db.aps::AP_CUSTOMER"]
} 
```

In this case, you’ll only need the namespace or package folder structure and the name of the analytic privilege entered into the "privileges" value string. If you’re referring to an external structured privilege that has a schema, you would use the syntax shown in [Listing 18.6](#18_004.html#l18.6).

```
"schema_analytic_privileges":[
   {
     "schema_reference":"APSchemaRef1",
     "privileges": ["AP1", "AP2"] }
 ]
```

**Listing 18.6**    Privilege Value String

As with external schemas, the schema reference must be defined in the supporting .hdbroleconfig file.

###### Additional Information on the Syntax of the .hdbrole File

For additional information on the complete syntax of the .hdbrole file, refer to the “SAP HDI Artifact Types and Build Plugins Reference” section in the SAP HANA Development Infrastructure Reference Guide for SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, available at [http://s-prs.co/v498223](http://s-prs.co/v498223).

Recall from [Chapter 6](#06_001.html#h6) that repository-based roles in the SAP HANA XS platform could not be directly granted to a grantee using GRANT or REVOKE statements. You had to execute a stored procedure and provide input parameters to grant repository roles. This limitation is because only the owner \_SYS\_REPO can grant the role as no other user has the WITH GRANT OPTION. However, most of the GUI interfaces would automatically execute the procedures when you selected repository roles within the GUI workflow. HDI roles have a similar reequipment. Only system-managed technical users can grant HDI container roles out of the box. With the SAP HANA XS repository roles, you simply need to grant EXECUTE on the \_SYS\_REPO schema to security administrators, allowing them to perform the action. That process was easy to execute because the SYSTEM account had these privileges including the WITH GRANT OPTION. You could also include them in repository roles without much effort.

Within the HDI platform, only the \_SYS\_DI user and a few other technical users have these privileges directly by default. Therefore, you only have two options for granting these privileges:

*   You can use the SAP HANA database explorer based on a service connection of the HDI container. Within that connection, you can right-click and select Open SQL Console (Admin), which will open the SQL console that impersonates a user that has EXECUTE access to the procedures.
    
*   You can leverage the stored procedure in the \_SYS\_DI schema called GRANT\_CONTAINER\_API\_PRIVILEGES\_WITH\_GRANT\_OPTION. By default, the SYSTEM account has EXECUTE privileges on this procedure. However, running this procedure is not straightforward since you must run a series of other SQL statements in the correct sequence to use this procedure properly.
    

Let’s look at each of these options in more detail starting with the first option.

#### Granting HDI Roles with the SAP HANA Database Explorer

To grant an HDI role using SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, you must first access the SAP HANA database explorer. In [Section 18.3](#18_003.html#h18.3), we provided details for accessing the SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA application. Once logged into the application, you’ll notice three icons on the vertical bar on the left side, as shown in [Figure 18.12](#18_004.html#f18.12). The icon that appears as a set of stacked cubes or boxes is the icon used to launch the SAP HANA database explorer view. You can also use the file menu option Tools • Database Explorer to launch the SAP HANA database explorer interface.

[![SAP HANA Database Explorer in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA](bilderklein/klein18_012.png)](img-f18.12.html) 

**Figure 18.12**    SAP HANA Database Explorer in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA

Before you can launch the Open SQL Console (Admin) option, you’ll need to create the correct type of connection to the database. To create the connection, locate the large plus sign (+) above the pane that contains the existing database connections shown in [Figure 18.12](#18_004.html#f18.12). If this is the first time you’re accessing the SAP HANA database explorer, you won’t have an existing connection. Once you click the plus sign (+), the Add Database window will appear. Choose the Database Type of HDI container. Search for your current container. In our environment, the correct container was prefixed with the current logon user’s name followed by a serial code, and then our project name was suffixed with hdi\_db, as shown in [Figure 18.13](#18_004.html#f18.13).

[![Adding a Database from an HDI Container Connection](bilderklein/klein18_013.png)](img-f18.13.html) 

**Figure 18.13**    Adding a Database from an HDI Container Connection

This connection will show you all the catalog objects in the HDI’s database schema. To access the SQL console as an admin, right-click the connection’s top node and choose Open SQL Console (Admin), as shown in [Figure 18.14](#18_004.html#f18.14).

The SQL console will open on the right, where you can execute a series of SQL statements that will grant HDI container roles to a specified user. The SQL that must be executed is somewhat complex. You must run five different statements to grant the role. In addition, you’ll need the technical name of the HDI container.

[![Accessing the SQL Console as an HDI Container Administrator](bilderklein/klein18_014.png)](img-f18.14.html) 

**Figure 18.14**    Accessing the SQL Console as an HDI Container Administrator

If you need the technical name of the HDI container, you can run a SQL statement to view the name, but you’ll need to use a different SQL console. The Admin user does not have the correct access to show the technical container name, so you’ll need to run the SQL statement in a SQL console connected with a user with SELECT access on the \_SYS\_DI schema. For example, the SYSTEM user has this access by default. The following statement will show you the technical name of the HDI container:

```
SELECT * FROM "_SYS_DI".M_ALL_CONTAINERS WHERE CONTAINER_NAME like 'MYPROJ%';
```
