After getting the technical name, make sure you’re in the SQL console connected as the HDI container admin before proceeding with the next steps. The first statement you’ll need to run sets the default schema used for your temporary tables:

```
SET SCHEMA "MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#DI";
```

The second statement will create a local temporary column table in the schema. You’ll use this temporary table to store role grant information used as an input parameter in the stored procedure:

```
CREATE LOCAL TEMPORARY COLUMN TABLE #ROLES LIKE _SYS_DI.TT_SCHEMA_ROLES;
```

The third statement will insert the role name information and target user into the temporary table named #ROLES. To grant the role MyProj.db.roles::TABLE\_READ\_ONLY\_ACCESS (input parameter 1) to the user SYSTEM (input parameter 3), you’ll need to adjust the following statement to match your use case:

```
INSERT INTO #ROLES ( ROLE_NAME, PRINCIPAL_SCHEMA_NAME, PRINCIPAL_NAME ) 
VALUES ( 'MyProj.db.roles::TABLE_READ_ONLY_ACCESS', '', 'SYSTEM' );
```

The fourth statement will call the stored procedure in the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1#DI schema. When crafting this statement, make sure you update the schema name to match the name of the #DI schema supporting your HDI container:

```
CALL MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#DI.GRANT_CONTAINER_SCHEMA_ROLES(#ROLES, _SYS_DI.T_NO_PARAMETERS, ?, ?, ?);
```

The output of this procedure will include multiple tabs of results. Look at the Results 1 tab to see a verbose message about the actions that were executed and to validate that the role was granted properly to the user.

Finally, you’ll drop the temporary table because it is no longer needed, as follows:

```
DROP TABLE #ROLES;
```

After running each of these statements correctly, your target user will be granted the HDI container role. Now let’s look at the second option in more detail.

#### Granting HDI Roles with a Database User

As a second option, you can also use a standard SAP HANA database user to grant the statements outlined above and effectively grant an HDI container role to a database user. However, the standard user must first be set up with the same privileges that the HDI container admin possesses. Fortunately, the \_SYS\_DI schema provides a procedure that you can use to grant the correct privileges to another user.

By default, only the SYSTEM account has the access necessary to execute the procedures in the \_SYS\_DI schema. Therefore, you’ll need to start by connecting to the SQL console as the SYSTEM user.

The first statement you’ll need to execute will set the default schema used in the example. Run the following SQL statement:

```
SET SCHEMA SYSTEM;
```

Next, you’ll temporarily move your HDI container to the \_SYS\_DI container group. This step is required because the procedure in the \_SYS\_DI container is hard-coded to reference this group and will not work on HDI containers in other groups. When we’re done, you’ll move the HDI container back to its original group. Before you move the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1 HDI container, you’ll need to query the database to capture its current container group with the following statement:

```
SELECT * FROM "_SYS_DI".M_ALL_CONTAINERS WHERE CONTAINER_NAME like 'MYPROJ%';
```

Look for the value in the CONTAINER\_GROUP\_NAME column. In our example, our column was named CG\_SYS\_XS\_HANA\_BROKER\_2. Again, we’ll move this container back to this group when we’re done granting the privileges.

Now, you can execute the SQL to temporarily move the HDI container into the required container group \_SYS\_DI with the following statement:

```
CALL _SYS_DI.MOVE_CONTAINER_TO_GROUP('MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1', '_SYS_DI', _SYS_DI.T_NO_PARAMETERS, ?, ?, ?);
```

Next, you’ll create a local temporary table in the SYSTEM schema named #PRIVILEGES with the following statement:

```
CREATE LOCAL TEMPORARY COLUMN TABLE #PRIVILEGES LIKE _SYS_DI.TT_API_PRIVILEGES;
```

Next, you’ll insert all the API privileges into the temporary table. This array is required as an input for the stored procedure. In the following script, replace the target user name JHAUN with your target user account name:

```
INSERT INTO #PRIVILEGES (PRINCIPAL_NAME, PRIVILEGE_NAME, OBJECT_NAME) SELECT 'JHAUN', PRIVILEGE_NAME, OBJECT_NAME FROM _SYS_DI.T_DEFAULT_CONTAINER_ADMIN_PRIVILEGES; 
```

Next, execute the stored procedure in the \_SYS\_DI schema that grants the array of privileges in the #PRIVILEGES temporary table. The name of the procedure is GRANT\_CONTAINER\_API\_PRIVILEGES\_WITH\_GRANT\_OPTION, which will grant all the API privileges to the user and include the WITH GRANT OPTION so that the user can selectively grant the same privileges to other users in the future. In your script, you’ll need to update the value for the first parameter to match the technical name of your HDI container, as follows:

```
CALL _SYS_DI.GRANT_CONTAINER_API_PRIVILEGES_WITH_GRANT_OPTION('MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1', #PRIVILEGES, _SYS_DI.T_NO_PARAMETERS, ?, ?, ?);
```

The results of this procedure include multiple output tabs. Review the first tab, which will contain a verbose information about each grant action.

Next, you’ll need to drop the temporary table #PRIVILEGES. Run the following SQL:

```
DROP TABLE #PRIVILEGES;
```

Finally, you’ll need to return our HDI container back to its original HDI container group. This step is critical and can’t be skipped.

```
CALL _SYS_DI.MOVE_CONTAINER_TO_GROUP('MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1', 'CG_SYS_XS_HANA_BROKER_2', _SYS_DI.T_NO_PARAMETERS, ?, ?, ?);
```

At this point, you can now log on to the SQL console as the target user and run the following statements. These examples are the same statements used in the previous section. Therefore, we’ll assume that you already understand each step and won’t go into detail about each step. Run the statements shown in [Listing 18.7](#18_004.html#l18.7), adjusting the syntax for your specific environment.

```
SET SCHEMA "MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#DI";
CREATE LOCAL TEMPORARY COLUMN TABLE #ROLES LIKE _SYS_DI.TT_SCHEMA_ROLES;
INSERT INTO #ROLES ( ROLE_NAME, PRINCIPAL_SCHEMA_NAME, PRINCIPAL_NAME ) 
VALUES ( 'MyProj.db.roles::TABLE_READ_ONLY_ACCESS', '', 'SYSTEM' );
CALL MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#DI.GRANT_CONTAINER_SCHEMA_ROLES(#ROLES, _SYS_DI.T_NO_PARAMETERS, ?, ?, ?);
DROP TABLE #ROLES; 
```

**Listing 18.7**    SQL Statements That Must Be Executed to Grant an HDI Container Role to a Database User

You should now have a basic understanding of the structure of the .hdbrole and the two dependent objects .hdbsynonym and .hdbroleconfig that are required when referencing external catalog objects. You should also understand the process for granting an HDI container role to a database user and also the process for creating an HDI container admin user. In the next section, we’ll provide you more details on .hdbsynonym files, which are also required when you develop calculation views against external tables. We’ll also show you the synonym GUI available in the latest version of SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA.

### 18.4.3    Granting the HDI Container Access to External Objects

When working within an HDI container using SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, two security considerations must be addressed: First, developers might need access to runtime catalog objects that are outside of the HDI container as well as access to objects in other HDI containers. By default, developers will only have access to catalog objects within the HDI container or project workspace.

If you’re building a business intelligence solution, your tables and schemas will likely be in a non-repository-based schemas or a schema owned by a standard user account. Therefore, your HDI container will probably need access to external objects or other HDI containers. Second, when you deploy HDI container content referencing external objects, the #OO user will require access to those external objects at runtime. SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA provides mechanisms that address both situations, but neither mechanism can be completed exclusively within SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA by developers. Therefore, you’ll need to explore each option and its requirements in detail. Let’s look first at the security considerations for external catalog objects, and then we’ll look at the considerations for other HDI containers.

#### Developer Access to External Catalog Objects at Design Time

SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA uses user-provided services and services instances to proxy access to external catalog objects or HDI containers. This service is part of the SAP HANA XSA architecture and can be created in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA or within the SAP HANA XSA cockpit. You can also use the SAP HANA XSA cockpit to manage the service after it is created. A service is effectively a snippet of code that provides a Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) access bridge to the SAP HANA database. The snippet of code is in JSON format, as shown in the example in [Figure 18.15](#18_004.html#f18.15).

[![Example Definition of a User-Provided Service within the SAP HANA XSA Cockpit GUI](bilderklein/klein18_015.png)](img-f18.15.html) 

**Figure 18.15**    Example Definition of a User-Provided Service within the SAP HANA XSA Cockpit GUI

Once defined and associated with your HDI container di-builder, you can configure your project to use this service. However, SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA also has a workflow to help you create the service, and we’ll walk you through this process in this section.

Before you build a service, let’s first discuss the security that the service user will require. The service bridge provides two features. First, at design time, the service can be selected when searching for external catalog objects. For example, when creating synonyms or SAP HANA calculation views, you might need to search for an external object using this service. Second, if you use .hdbgrants files to grant privileges to the #OO user, this service bridge will grant the permissions to the #OO user. Therefore, when using .hdbgrants, the service user must have the required privileges for both scenarios including the WITH GRANT OPTION. This service user will also become a permanent component of the project once referenced in .hdbgrants project files. The security team must carefully design the service account user on the SAP HANA database and ensure that the account only possesses the privileges necessary to support the application.

Now, let’s look at the process of creating a user-provided service using SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA GUI. Before starting this step, make sure your project has an assigned space and di-builder. Within your SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA project, right-click the db folder and choose New • SAP HANA Service Connection, as shown in [Figure 18.16](#18_004.html#f18.16).

[![Creating an SAP HANA Service Connection](bilderklein/klein18_016.png)](img-f18.16.html) 

**Figure 18.16**    Creating an SAP HANA Service Connection

The Add External SAP HANA Service window will appear. Enter the details for the SAP HANA database, as shown in [Figure 18.17](#18_004.html#f18.17), including the connection information and the credentials of a user in the local database.

[![Defining the Service Connection](bilderklein/klein18_017.png)](img-f18.17.html) 

**Figure 18.17**    Defining the Service Connection

Click OK to continue. The service will now be available to help you search for external objects outside the HDI container. For example, when creating a synonym, you can connect to the service and search for objects within the GUI. Again, from a security standpoint, only objects that the service has SELECT access on will be displayed. A developer doesn’t have to create this service if you are concerned about the developer having the credentials of the service user. A security admin and SAP HANA XSA admin can define the service using the SAP HANA XSA cockpit. The developer can then update the mta.yaml file and reference the service. For example, you can use the mta.yaml GUI editor to create or change the service value at any time.

[Figure 18.18](#18_004.html#f18.18) shows an example of editing this value using the mta.yml GUI. You’ll find the mta.yaml file within the workspace of your project. By default, opening the file will launch the GUI editor. Select the Resources option and then choose the cross-container-servcie-1 to reveal the service-name attribute. Change the value to match the value of the user-defined service. Note that changing this value might impact any existing .hdbgrants files within the project because .hdbgrants files reference services for granting access to the #OO user at runtime.

[![Changing the Service-Name Associated with Our MTA Project within the mta.yaml File](bilderklein/klein18_018.png)](img-f18.18.html) 

**Figure 18.18**    Changing the Service-Name Associated with Our MTA Project within the mta.yaml File

#### Developer Access to Additional HDI Containers

We’ll use a similar process to provide design-time access to another HDI container. When defining the SAP HANA service connection, choose the option HDI Container and then select an existing HDI container. The list will only show HDI containers that are fully built and deployed to the database and have a service instance in SAP HANA XSA. A new service will be defined in the mta.yaml file that will also be selectable when defining calculation views and synonyms in the GUI. Note that you’ll need to grant the local project #OO user access to the remote container before you can build referencing objects. In the next section, we’ll explain how you can use the .hdbgrants file and HDI roles to grant the necessary access.

#### #OO Service User Access to Objects at Runtime

Before you can fully deploy or build content files in a project, the #OO user of the container must have access to the remote content it references. Remote content includes classic SAP HANA database objects as well as other HDI containers. You can create this access in three ways. Let’s look at each option available for a given scenario:

*   When access to external objects in the classic SAP HANA database is required, the security team can directly grant privileges. In short, they can grant the #OO user access to the external catalog objects using the SQL console or SAP HANA cockpit. This step can be completed independent of the developer and SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA artifacts. This option is the more secure option because the developer won’t need access to a user-provided service that can grant privileges.
    
*   Security admins can create standard roles within the database that can then be granted to the #OO user, using .hdbgrants files defined by the developers. In this case, the user-provided service will require the ability to grant these roles to the #OO user. The service user is the user that grants these roles to the #OO accounts based on the information in the .hdbgrants file. This approach can be less secure because a crafty developer could grant the #OO user access to an object and then update an HDI roles in that container, which is assigned to their account, to elevate their own privileges.
    
*   When developers require access to a remote HDI container, they can again use .hdbgrants files to provide the local #OO user access to remote HDI container objects. In this case, the remote HDI container will need two HDI roles created within their HDI container by a developer as well. With this scenario, developers can build the solution without any involvement from the SAP HANA database security team.
    

To better understand each of these options, let’s walk through an example setup scenario for each option. Let’s start with a detailed view of the first option where the SAP HANA database security team grants the privileges to the #OO user directly.

##### Directly Granting Privileges to the #OO User

When directly granting privileges to the #OO user, the SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA developer does not need to create .hdbgrant files within their project but will still need a service for design-time access to database objects outside of the HDI container. They will also need to communicate a list of external objects that they that their HDI container will access. Let’s start by explaining the process and requirements necessary to set up a service user.

In this scenario, the developer will use the service to view and read metadata from objects outside of the HDI container. The service account will need SELECT access to views and tables in the external schema as well as EXECUTE access to table valued functions and stored procedures. Let’s assume that the external schema is named SAPABAP1 and that the developers need to query all tables, views, and tabled valued functions in this schema. To achieve this setup, the administrator will execute the SQL shown in [Listing 18.8](#18_004.html#l18.8).

```
CREATE USER SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1 PASSWORD "<some password>" NO FORCE_FIRST_PASSWORD_CHANGE;
CREATE ROLE SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1_ROLE;
GRANT SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1_ROLE TO SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1;
GRANT SELECT, EXECUTE ON SCHEMA SAPABAP1 TO SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1_ROLE;
```

**Listing 18.8**    Four Example SQL Statements Creating a Service Account and Roles for Design-Time Access to Catalog Objects outside the HDI Container

As shown in [Listing 18.8](#18_004.html#l18.8), the first statement will create a service account user named SVC\_FOR\_HDI\_PRJ\_SAPABAP1 that the developer or SAP HANA XSA admin can utilize when creating the user-provided service. You’ll then create a standard role and then grant that role the privileges necessary to access the SAPABAP1 schema. Finally, we’ll grant the role SVC\_FOR\_HDI\_PRJ\_SAPABAP1\_ROLE to the user account.

Next, you’ll need to grant the same privileges to the #OO user allowing the HDI content to access the same tables at runtime. The SQL shown in [Listing 18.9](#18_004.html#l18.9) can be utilized to set up the necessary security.

```
CREATE ROLE SVC_FOR_HDI_#OO_SAPABAP1_ROLE;
GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA SAPABAP1 TO SVC_FOR_HDI_#OO_SAPABAP1_ROLE WITH GRANT OPTION;
GRANT SVC_FOR_HDI_#OO_SAPABAP1_ROLE TO MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#OO;
```

**Listing 18.9**    Three Example SQL Statements Granting the #OO User Access to a Catalog Schema at Run-time

As shown in [Listing 18.9](#18_004.html#l18.9), you’ll start by creating a role that will be granted to the HDI container MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1#OO or object owner user. You’ll then grant SELECT access to the role and include the WITH GRANT OPTION. The WITH GRANT OPTION is required as the #OO user is delegating access to the remote schema. Finally, you’ll grant the SVC\_FOR\_HDI\_#OO\_SAPABAP1\_ROLE to the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1#OO user.

Again, with this option, the developer does not need to use .hdbgrants files within their project, nor does the service user require the ability to grant these same privileges to other users. The service account, used by the user-provided service, has limited access to the database.

##### Using .hdbgrants to Provide Access to External Catalog Objects

A second option, similar to the first option, is to leverage the .hdbgrants files within a project. However, one key difference is that the user-provided service must have the ability to grant two specific roles to the #OO user. In this scenario, the service user will require elevated privileges. Let’s start by examining the SQL that the SAP HANA security team will execute to create the service user, roles, and permissions.

First, you’ll need to create a service user SVC\_FOR\_HDI\_PRJ\_SAPABAP1 like we did in the previous section’s example. Execute the following SQL to create the service account user:

```
CREATE USER SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1 PASSWORD "<some password>" NO FORCE_FIRST_PASSWORD_CHANGE;
```

Next, you’ll need to create two roles like you did in the previous section’s example. Execute the following SQL to create the two roles:

```
CREATE ROLE SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1_ROLE;
CREATE ROLE SVC_FOR_HDI_#OO_SAPABAP1_ROLE;
```

Next, you’ll need to grant access to the two roles. The first role would be used by the application layer user in the .hdbgrants file. The second role will be used for the object owner in the .hdbgrants file. The object owner will require the WITH GRANT OPTION. Execute the following SQL to grant permissions to the two roles:

```
GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA SAPABAP1 TO SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1_ROLE;
GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA SAPABAP1 TO SVC_FOR_HDI_#OO_SAPABAP1_ROLE WITH GRANT OPTION;
```

Finally, you’ll need to grant both roles to the SVC\_FOR\_HDI\_PRJ\_SAPABAP1 user account including the WITH ADMIN OPTION. The .hdbgrants file will use the service user to grant these roles to the #OO user. Therefore, the service account now needs elevated access to accomplish this. This arrangement is a major difference from the first option, where a security team member grants directly to the #OO user. When using .hdbgrants files, the service user does this task and therefore needs the required privileges. Execute the following SQL to grant the two roles to the service account, including the WITH ADMIN OPTION:

```
GRANT SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1_ROLE TO SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1 WITH ADMIN OPTION;
GRANT SVC_FOR_HDI_#OO_SAPABAP1_ROLE TO SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1 WITH ADMIN OPTION;
```

Now, let’s walk through the process the developer would follow in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA to create the user-provided service, synonyms, and .hdbgrants files. Let’s start by accessing SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA and opening the existing project MyProj for this example. Start by creating the user-provided service needed to access the SAPABAP1 schema at design time and to grant the created roles at runtime to the #OO user.

Right-click the folder db within the project and choose SAP HANA Service Connection, as shown in [Figure 18.19](#18_004.html#f18.19).

[![Creating a New User-Provided Service within Our Project](bilderklein/klein18_019.png)](img-f18.19.html) 

**Figure 18.19**    Creating a New User-Provided Service within Our Project

Using the service account credentials created by the SAP HANA security team in our example, create a service named SAPABAP1, as shown in [Figure 18.20](#18_004.html#f18.20). We recommend using the target schema name for the service to help other developers identify the right service.

[![Defining the User-Provided Service](bilderklein/klein18_020.png)](img-f18.20.html) 

**Figure 18.20**    Defining the User-Provided Service

To further demonstrate the example, let’s assume that the developer is creating a calculation view based on the table /SDF/SQLCUST in the SAPBAP1 schema. Assume that the developer is adding a new table to a project node within the calculation view. The Find Data Source window will appear, as shown in [Figure 18.21](#18_004.html#f18.21). In this window, choose the External Services and then SAPABAP1 as the service name. Search for the table /SDF/SQLCUST. Select the table in the list and then click the Create Synonym button.

[![Using the External Service to Find the External Table and then Create a Synonym](bilderklein/klein18_021.png)](img-f18.21.html) 

**Figure 18.21**    Using the External Service to Find the External Table and then Create a Synonym

SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA provides options to help developers easily create synonyms and .hdbgrant files. All a developer needs to know are the names of the two roles provided by the SAP HANA security team. On the next screen, shown in [Figure 18.22](#18_004.html#f18.22), enter the desired Synonym Name in the provided field. The synonym is required to link the local HDI container to the external table.

In the section below the synonym list, choose the generate .hdbgrants file option and then enter the role “SVC\_FOR\_HDI\_#OO\_SAPABAP1\_ROLE” in the Object Owner Role field. Then, enter “SVC\_FOR\_HDI\_PRJ\_SAPABAP1\_ROLE” in the Application User Role field. Note that you only need to choose these options the first time you use the service. Click Finish, and the development infrastructure builder will partially deploy to validate that the service user has the necessary access. In most cases, errors at this stage result from the service account not having the necessary privileges to grant items to the #OO user.

[![Defining the Synonym and Creating the .hdbgrants File in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA](bilderklein/klein18_022.png)](img-f18.22.html) 

**Figure 18.22**    Defining the Synonym and Creating the .hdbgrants File in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA

Now, let’s look at the two files that were generated by the workflow. The first is the SAPABAP1.hdbgrants file, as shown in [Figure 18.23](#18_004.html#f18.23). The syntax of the file links directly to the user-provided service name SAPBAP1 in the first value, which tells the builder to use that service connection and those credentials when granting privileges to the #OO user.

The next two values object\_owner and application\_user, define the roles that will be granted and their intended targets. The role entered into the object\_owner value will be granted to the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1#OO user, and the application\_user value will be granted to the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1::access\_role role. This role is granted to system-managed user accounts tied to the HDI container only but can provide runtime access to developers in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA. Therefore, this role should only have limited privileges to view, excluding the WITH GRANT OTION. When this file is built in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, the specified roles will be granted by the service user SVC\_FOR\_HDI\_PRJ\_SAPABAP1 to the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1#OO and the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1::access\_role role.

[![The SAPABAP1.hdbgrants File](bilderklein/klein18_023.png)](img-f18.23.html) 

**Figure 18.23**    The SAPABAP1.hdbgrants File

The next file is the SAPABAP1.hdbsynonym file, as shown in [Figure 18.24](#18_004.html#f18.24). This file defines synonyms for the HDI container that reference external catalog objects. Again, all development artifacts within the HDI container assume that objects in the HDI container schema. Therefore, you’ll need to use synonyms to link to external objects.

[![The SAPABAP1.hdbsynonym File](bilderklein/klein18_024.png)](img-f18.24.html) 

**Figure 18.24**    The SAPABAP1.hdbsynonym File

When this file is built, a runtime synonym will be created in the MYPROJ\_HDI\_DB\_1 schema.

In summary, this option requires SAP HANA security team members and developers work jointly in finalizing the solution. The security team will create the service account users and roles. Then, developers will set up the .hdbgrants file referencing these roles. While developers can also create the service, SAP HANA XSA admins can create the service in the SAP HANA XSA cockpit, which prevents the developers from obtaining service account credentials.

###### More Information on Using .hdbgrants Files

The SAP HANA Developer Guide for XS Advanced Model includes a section called “Using Synonyms to Access External Schemas and Objects in XS Advanced.” The guide walks you through the complete example using an external classic schema or schema not maintained by the HDI container. The following link references this document and section: [http://s-prs.co/v498224](http://s-prs.co/v498224).

The “Syntax Options in the hdbgrants File” section provides more details on the various options available in the .hdbgrants file and is available at [http://s-prs.co/v498225](http://s-prs.co/v498225).

In the next section, we’ll review the processes used to manage security between HDI containers.

##### Using .hdbgrants to Provide Access between HDI Containers

Establishing access between two containers can be accomplished by developers without little intervention by the security team. This process assumes that developers have access to the spaces or organizations where the HDI containers are stored. While convenient, this arrangement also violates most segregation of duties standards. Despite this lack of control, organizations often find creating multiple containers and then granting access between the containers necessary. To help you understand this process, let’s establish the names of two containers within an example SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA workspace. The name of the first HDI container will be MyProj, an example we’ve already used many times throughout this chapter. The name of the second example HDI container will be EXAMPLE. We’ll refer to MyProj as the primary HDI container and EXAMPLE as the target HDI container.

To begin the setup process, you’ll need to create two HDI container roles in the primary container MyProj. These roles should be set up exclusively to manage the universal connection between containers. The following list includes runtime names of the two roles that will be created in the MyProj project:

*   MYPROJ\_EXT\_HDI\_APP\_ACCESS
    
*   MYPROJ\_EXT\_HDI\_OO\_ACCESS#
    

In addition to the two roles, you’ll also need to create an .hdbroleconfig file that will map these two roles to a schema alias or schema reference. This step is required because you’ll grant external schema access to the target HDI container. Effectively, you’ll use the MyProj schema as a proxy to the external schema in the .hdbroleconfig file.

Within the project, you’ve created the folder structure db • src • roles and will be placing the role scripts in that folder. The design-time name of the first role will be MYPROJ\_EXT\_HDI\_APP\_ACCESS.hdbrole. Its runtime name will be MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ\_EXT\_HDI\_APP\_ACCESS, and the role will be configured with JSON syntax shown in [Listing 18.10](#18_004.html#l18.10).

```
{ 
  "role":{ 
    "name":"MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_APP_ACCESS", 
      "object_privileges":[ 
      { 
       "name":"MyProj.db::CUSTOMERS", 
       "type":"TABLE", 
       "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
      } ,
      { 
       "name":"MyProj.db::CS_CUSTOMERS", 
       "type":"TABLE", 
       "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
      }
    ],
      "schema_privileges":[  
{  
    "reference":"REF_SYSTEM",
    "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
},
{  
    "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
}
  ],
 "schema_analytic_privileges":[
   {
     "privileges": ["MyProj.db.aps::AP_CUSTOMER"]
    }
          ]
    }
   }
```

**Listing 18.10**    The MYPROJ\_EXT\_HDI\_APP\_ACCESS.hdbrole Script

The script shown in [Listing 18.10](#18_004.html#l18.10) will grant the following:

*   SELECT to the HDI table "MyProj.db::CUSTOMERS"
    
*   SELECT to the HDI synonym "MyProj.db::CS\_CUSTOMERS" which actually points to the SYSTEM.CUSTOMER table.
    
*   SELECT to the schema reference REF\_SYSTEM which actually points to the SYSTEM schema.
    
*   SELECT to the HDI container schema MYPRJ\_HDI\_DB\_1
    
*   The HDI container analytic privilege MyProj.db.aps::AP\_CUSTOMER
    

Note that, in the script found shown in [Listing 18.10](#18_004.html#l18.10), anything granted in the "schema\_privileges" value array that does not include a "reference" value is assumed to be a grant on the HDI container schema MYPRJ\_HDI\_DB\_1.

The second role will similar to the first but will require the "privileges\_with\_grant\_option" in the script for each privilege. This option will allow the grantee to also grant the same privilege to others. Recall that this ability is a requirement when granting privileges to the container’s #OO user. In addition, you must end the runtime name of the role with a #, which signifies that the roles contain the "privileges\_with\_grant\_option" and the HDI infrastructure will only allow this privilege to be granted to the #OO user of a target container via an .hdbgrants file.

The design-time name of the second role will be MYPROJ\_EXT\_HDI\_OO\_ACCESS.hdbrole. Its runtime name will be MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ\_EXT\_HDI\_OO\_ACCESS#, and the role will be configured with JSON syntax shown in [Listing 18.11](#18_004.html#l18.11).

```
{ 
  "role":{ 
    "name":"MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_OO_ACCESS#", 
      "object_privileges":[ 
      { 
       "name":"MyProj.db::CUSTOMERS", 
       "type":"TABLE", 
       "privileges_with_grant_option":[ "SELECT" ]
      } ,
      { 
       "name":"MyProj.db::CS_CUSTOMERS", 
       "type":"TABLE", 
       "privileges_with_grant_option":[ "SELECT" ]
      }
    ],
      
      "schema_privileges":[  
{  
    "reference":"REF_SYSTEM_2",
    "privileges_with_grant_option":[ "SELECT" ]
},
{  
    "privileges_with_grant_option":[ "SELECT" ]
}
  ]
    }
   }
```

**Listing 18.11**    MYPROJ\_EXT\_HDI\_OO\_ACCESS.hdbrole Script

The script shown in [Listing 18.11](#18_004.html#l18.11) will grant the following access:

*   SELECT to the HDI table "MyProj.db::CUSTOMERS" including the WITH GRANT OPTION
    
*   SELECT to the HDI synonym "MyProj.db::CS\_CUSTOMERS", which actually points to the SYSTEM.CUSTOMER table including the WITH GRANT OPTION.
    
*   SELECT to the schema reference REF\_SYSTEM including the WITH GRANT OPTION which points to the SYSTEM schema.
    
*   SELECT to the HDI container schema MYPRJ\_HDI\_DB\_1 including the WITH GRANT OPTION
    

Before you can build roles within your project, you’ll create the MYPROJ\_EXT\_HDI\_ROLREF.hdbroleconfig file to provide link to the SYSTEM schema referenced in the [Listing 18.10](#18_004.html#l18.10) and [Listing 18.11](#18_004.html#l18.11) files. The file must contain the JSON statement shown in [Listing 18.12](#18_004.html#l18.12).

```
{ 
 "MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_APP_ACCESS":{ 
    "REF_SYSTEM":{ 
      "schema":"SYSTEM" 
        }
  },
   "MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_OO_ACCESS#":{ 
    "REF_SYSTEM_2":{ 
      "schema":"SYSTEM" 
        }
  }
 }
```

**Listing 18.12**    MYPROJ\_EXT\_HDI\_ROLREF.hdbroleconfig File

Within your project, you can now build the three files that will deploy these roles at runtime. These roles will need to be active at runtime so that the EXAMPLE container can access them.

To complete the process, you’ll now need to access the target EXAMPLE project in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA. In this project, we’ll create two items. First, you’ll need to create an SAP HANA service connection to the primary HDI container MyProj. Second, you’ll need to create the MYPROJ.hdbgrants file that will reference the two HDI roles you created in the prior steps.

Let’s start by creating the service connection to the primary HDI container MyProj. Access SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA and expand the EXAMPLE project node to reveal the db folder. Right-click the db folder and choose the option New • SAP HANA Service Connection. Choose the HDI container option and then select the service in the list that references the MyProj container. The name of the service will start with the name of the user that activated it, followed by a serialized number and letter string and then end with \-MyProj-hdb\_db, as shown in [Figure 18.25](#18_004.html#f18.25).

[![Choosing the MyProj Service When Creating an SAP HANA Service Connection](bilderklein/klein18_025.png)](img-f18.25.html) 

**Figure 18.25**    Choosing the MyProj Service When Creating an SAP HANA Service Connection

Click OK to add this service to your mta.yaml file. Note the name of the service because you’ll need to reference this name when defining your .hdbgrants file.

Next, you’ll need to define the MYPROJ.hdbgrants file. This file will grant the primary container MyProj roles to various HDI container systems users. This step is required to so that runtime content within the target EXAMPLE container can access runtime content within the MyProj container. Within the db • src folder, create the file MYPROJ.hdbgrants. The file should contain the JSON text shown in [Listing 18.13](#18_004.html#l18.13).

```
{
  "XSA_ADMIN-x6o70e6hj4yiatlu-MyProj-hdi_db" : {
   "object_owner" : { 
      "schema_roles" : [
       "MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_OO_ACCESS#"
      ]
    },
    "application_user" : {
      "schema_roles" : [
        "MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_APP_ACCESS"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

**Listing 18.13**    The MYPROJ.hdbgrants File in the EXAMPLE Project

Within the script, you’ll start by referencing the service name "XSA\_ADMIN-x6o70e6hj4yiatlu-MyProj-hdi\_db" : { . This name is specific to the name you set up in the mta.yaml project or when creating the SAP HANA service connection. You’ll then assign the two roles to the different service account users. The role "MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ\_EXT\_HDI\_OO\_ACCESS#" is the role with the highest level of access and must be granted to the #OO user within the "object\_owner" JSON value array. The "application\_user" JSON value array will be mapped to the "MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ\_EXT\_HDI\_APP\_ACCESS" role.

Once the MYPROJ.hdbgrants is built and deployed to runtime, you can now reference MyProj runtime objects within the EXAMPLE project. Keep in mind that you’ll first also need to create synonyms in the EXAMPLE project that reference objects in the MyProj container. However, the GUI will walk you thought this process any time you browse for objects from the HDI container service connection. Again, the service connection allows developers to search for objects native to the primary HDI container MyProj at design time. In addition, the service connection allows the MYPROJ.hdbgrants file to grant its roles to the EXAMPLE\_HDI\_DB\_1#OO user at runtime.

## 18.5    Summary

You should now have a basic understanding of the difference scenarios and options that security teams need to understand when supporting security in the SAP HANA XSA environment. The SAP HANA XSA cockpit is used to configure SAP HANA XSA users, access to organizations, and access to spaces. Many other options are available, including the management of the service connections key to providing security within SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA and with HDI containers. SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA is primarily a developer’s tool, but the security team will need to understand how to create HDI container roles and manage the .hdbgrants file. In addition, we discussed the complex options for granting database users access to objects within an HDI container using .hdbrole files, granting access between containers and classic database objects in the .hdbgrants file, granting access to the #OO user directly, and finally granting access between containers.

# Service Pages

The following sections contain notes on how you can contact us. In addition, you are provided with further recommendations on the customization of the screen layout for your e-book.

## Praise and Criticism

We hope that you enjoyed reading this book. If it met your expectations, please do recommend it. If you think there is room for improvement, please get in touch with the editor of the book: [Meagan White](mailto:meaganw@rheinwerk-publishing.com). We welcome every suggestion for improvement but, of course, also any praise! You can also share your reading experience via Twitter, Facebook, or email.

## Technical Issues

If you experience technical issues with your e-book or e-book account at SAP PRESS, please feel free to contact our reader service: [support@rheinwerk-publishing.com](mailto:support@rheinwerk-publishing.com).

Please note, however, that issues regarding the screen presentation of the book content are usually not caused by errors in the e-book document. Because nearly every reading device (computer, tablet, smartphone, e-book reader) interprets the EPUB or Mobi file format differently, it is unfortunately impossible to set up the e-book document in such a way that meets the requirements of all use cases.

In addition, not all reading devices provide the same text presentation functions and not all functions work properly. Finally, you as the user also define with your settings how the book content is displayed on the screen.

he EPUB format, as currently provided and handled by the device manufacturers, is actually primarily suitable for the display of mere text documents, such as novels. Difficulties arise as soon as technical text contains figures, tables, footnotes, marginal notes, or programming code. For more information, please refer to the section [Notes on the Screen Presentation](#notes.html#screenpresentation) and the following section.

Should none of the recommended settings satisfy your layout requirements, we recommend that you use the PDF version of the book, which is available for download in your online library.

## Recommendations for Screen Presentation and Navigation

We recommend using a sans-serif font, such as Arial or Seravek, and a low font size of approx. 30–40% in portrait format and 20–30% in landscape format. The background shouldn’t be too bright.

Make use of the hyphenation option. If it doesn't work properly, align the text to the left margin. Otherwise, justify the text.

To perform searches in the e-book, the index of the book will reliably guide you to the really relevant pages of the book. If the index doesn't help, you can use the search function of your reading device.

Since it is available as a double-page spread in landscape format, the table of contents we’ve included probably gives a better overview of the content and the structure of the book than the corresponding function of your reading device. To enable you to easily open the table of contents anytime, it has been included as a separate entry in the device-generated table of contents.

If you want to zoom in on a figure, tap the respective figure once. By tapping once again, you return to the previous screen. If you tap twice (on the iPad), the figure is displayed in the original size and then has to be zoomed in to the desired size. If you tap once, the figure is directly zoomed in and displayed with a higher resolution.

For books that contain programming code, please note that the code lines may be wrapped incorrectly or displayed incompletely as of a certain font size. In case of doubt, please reduce the font size.

## About Us and Our Program

The website [http://www.sap-press.com](http://www.sap-press.com) provides detailed and first-hand information on our current publishing program. Here, you can also easily order all of our books and e-books. Information on Rheinwerk Publishing Inc. and additional contact options can also be found at [http://www.sap-press.com](http://www.sap-press.com).
